items.title: The Challenge and Opportunity of Our Ageing Population

speakers.name: David Weinkove
speakers.organisation: British Society for Research on Ageing (BSRA); Durham University
speakers.role: Emeritus Chair, British Society for Research on Ageing; Professor, Durham University

items.to_check: Whether Nathan attended. No recording; slides only. The second person pictured on the call-to-action slide (slide 9) is not named.
items.added_by: Claude (from the printed agenda, Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
David Weinkove, Professor at Durham University and Emeritus Chair of the British Society for Research on Ageing (BSRA), gave the first talk on the day's agenda. His subject was why slowing ageing matters, and why it is hard to prove.

He opened with a strong claim: our ageing population is a bigger threat than climate change, through the cost of living, pressure on health services and tension in society. A population pyramid of the UK in 2026 set the scene.

He then set prevention against treatment and argued that ageing is malleable. In England, people in the least deprived areas live 70.7 years in good health; in the most deprived, 51.9.

The science has three fundamentals. Ageing speeds up with time, people grow more different from each other, and the body holds its balance less well. That makes trials hard: they need large numbers of healthy but ageing people over several years, and funding and approval are difficult.

His call to action had three parts. Make the case that keeping people healthy for longer is good for everyone. Make trials long enough to measure ageing. Bring industry, charities, government and universities together. The BSRA, with over 300 members from academia and industry, asked the room to talk to it.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The frame: "Our ageing population is a bigger threat than climate change", because of the cost of living, pressure on health services and societal tensions (slide 2).
- Ageing is malleable: in England (ONS, 2018 to 2020, in the Chief Medical Officer's Annual Report 2023), the least deprived 10% of small areas live 70.7 years in good health and 15.6 in poorer health; the most deprived 51.9 and 26.4 (slide 5).
- Three fundamentals of ageing: the rate of ageing accelerates with time, variation between individuals increases, and homeostasis declines (slide 6).
- Trials to slow ageing need large numbers and several years, ideally in people who are healthy but ageing, and funding and approval are challenging (slide 7).
- The call to action: make the case for healthy longevity, make trials long enough to measure ageing, and have industry, charities, government and universities work together (slide 9).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance low: no ingredient or product is named. The talk sets the public-health and research frame for healthy ageing, not a market (slide 2) (slide 9).
- My reading: years in good health, not lifespan, is the frame our healthy-ageing pitches for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea already use. The healthy-life-expectancy gap is a public figure (ONS, Chief Medical Officer) a brand deck could cite (slide 5).
- His point on trials (slide 7). My reading: "slowing ageing" stays out of reach as a supplement claim for years; muscle, strength and function endpoints remain the practical route for creatine and protein.
- The BSRA invites industry to talk to it and counts industry among its members (slide 8) (slide 9). My reading: a route to academic partners if we ever fund a long healthy-ageing study.
- Context from the next talk: Nick Stene of Euromonitor said 2026 is the first year more is spent on prevention than on treatment, and that demographics explain about 30 to 40% of consumer-health growth through people entering a new life stage, not the size of the ageing population (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). Weinkove's slides frame the ageing population itself as the challenge; the two views differ in emphasis.

- "Make trials long enough to measure ageing" (slide 9)

items.title: Fewer products, more proof: who is winning the healthspan economy?

speakers.name: Nick Stene
speakers.role: Senior Global Insight Manager, Consumer Health

items.to_check: Room not on the agenda. Billed 09:20 to 09:40 on the printed agenda (Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026); his recording ran 09:24 to 09:47, as the day ran late.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recording, 10 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Nick Stene, Senior Global Insight Manager for consumer health at Euromonitor International, opened the Healthspan Summit. His question was where the money in healthspan is going and which messages earn a premium.

He started with the market. Consumer health grows about 5%, only 1.5% without inflation, and this is the first year more is spent on prevention than on treatment. Medicines sold over the counter and sports protein are both under profit pressure, so money, including billions in deal finance, is moving to premium dietary supplements.

Within healthspan, products that name a specific need or life stage earn a premium, while broad wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike. Ingredients follow a life cycle: proof brings a premium, popularity brings scale, then a price war. Magnesium forms have gone that way and NAD+ is close, with postbiotics leading what queues behind it. IM8, one product meant to replace a shelf of supplements, was his example of a brand winning on proof and trust.

His conclusion: lead with proof, know where each ingredient is in its life cycle, segment and price for specific groups such as women entering perimenopause, and design proof for shoppers, healthcare professionals and the AI agents that will increasingly shop for them.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20] (photo 2).
- Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].
- Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].
- Ingredient life cycle: proof of benefit, then premium, then popularity, then price war. Magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price, while L-threonate, the cognitive form, still holds a premium; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20] (photo 3).
- NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream (US price index 1.84 in 2024, 1.43 in 2026 to date); postbiotics lead what queues behind it, with share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 [00:20] (photo 4).
- IM8 is the fastest year-one growth he has seen: one product of 90 ingredients positioned to replace 16 supplements, with year-two revenue guidance of USD 220 to 230 million [00:20] (photo 7).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- He expects premium whey supply to start being solved around the back end of 2027, 2028 at the earliest, and sees sports protein brands passing on 20% or more on shelf, 30 to 40% with smaller packs [00:20]. Alan Johnstone at SANS Europe expects whey to stay structurally expensive, with announced capacity running to 2028 (unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of). My reading: both views point to protein margins staying tight through 2027, which keeps blends and alternatives such as IsoClr: Pea on brands' agendas.
- His ingredient life cycle applies to creatine: proof brings a premium and popularity erodes it [00:20] (photo 3). My reading: CreaWin's case to brands should rest on its own evidence and a clear benefit, not on creatine's popularity.
- Healthy-ageing customers pay for named needs and proof, and in Europe mitochondrial wording is already established [00:20]. My reading: our healthy-ageing pitches should name the need and the evidence.
- AI shopping agents read proof differently [00:20]. My reading: our evidence files should be structured and machine-readable.
- Relevance high: healthy-ageing market structure and sports protein economics.
summary.Quotes:
- "...this is the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment." Speaker 1 (Nick Stene) [00:20]
- "...we've got to name the need, and the more we name the need, the more we get the benefits out of this space" Speaker 1 (Nick Stene) [00:20]
- "...popularity is the death knell on premium." Speaker 1 (Nick Stene) [00:20]
- "...the agent looks at proof through a completely different lens to a human being." Speaker 1 (Nick Stene) [00:20]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Nick Stene (Euromonitor): ask for the deck and the premium-versus-launch data for sports protein and creatine [00:20].
- The next speaker, introduced as "Emma Hudson, senior insights director" in Otter's transcript, was Ewa Hudson of Lumina Intelligence; her talk is filed as lumina-new-longevity-consumer [23:16].
- The track, once the programme is published.

- (photo 2) The market in 2026: USD 373 billion, +5% in current terms but +1.5% without inflation, growth by category.
- (photo 3) Magnesium forms in Europe: share growth against price premium, and the cycle from proof to price war.
- (photo 4) NAD+ losing its premium in the US and Europe, and the ingredients queuing behind it.
- (photo 7) IM8: fastest year-one growth, guidance, and the four reasons it wins.
summary.Detail:
- The speaker was introduced as Nick Steen; the title slide gives Nick Stene, Senior Global Insight Manager, Consumer Health, Euromonitor International [00:00] (photo 1).
- Market: he gave consumer health as "373 billion", growing about 5%, or 1.5 without inflation, half a point down; treatment has gone negative in real terms [00:20]. The slide gives USD 373 billion, +5% in current terms (3.5% price rises) and +1.5% without inflation ("demand stagnation") (photo 2).
- Growth by category, 2025 then 2026: vitamins and dietary supplements 5.9% and 5.6%; OTC 3.4% and 3.2%; sports nutrition 13.3% and 12.5%; weight management and wellbeing 0.2% and 0.3%. Shares of the market: vitamins and supplements 42%, OTC 42%, sports nutrition 11%, weight management and wellbeing 5%. The slide's line: "2026 is the year when we started spending more on prevention than we do on treatment" (photo 2).
- OTC is hit hardest by tariffs, by dependence on active pharmaceutical ingredients from India and China, and, next, by European wastewater rules [00:20].
- Sports protein, as he said it: he has shelf data showing a 20% plus pass-through in physical pricing, 30 to 40% overall once pack shrinkage and other absorption moves are counted. On premium whey supply: "So the protein one probably starts to get solved in supply because it's scarcity driven around premium way around 2027 back end, 2028 earliest", with "years of trauma" left [00:20].
- Growth is stronger in shops than online, where trust is leaking; demographics explain about 30 to 40% of growth (people entering a new life stage, not the size of the ageing population), brand push about another third, and employers' attitudes to time off work more [00:20].
- On the US shelf, longevity and healthy ageing grow fastest and earn a strong premium; menopause is losing its premium while 40-plus and perimenopause still earn one; prostate has lost its premium; skin peaked in 2025 and hair is next; immune has peaked but remains a workhorse [00:20].
- Europe follows the same pattern, but mitochondrial messaging is already stronger than in the US, partly because of what the regulatory framework allows, and healthy-ageing messaging is "a tougher sell", some of it only online [00:20].
- Magnesium forms in Europe, January to August 2026 against 2025, read approximately from the chart (price index against matched peers, change in share of products): carbonate about 1.4 and 0%; oxide about 0.75 and 3%; citrate about 0.95 and 13%; bisglycinate about 0.65 and 42%; taurate about 0.55 and 43%; malate about 0.55 and 48%; L-threonate (cognitive) about 1.17 and 49%. The slide's line: "Popularity is a consistent death [k]nell for premium [achieve]ment." (photo 3). Otter heard L-threonate as "L3 and eight" [00:20].
- NAD+ escaped niche last year and grew three times on the US shelf in 18 months; stacks with spermidine and resveratrol won back some premium in 2026, but it is near price war [00:20]. The slide's NAD+ family price index (NAD+, NADH, NR, NMN, NMNH): US 1.84 in 2024, 1.28 in 2025, 1.43 in 2026 to date; Europe 1.68, 1.50 and 1.32 (photo 4).
- Queuing behind NAD+, US 2026 (share growth, price index): postbiotics +48%, 2.83; urolithin A +17%, 1.37; TMG +19%, 1.23; fisetin +22%, 1.14; spermidine +45%, 1.13. The slide's line: "What's next? Because nothing stays shiny and new forev[er]" (photo 4).
- Postbiotics are growing fast, have "really strong connections into GLP-1" and earn one of the strongest premiums; he is watching them most closely. In his words: "But postbiotics is at this moment in time kicking ass" [00:20].
- Life stage, US products per 10,000 supplement products, 2024, 2025 and 2026 to date: testosterone 171, 182, 163; prostate 70, 85, 98; menopause 46, 64, 73; andropause 0, 1, 2. The slides: perimenopause is picking up fast while menopause slows; andropause is "near non-existent on the shelf"; testosterone is more than twice the size of menopause on the shelf, stalled in the US, still rising in Europe and getting cheaper, with fading spikes in tongkat ali, tribulus and shilajit; prostate support now rises fast (photo 5) (photo 6).
- Men do not buy into an andropause label; they respond to testosterone, performance and prostate messages [00:20] (photo 6).
- IM8, as he said it: over 100 million in year one, on target for 220 to 230 in year two, 400 million projected for year three, and a billion raised on a profitable subscription model [00:20]. The slide: year-two revenue guidance USD 220 to 230 million and 2027 full-year guidance over USD 400 million; US online sales peaked in Q4 2025 and eased slightly in Q1 and Q2 2026; the US is by far its largest market, ahead of the UK and Canada (photo 7).
- Why IM8 wins, from the slide: one product replaces a shelf (90 ingredients, positioned to replace 16 other supplements); celebrity equity and a science council, driving word of mouth; subscription economics a lender can fund, with USD 1.44 of declared gross profit per USD 1 of acquisition; and an AI-native acquisition engine across 43 markets. "IM8 nailed "trust" in all its flavours" (photo 7).
- He named IM8 and Ancient + Brave as brands nailing proof [00:20]. Nathan's note: IM8 "is winning a lot in the market, alongside Ancient+Brave" (notes).
- Positioning that facilitates "someone's perfect life" lasts longer than solving a problem, which ends when it is fixed or fails; collagen can be sold either way [00:20]. The slide sets "something wrong [with] you our product can fix" (joints, wrinkles, ageing, collagen deficiency) against "Aspire to a life free of imperfection" (vitality, performance, radiance, wellbeing): "you never stop taking something that is part of who you want to be" (photo 8).
- His takeaways: lead with proof; know the ingredient's life stage and the pipeline behind it; segment and price, with women heading into perimenopause badly served; and design proof for three gatekeepers: shoppers, healthcare professionals and agentic commerce [00:20].

items.title: Too Young to Age? The New Consumer Rules of Longevity
items.to_check: The room is not confirmed. Title and slot (09:40 to 09:55) from the printed agenda (Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026) and the deck; her recording ran 09:47 to 10:05. The deck does not show the 18% who want to stay as they are, nor label the lighter series on the age chart (photo 1, slide 4).
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's slide photos and Otter recording, 10 Nov 2026; deck added 23 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Ewa Hudson, Strategy & Insight Director at ReThink Global, Lumina Intelligence, presented a July 2026 survey of 10,500 consumers in nine countries. Her question: consumers are rewriting the rules of ageing, so is the industry ready to rewrite its own?

Her first point was that the longevity consumer is no longer old. Retired people mostly began thinking seriously about ageing in their 60s; people in full-time work mostly in their 30s. Younger people blame their genes less and put more faith in supplements, and one in four is actively pursuing anti-ageing.

Ageing well, she said, means having the vitality to keep reinventing yourself. Energy, stamina and physical strength is a top-three concern in every age band, and mobility, joint and bone health comes first for women from their mid-thirties. Needs shift with life stage and country, and GLP-1 treatment is moving UK users towards healthier habits.

Trust is the gap: in the UK, not enough proof was the most common hesitation about longevity supplements. Brands such as Niagen, Life Extension and Novos are moving from selling supplements to measuring and managing biological ageing. Her conclusion: applied and communicated science will be the number one trust creator, and the healthspan leaders of the next decade may be platforms that measure, manage and optimise ageing.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Concern about ageing starts younger: retired respondents mostly began thinking seriously about it in their 60s (36%); in the deck's version of the chart, people working full-time mostly began in their 30s (about 30%, read from the chart). She called it "a generational shift" [00:04] (photo 1) (slide 4).
- The younger the respondent, the less they credit genetics and the more they credit supplements: genetics from 39% at 65 plus down to 21% at 18 to 24; supplements from 20% at 25 to 34 down to 12% at 65 plus [00:04] (slide 2) (slide 3).
- One in four is actively pursuing anti-ageing: 16% want to prevent premature ageing and 11% to reverse it, beside 52% who want to age slowly and healthily [00:04] (photo 2) (slide 5).
- Energy, stamina and strength is in the top three concerns of every age band, for men and women; mobility, joint and bone health is in the top three of every band from 35 to 44 up for both, and from 25 to 34 for women (photo 3) (slide 8).
- Trust is the gap. Biggest hesitation about longevity supplements in the UK: not enough proof 22%, cost 21%, don't believe claims 20%, safety concerns 20%. Across the survey, 36% already take supplements to counteract natural ageing [00:04] (slide 17) (slide 18).

summary.Summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired two retailers, a brand and a marketplace: Jessica Pasco of Holland & Barrett, Rachel Kreider of GNC, Federico Luna of Timeline and Jennifer Wang of Alibaba's Taobao Tmall. His question: is longevity a real category, or an umbrella for outcomes consumers already understand?

They agreed that shoppers pay for benefits they can feel or see. Prevention alone is hard to sell, so proof and a tangible result, such as stronger muscles or better skin, matter most. They also agreed that GLP-1 medicines move people into a proactive mindset, and that creatine and muscle are a way into healthy ageing.

They differed on the category itself. Luna said longevity is absolutely a category, defined by the hallmarks of ageing and four pillars, and that bundling a generic vitamin C into it does consumers a disservice. Pasco said Holland & Barrett's new in-store longevity category is small but growing fast, driven mainly by NAD, while most proactive shopping is not badged longevity. Kreider said GNC treats healthy ageing as a demand space and links new ingredients to condition-specific products. Wang said nobody in China searches for longevity online: men search for sexual vitality and women for sagging skin, and premium shoppers ask for patents and clinical studies.

items.title: Microbiome modulation through nutritional interventions to extend healthy lifespan

speakers.name: Jens Walter
speakers.organisation: APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork
speakers.role: Professor of Ecology, Food, and the Microbiome; founder and co-owner of Synbiotic Health

items.to_check: The room is not confirmed. Slot (10:25 to 10:45) from the printed agenda (Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026), which listed it as "Synbiotic Health Presentation"; the title is as billed on the deck. His recording ran 10:38 to 11:04.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recording, 10 Nov 2026; deck added 23 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Professor Jens Walter of APC Microbiome Ireland and University College Cork, founder and co-owner of Synbiotic Health, asked whether nutrition that targets the gut microbiome can extend healthy lifespan.

He started with animal studies. Germ-free rodents live longer than normal ones, but with calorie restriction the microbiome becomes beneficial, so its effect depends on diet. In humans, large observational studies link healthy eating patterns to healthy ageing; one UK study suggests sustained shifts to a healthier diet can add up to ten years, most if made in your 40s and 50s.

His own trial in Cell put healthy adults on a high-fibre, non-industrialised diet for three weeks. Bifidobacteria rose, inflammatory bacteria fell, and LDL cholesterol dropped by 16.8%. Older people rarely change their whole diet, so he sees room for alternatives: Bifidobacterium adolescentis, which falls with age and is linked with healthy ageing, paired with fibre.

He kept his hedges. Causality is clearly established in animals only, current human evidence does not prove the microbiome mediates diet's effects, and clinical trials are needed. His company's trials in older people have not reported. In questions he doubted that postbiotics can change gut ecology.
summary.Key takeaways:
- In animal studies, rodents without a microbiome live longer. He said normal mice live about 25 months and germ-free mice almost ten months longer [00:24]. In the 1991 study on his slide, mean lifespan was 88.9 weeks germ-free against 75.9 weeks conventional on a full diet, and 117.5 weeks, the longest, for conventional mice on a restricted diet (slide 6) (slide 7).
- Observational studies link healthy dietary patterns to healthy ageing, with the Alternative Healthy Eating Index performing "consistently best" (slide 8). A UK study is titled "Life expectancy can increase by up to 10 years following sustained shifts towards healthier diets" (slide 9); he described it as ten years of healthier lifespan, and "probably" five to six years if the shift comes in the 70s [00:24].
- His Cell trial of the non-industrialised "Restore" (NiMe) diet, 45 g of fibre a day, against participants' usual diet: LDL cholesterol down 16.8% (he said 17%), glucose down 6.3%, CRP down 14.0%, BMI down 1.4%; faecal pH and the ratio of branched-chain to short-chain fatty acids also fell [00:24] (slide 14) (slide 15).
- Bifidobacterium adolescentis falls with age and is linked with healthy ageing: it peaks at about 4.8% of the gut microbiome around age 40 in healthy people (read from the chart, Synbiotic Health's data on 8,942 people), it was the strongest predictor of slower epigenetic ageing in 123 adults, and in animal studies it improved healthspan and lifespan. Synbiotic Health's human trials in older people are ongoing, with no data yet [00:24] (slide 17) (slide 20) (slide 21).
- His take-home: the gut microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy ageing, "but human causality remains incompletely established"; complementary microbiome-targeted interventions are promising, but clinical trials are needed [00:24] (slide 22).
- He is doubtful that a postbiotic can change gut ecology or raise short-chain fatty acids, prefers probiotic bifidobacteria with fibre, and sees a possible role for postbiotics in a direct immune effect [22:01] [22:52].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- He sees the next healthy-ageing supplements as probiotic bifidobacteria combined with fibre, because dietary change is hard to sustain in older people [00:24] (slide 22). My reading: fibre for healthy ageing may be pitched as a partner to probiotics, within what the evidence supports, which he says is not yet proven in humans.
- He showed the title of a Cell Reports paper, "Bifidobacterium adolescentis-derived nicotinic acid improves host skeletal muscle mitochondrial function to ameliorate sarcopenia" (slide 21); Otter heard "amyloid sarcopenia" [00:24]. He gave no data from it. My reading: gut-to-muscle claims may reach muscle-ageing products where CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea sit; worth watching, not borrowing.
- He cited animal research in which high-protein diets shorten lifespan, and said he is not sure how far it translates to humans [00:24]. His review figure lists plant-based protein foods among microbiome-compatible foods and red meat "in moderation" (slide 11). My reading: brands selling protein for healthy ageing may hear this; our answer should rest on human muscle evidence, and the review is about whole foods, not protein isolates.
- Postbiotics divide the speakers: Nick Stene of Euromonitor sees them leading the ingredients queuing behind NAD+, with US share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan); Walter doubts they can change gut ecology [22:01]; and 5% of consumers in Lumina's survey name them as most helpful for healthspan (lumina-new-longevity-consumer, slide 17). All three are given.
- Relevance medium: healthy-ageing science around fibre and probiotics; protein and muscle come up only through animal and mechanistic papers.
summary.Quotes:
- "...the microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy aging in animal model." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
- "...we don't really have any direct evidence that the microbiome is mediating these these diet effects." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
- "...by eating a healthy diet, you can extend your healthier lifespan by 10 years." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
- "...I'm not sure a postbiotic can achieve that." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [22:52]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Jens Walter: Synbiotic Health's trials in older people, when they report, and what its B. adolescentis and fibre combination is; the deck shows neither [00:24].
- Read the Cell Reports sarcopenia paper on B. adolescentis-derived nicotinic acid, for any human muscle data (slide 21).
summary.Detail:
- Billing: "Microbiome modulation through nutritional interventions to extend healthy lifespan"; Jens Walter, Professor of Ecology, Food, and the Microbiome, APC Microbiome Ireland, School of Microbiology, and Department of Medicine, University College Cork (slide 1). The printed agenda listed the slot as "Synbiotic Health Presentation". No slide is marked Confidential.
- The talk is one Otter turn from [00:24] to the questions at [20:46]. Stephen Daniells introduced him as "Professor Jens Walder" of "University College Corp" and co-founder of "Symbiotic Health" [00:00]. Otter's labels: Speaker 1 is Jens Walter; Speakers 2 and 3 are questioners. At [23:31] and [23:38] the Speaker 1 label also carries George's question before Walter's answer.
- Disclosures on the slide: "J.W. is a founder and co-owner of Synbiotic Health"; "Support and consultancy from companies that market or use dietary fiber (MGP Ingredients, Nestlé, Ingredion, Agrifiber)" (slide 2). As he said it: co-founder, with consultancy support from companies that "do both pro and prebiotics" [00:24]. The two wordings differ; both are given.
- Paul O'Toole's work: the 2013 Nature paper "Gut microbiota composition correlates with diet and health in the elderly" (slide 3). With age, pathogens rise and healthy bacteria fall, with links to inflammation and lower barrier function; the microbiome declines further when older people move into nursing homes, probably linked to diet [00:24].
- In a literature survey (Ghosh et al., 2022), Bifidobacterium is in the group that declines with age and is linked to healthy ageing; pathobionts rise, especially in unhealthy ageing (slide 4). Observational research cannot establish cause and effect [00:24].
- Animal studies: survival curves of germ-free and conventional mice from 1966 (slide 6); read from the chart, half the conventional mice had died by about 15 to 17 months and half the germ-free mice by about 23 to 25 months. A 1991 study added food restriction: mean lifespan 75.9 weeks conventional full-fed, 117.5 conventional restricted, 88.9 germ-free full-fed, 109.6 germ-free restricted (slide 7). The finding has been repeated in mice, rats and other species; "in a lot of animal models, high protein diets actually shorten lifespan. Not sure to what degree this then translates to human." [00:24]
- Nature Medicine, "Optimal dietary patterns for healthy aging" (published 24 March 2025): the AHEI performs best; his reasons are high-quality plant foods, fat quality (PUFA, omega-3, low trans fat) and avoiding industrial risk foods such as sugary drinks, red and processed meat, sodium and trans fat (slide 8). In the talk: an unhealthy vegetarian pattern does the least good, and small amounts of wine are linked to healthier ageing [00:24].
- The UK study is Nature Food, published 20 November 2023 (slide 9). He said healthier lifespan; the paper's title says life expectancy. He added that the 40s and 50s are when to adopt the pattern [00:24].
- A systematic review in Nutrition Reviews, "Mediterranean Diet Adherence and Markers of Healthy Aging" (slide 10), published "a week or two ago" as he said it, partly from intervention studies [00:24].
- His Cell Host Microbe review of 2022, "Rethinking healthy eating in light of the gut microbiome": "Healthy Ageing Diets Are Also Microbiome-Compatible Diets!" (slide 11).
- NU-AGE (Gut, 2020): a Mediterranean diet in 612 older adults in five European countries, sampled at 0 and 12 months. It lowered bacteria associated with frailty and cognition, raised taxa linked to lower frailty, better cognition and lower CRP and IL-17, and was associated with more short-chain fatty acids and fewer secondary bile acids. The slide questions how practical the diet is for older people ("dentition, saliva, ingredients") (slide 12). He said secondary bile acids drive colon cancer [00:24]; the slide cites a Gut 2025 paper titled "Secondary bile acid production by gut bacteria promotes Western diet-associated colorectal cancer" (slide 14).
- The Cell paper: "Cardiometabolic benefits of a non-industrialized-type diet are linked to gut microbiome modulation", a randomised controlled feeding trial in healthy adults (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03501082). The Restore diet was given with a "lost microbe", Limosilactobacillus reuteri, which the talk did not mention (slide 13). He described the cohort as students and as healthy adults, three weeks on the diet, and said it was published two years ago [00:24].
- The NiMe diet: primarily plant-based; no dairy, beef or wheat; limited highly processed foods; low glycaemic index; 45 g of fibre a day (slide 15). He said the pH drop is "clearly fiber fermentation" [23:38].
- Restore diet results with p-values: BMI p=0.002, LDL p=0.003, glucose p<0.001, CRP p=0.014 (slide 15); faecal pH p=0.003 and branched-chain to short-chain fatty acids p=0.007 against no change on the usual diet (slide 14). In the talk: bifidobacteria including B. adolescentis and B. longum rose; inflammatory bacteria such as Bilophila fell; indole-3-propionic acid, a neuroprotective antioxidant with consistent benefits "specifically in mice", rose; participants lost weight [00:24].
- Possible mediators from diet to healthy ageing: saccharolytic fermentation and short-chain fatty acids; tryptophan-derived metabolites; less proteolytic fermentation and mucus degradation; fewer harmful metabolites; altered microbiome functions; ecological restructuring (slide 16).
- Bifidobacteria as fibre "amplifiers": they respond strongly to specific carbohydrates and make acetate and lactate that feed butyrate producers; B. adolescentis is adult-adapted and linked to complex carbohydrate metabolism (slide 17). Read from Synbiotic Health's charts, in unhealthy people B. adolescentis stays near 1% or below at every age (slide 17).
- The oldest living person when sampled, aged 116 as he recalled it [00:24]: Bifidobacterium at about 52% of the gut microbiome, against about 11 to 12% in 250 women and 195 men, read from the chart (Santos-Pujol et al., 2025, Cell Reports Medicine) (slide 18). He said "almost 50%" and "an N of one" [00:24].
- Sardinian centenarians (mSystems): 19 centenarians, 23 older adults and 17 young adults; read from the chart, B. adolescentis is a large share of total bifidobacteria in several centenarians (slide 19). He said it is "dramatically actually increased" in centenarians against healthy older people [00:24].
- Slower epigenetic ageing (Kunihiro et al., Scientific Reports, 2026): 123 adults, 63.4% Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander; B. adolescentis was the strongest predictor of a slower DunedinPACE. The slide's take-home: signatures "may track biological ageing pace" (slide 20).
- Mechanism papers on one slide: B. adolescentis and GABA production (Scientific Reports); his group's Microbiome paper of 2018, "Probiotic Bifidobacterium strains and galactooligosaccharides improve intestinal barrier function in obese adults but show no synergism when used together as synbiotics"; the Cell Reports sarcopenia paper; and Nature Aging (16 November 2021), B. adolescentis "improves healthspan and lifespan in multiple species" (slide 21). In the talk he gave the barrier result without the no-synergism finding [00:24].
- Lumina's earlier talk came up: he recalled that "40% of men now in the 40s think healthy eating is actually important" [00:24]. Lumina's deck shows 21% of US men in their late 40s choosing healthy eating as the single most important to long-term health goals (lumina-new-longevity-consumer, slide 14). The figures differ; both are given.
- Human milk oligosaccharides: studies show they can raise bifidobacteria in older people, but "the jury is completely out" on stimulating infant-associated species and on clinical benefit [21:22].
- Short-chain fatty acids are "very very hard to increase", even with extreme diet shifts [22:52].
- Causality: he has been on three or four papers on it; transplant models and C. elegans have limits; causal inference in humans "comes with its own bag of limitations" [23:38].
- Funders and partners include the Weston Family Foundation, Alberta Innovates, CIHR, PrecisionBiotics and the Killam Laureates; most collaborators are at the University of Alberta (slide 23). He said his interest in bifidobacteria started when he was a professor at the University of Nebraska [00:24].
- The book "The NiMe Diet: Scientific Principles and Recipes" by Anissa M. Armet and Jens Walter is free online via the University of Alberta Library (thenimediet.com) (slide 24).

takeaways.text: In animal studies, rodents without a microbiome live longer. He said normal mice live about 25 months and germ-free mice almost ten months longer [00:24]. In the 1991 study on his slide, mean lifespan was 88.9 weeks germ-free against 75.9 weeks conventional on a full diet, and 117.5 weeks, the longest, for conventional mice on a restricted diet (slide 6) (slide 7).

Observational studies link healthy dietary patterns to healthy ageing, with the Alternative Healthy Eating Index performing "consistently best" (slide 8). A UK study is titled "Life expectancy can increase by up to 10 years following sustained shifts towards healthier diets" (slide 9); he described it as ten years of healthier lifespan, and "probably" five to six years if the shift comes in the 70s [00:24].

His Cell trial of the non-industrialised "Restore" (NiMe) diet, 45 g of fibre a day, against participants' usual diet: LDL cholesterol down 16.8% (he said 17%), glucose down 6.3%, CRP down 14.0%, BMI down 1.4%; faecal pH and the ratio of branched-chain to short-chain fatty acids also fell [00:24] (slide 14) (slide 15).

Bifidobacterium adolescentis falls with age and is linked with healthy ageing: it peaks at about 4.8% of the gut microbiome around age 40 in healthy people (read from the chart, Synbiotic Health's data on 8,942 people), it was the strongest predictor of slower epigenetic ageing in 123 adults, and in animal studies it improved healthspan and lifespan. Synbiotic Health's human trials in older people are ongoing, with no data yet [00:24] (slide 17) (slide 20) (slide 21).

His take-home: the gut microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy ageing, "but human causality remains incompletely established"; complementary microbiome-targeted interventions are promising, but clinical trials are needed [00:24] (slide 22).

He is doubtful that a postbiotic can change gut ecology or raise short-chain fatty acids, prefers probiotic bifidobacteria with fibre, and sees a possible role for postbiotics in a direct immune effect [22:01] [22:52].

quotes.text: "...the microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy aging in animal model." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
"...we don't really have any direct evidence that the microbiome is mediating these these diet effects." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
"...by eating a healthy diet, you can extend your healthier lifespan by 10 years." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
"...I'm not sure a postbiotic can achieve that." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [22:52]

followups: Jens Walter: Synbiotic Health's trials in older people, when they report, and what its B. adolescentis and fibre combination is; the deck shows neither [00:24].
Read the Cell Reports sarcopenia paper on B. adolescentis-derived nicotinic acid, for any human muscle data (slide 21).

detail.text: Billing: "Microbiome modulation through nutritional interventions to extend healthy lifespan"; Jens Walter, Professor of Ecology, Food, and the Microbiome, APC Microbiome Ireland, School of Microbiology, and Department of Medicine, University College Cork (slide 1). The printed agenda listed the slot as "Synbiotic Health Presentation". No slide is marked Confidential.

The talk is one Otter turn from [00:24] to the questions at [20:46]. Stephen Daniells introduced him as "Professor Jens Walder" of "University College Corp" and co-founder of "Symbiotic Health" [00:00]. Otter's labels: Speaker 1 is Jens Walter; Speakers 2 and 3 are questioners. At [23:31] and [23:38] the Speaker 1 label also carries George's question before Walter's answer.

Disclosures on the slide: "J.W. is a founder and co-owner of Synbiotic Health"; "Support and consultancy from companies that market or use dietary fiber (MGP Ingredients, Nestlé, Ingredion, Agrifiber)" (slide 2). As he said it: co-founder, with consultancy support from companies that "do both pro and prebiotics" [00:24]. The two wordings differ; both are given.

Paul O'Toole's work: the 2013 Nature paper "Gut microbiota composition correlates with diet and health in the elderly" (slide 3). With age, pathogens rise and healthy bacteria fall, with links to inflammation and lower barrier function; the microbiome declines further when older people move into nursing homes, probably linked to diet [00:24].

In a literature survey (Ghosh et al., 2022), Bifidobacterium is in the group that declines with age and is linked to healthy ageing; pathobionts rise, especially in unhealthy ageing (slide 4). Observational research cannot establish cause and effect [00:24].

Animal studies: survival curves of germ-free and conventional mice from 1966 (slide 6); read from the chart, half the conventional mice had died by about 15 to 17 months and half the germ-free mice by about 23 to 25 months. A 1991 study added food restriction: mean lifespan 75.9 weeks conventional full-fed, 117.5 conventional restricted, 88.9 germ-free full-fed, 109.6 germ-free restricted (slide 7). The finding has been repeated in mice, rats and other species; "in a lot of animal models, high protein diets actually shorten lifespan. Not sure to what degree this then translates to human." [00:24]

Nature Medicine, "Optimal dietary patterns for healthy aging" (published 24 March 2025): the AHEI performs best; his reasons are high-quality plant foods, fat quality (PUFA, omega-3, low trans fat) and avoiding industrial risk foods such as sugary drinks, red and processed meat, sodium and trans fat (slide 8). In the talk: an unhealthy vegetarian pattern does the least good, and small amounts of wine are linked to healthier ageing [00:24].

The UK study is Nature Food, published 20 November 2023 (slide 9). He said healthier lifespan; the paper's title says life expectancy. He added that the 40s and 50s are when to adopt the pattern [00:24].

A systematic review in Nutrition Reviews, "Mediterranean Diet Adherence and Markers of Healthy Aging" (slide 10), published "a week or two ago" as he said it, partly from intervention studies [00:24].
His Cell Host Microbe review of 2022, "Rethinking healthy eating in light of the gut microbiome": "Healthy Ageing Diets Are Also Microbiome-Compatible Diets!" (slide 11).

NU-AGE (Gut, 2020): a Mediterranean diet in 612 older adults in five European countries, sampled at 0 and 12 months. It lowered bacteria associated with frailty and cognition, raised taxa linked to lower frailty, better cognition and lower CRP and IL-17, and was associated with more short-chain fatty acids and fewer secondary bile acids. The slide questions how practical the diet is for older people ("dentition, saliva, ingredients") (slide 12). He said secondary bile acids drive colon cancer [00:24]; the slide cites a Gut 2025 paper titled "Secondary bile acid production by gut bacteria promotes Western diet-associated colorectal cancer" (slide 14).

The Cell paper: "Cardiometabolic benefits of a non-industrialized-type diet are linked to gut microbiome modulation", a randomised controlled feeding trial in healthy adults (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03501082). The Restore diet was given with a "lost microbe", Limosilactobacillus reuteri, which the talk did not mention (slide 13). He described the cohort as students and as healthy adults, three weeks on the diet, and said it was published two years ago [00:24].

The NiMe diet: primarily plant-based; no dairy, beef or wheat; limited highly processed foods; low glycaemic index; 45 g of fibre a day (slide 15). He said the pH drop is "clearly fiber fermentation" [23:38].

Restore diet results with p-values: BMI p=0.002, LDL p=0.003, glucose p<0.001, CRP p=0.014 (slide 15); faecal pH p=0.003 and branched-chain to short-chain fatty acids p=0.007 against no change on the usual diet (slide 14). In the talk: bifidobacteria including B. adolescentis and B. longum rose; inflammatory bacteria such as Bilophila fell; indole-3-propionic acid, a neuroprotective antioxidant with consistent benefits "specifically in mice", rose; participants lost weight [00:24].

Possible mediators from diet to healthy ageing: saccharolytic fermentation and short-chain fatty acids; tryptophan-derived metabolites; less proteolytic fermentation and mucus degradation; fewer harmful metabolites; altered microbiome functions; ecological restructuring (slide 16).

Bifidobacteria as fibre "amplifiers": they respond strongly to specific carbohydrates and make acetate and lactate that feed butyrate producers; B. adolescentis is adult-adapted and linked to complex carbohydrate metabolism (slide 17). Read from Synbiotic Health's charts, in unhealthy people B. adolescentis stays near 1% or below at every age (slide 17).

The oldest living person when sampled, aged 116 as he recalled it [00:24]: Bifidobacterium at about 52% of the gut microbiome, against about 11 to 12% in 250 women and 195 men, read from the chart (Santos-Pujol et al., 2025, Cell Reports Medicine) (slide 18). He said "almost 50%" and "an N of one" [00:24].

Sardinian centenarians (mSystems): 19 centenarians, 23 older adults and 17 young adults; read from the chart, B. adolescentis is a large share of total bifidobacteria in several centenarians (slide 19). He said it is "dramatically actually increased" in centenarians against healthy older people [00:24].

Slower epigenetic ageing (Kunihiro et al., Scientific Reports, 2026): 123 adults, 63.4% Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander; B. adolescentis was the strongest predictor of a slower DunedinPACE. The slide's take-home: signatures "may track biological ageing pace" (slide 20).

Mechanism papers on one slide: B. adolescentis and GABA production (Scientific Reports); his group's Microbiome paper of 2018, "Probiotic Bifidobacterium strains and galactooligosaccharides improve intestinal barrier function in obese adults but show no synergism when used together as synbiotics"; the Cell Reports sarcopenia paper; and Nature Aging (16 November 2021), B. adolescentis "improves healthspan and lifespan in multiple species" (slide 21). In the talk he gave the barrier result without the no-synergism finding [00:24].

Lumina's earlier talk came up: he recalled that "40% of men now in the 40s think healthy eating is actually important" [00:24]. Lumina's deck shows 21% of US men in their late 40s choosing healthy eating as the single most important to long-term health goals (lumina-new-longevity-consumer, slide 14). The figures differ; both are given.
Human milk oligosaccharides: studies show they can raise bifidobacteria in older people, but "the jury is completely out" on stimulating infant-associated species and on clinical benefit [21:22].
Short-chain fatty acids are "very very hard to increase", even with extreme diet shifts [22:52].
Causality: he has been on three or four papers on it; transplant models and C. elegans have limits; causal inference in humans "comes with its own bag of limitations" [23:38].

Funders and partners include the Weston Family Foundation, Alberta Innovates, CIHR, PrecisionBiotics and the Killam Laureates; most collaborators are at the University of Alberta (slide 23). He said his interest in bifidobacteria started when he was a professor at the University of Nebraska [00:24].
The book "The NiMe Diet: Scientific Principles and Recipes" by Anissa M. Armet and Jens Walter is free online via the University of Alberta Library (thenimediet.com) (slide 24).

summary.Summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired eight members of the public, who gave their first names and ages: Robert (38), Matt (27), Mike (51), Michelle (64), Rahav (25), Donella (51), Nadine (46) and Kane. He asked what they focus on, where they get their information and how they would take a supplement pitch. The audience asked about the long term, AI and trust.

They agreed on most things. All try to exercise and eat well; supplement use runs from none to four. Natural ingredients win attention; pills and synthetic ingredients put several of them off. They want proof before they buy: the science, an effective dose and independent research. Holland & Barrett earns trust by being long established, and most distrust influencers. Nobody raised price.

They differed in their concerns and their sources. The men named heart, colon and mental health; the women named sleep, menopause, hormones and bones. Michelle follows Ayurveda, Donella wants natural and regenerative sourcing, and Kane takes creatine and protein powder for training. Rahav, the youngest, does not mind non-natural products if a brand explains why she needs them today, and wants trials to say whom they did not test. On AI, Mike checks supplements with ChatGPT and Claude and asks for the evidence; Matt scrolls past AI health answers.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Naturalness opens the conversation: Robert listens more the more natural the product and shuts off at pills [23:46], Matt and Mike said much the same [24:01] [24:34], and Robert named naturalness as the main thing to build into a new product [45:44]. Rahav was the exception: she does not mind non-natural products if she is told how they help her [47:02].
- Proof decides: Michelle wants the science and a dose high enough to be effective [25:28] [25:59], Nadine wants to know whether the research was independent or paid for by a company with a vested interest [31:00], Mike wants clinical trials on the brand's site [42:40], and Rahav wants trials to say honestly whom they were not tested on [43:43].
- Trust comes from time and brand: Mike and Kane trust Holland & Barrett because it has been around a long time [24:34] [31:45]; a new brand, Mike said, needs a mix of advertising, proof on its site and a brand story, and cannot be built overnight [42:40] [47:44].
- Influencers are distrusted: Matt avoids health advice from social media [18:23], Mike asks "what's in it for them" [42:40], and Kane said what works for an influencer may not work for him [31:45]. Their sources are friends, Ayurvedic doctors, an Instagram feed and a Netflix documentary on Blue Zones [10:12] [17:45] [16:37] [20:32].
- AI is used with checks: Mike asks ChatGPT and Claude for evidence and checks it on Google [36:58], Rahav uses AI for low-stakes questions only [38:15], Nadine said AI has to be verified [38:53], and Matt ignores AI on health [37:33].
- Collagen needs a reason today: Rahav wants a collagen pitch to explain why she needs it when her great-grandmother did not [26:18], and Donella wants to know what to take with collagen and where it comes from [28:18].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: these are supplement purchase drivers from consumers themselves, with collagen, protein powder and creatine named [05:22] [26:18].
- Origin, naturalness and sustainability came up without prompting [23:46] [28:18] [29:29]. My reading: our ingredients' source, processing and sustainability story should be ready for brand customers' consumer copy, stated only as far as the facts go.
- Dose and independent proof were asked for directly [25:59] [31:00]. My reading: clinically documented ingredients at a stated effective dose give our customers the answer these shoppers asked for.
- Donella asked where collagen comes from, fish or bovine, and what the animals eat [28:18]. My reading: a clear origin and traceability sheet for our collagen would help brands answer that question.
- These are eight people speaking about their own habits: personal experience, not evidence or a market sample (my reading).

items.title: Nutrition to Improve Mitochondrial Functions During Ageing
items.to_check: Whether Nathan attended. No recording; slides only. The PDF has no text layer, so all slide text was read from the slide images. The speaker's name is spelled "Philipp Gut, M.D." on the title slide (the upload's file name has "Phillip"); his role beyond M.D. is not given. Slide 8 cites Hojfeldt et al. as Advanced Science 2026, slide 9 as Science Advances 2026.
items.added_by: Claude (from the printed agenda, Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Philipp Gut of Nestlé Research asked how nutrition can keep mitochondria working as we age.

He framed healthy-ageing nutrition across four need states, from prevention and peri-menopause to geriatric care, and three toolkits: nutrients, biotics and bioactives.

Calorie restriction is his reference point. In a 14-year study in dogs, a diet with 25% fewer calories gave a median life of 13 years against 11.2. Unpublished human data link a higher BMI to an older biological age, and weight loss, including on meal replacements, to a younger one. Mitochondria are vulnerable to ageing, and calorie restriction works partly through them.

He then showed four supplements aimed at mitochondria, creatine first, then nicotinamide riboside, urolithin A, and N-acetylcysteine with glycine. Nestlé's own research followed. Nicotinamide and vitamin B6 activated muscle stem cells in a human trial, by no direct mitochondrial route. Two NAD+ precursors raised blood NAD+ within two weeks, partly through the gut microbiome. Thymol, a plant compound, activated mitophagy and slowed functional decline in fast-ageing mice.

His conclusion was measured. Some benefits of calorie restriction can be mimicked with natural molecules, but more human evidence is needed, and biomarkers of ageing can serve as trial endpoints. He closed on Nestlé's new Healthy Longevity Academy for health professionals and a partnership with Nanyang Technological University.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Calorie restriction: in a 14-year lifetime study in dogs, 25% calorie restriction against pair-fed controls gave a median life span of 13 years against 11.2, "+ 15% longer life", with better insulin sensitivity and immune function and later disease onset (Lawler et al., 2008) (slide 4).
- Weight and biological age, unpublished: biological age (PhenoAge) rises with BMI, weight loss in people with obesity lowers it, and meal-replacement regimens lowered it with weight loss, against baseline at weeks 26 and 52 (read from the chart) (slide 5).
- Creatine is the first of four "Examples of supplements to improve mitochondrial functions", with nicotinamide riboside, urolithin A, and N-acetylcysteine and glycine, each shown beside a Solgar or Pure Encapsulations pack (slide 7).
- Muscle: nicotinamide and vitamin B6 activated muscle stem cells and enhanced regeneration in a human RCT, with 29% more activated Pax7+ cells and 37% more regenerating myofibres against placebo; the deck says there is no direct mitochondrial mechanism (slide 8) (slide 9).
- NAD+: two weeks of daily nicotinamide riboside (1 g) or NMN (1 g) raised blood NAD+ against placebo; nicotinamide (0.5 g) did not. The route runs through low absorption and conversion by gut microbes (Christen et al., Nature Metabolism 2026) (slide 10).
- Thymol (20 mg/kg a day) lowered biological age, improved running distance, preserved grip force and raised the mitophagy protein Pink1 in fast-ageing SAMP8 mice; his translational verdict is that more evidence in humans is needed (slide 13) (slide 15).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: a Nestlé Research scientist puts creatine first among supplements to improve mitochondrial function, shown with Solgar's Vitality Creatine Complex (slide 7). My reading: creatine's healthy-ageing case now runs on cellular energy as well as muscle, which supports CreaWin pitches to healthy-ageing brands, within CreaWin's own evidence. The deck gives no creatine data.
- My reading: Solgar and Pure Encapsulations, whose packs fill slide 7, are both Nestlé Health Science brands; the slide does not say so. Solgar already sells a creatine product, so it is a natural CreaWin prospect (slide 7).
- Muscle in ageing is the strongest human result here, from nicotinamide and vitamin B6 rather than protein (slide 9). My reading: a stacking partner for CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea in a healthy-ageing muscle formula, not a rival.
- Weight loss, biological age and obesity-related "hidden" malnutrition sit side by side (slide 2) (slide 5). My reading: keeping muscle and nutrient density during weight loss is where protein and creatine fit; the biological-age data are unpublished.
- NAD+ precursors raise blood NAD+ (slide 10), but Euromonitor's Nick Stene said NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream, with urolithin A among the ingredients queuing behind it (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). The two talks are about different things: Gut's is human blood data, Stene's is US shelf prices.
summary.Quotes:
- "Calorie restriction mediates benefits partially through mitochondria" (slide 6)
- "No direct mitochondrial mechanism !" (slide 8)
- "Can we identify natural bioactives that mimic benefits of fasting to prevent age-related decline of mitochondrial functions?" (slide 11)
- "Some benefits of calorie restriction can be mimicked with natural molecules, but more evidence in humans is needed" (slide 15)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Philipp Gut (Nestlé Research): ask whether Nestlé has creatine data on mitochondrial or muscle endpoints in older adults, and for the unpublished weight-loss and biological-age data when published.
- Solgar (Vitality Creatine Complex): find who supplies its creatine; a CreaWin prospect, my reading.
- Find Højfeldt et al., 2026 (nicotinamide and vitamin B6 RCT) and Christen et al., Nature Metabolism 2026 (NAD+ precursors).
- Look at the Healthy Longevity Academy's "Fuel and Frame" pillar for how Nestlé talks to health professionals about strength in ageing.
- Confirm whether Nathan attended.
summary.Detail:
- The PDF has no text layer; the slide text below was read from the slide images. Slide numbers are the PDF's pages and match the numbers printed on the slides.
- Title slide: "Philipp Gut, M.D.", Nestlé Research, November 2026 (slide 1).
- Four need states: preventive nutrition for healthy ageing, peri-menopause related nutrition needs, obesity-related "hidden" malnutrition, and geriatric and acute care nutrition. Subtitle: "Understanding the biology of ageing can benefit health across need states" (slide 2).
- Three toolkits: macro- and micronutrients (ultra-dense protein micelles from dairy; calorie-optimised, high-NRF-index foods and supplements); biotics (synbiotics mediating gut-organ signalling; live bacterial spores as microbiome therapeutics, FMT, pharma); molecular nutrition bioactives (plant-derived mitophagy activators, α-acarbose mimetics and stem cell activators; endogenous metabolites such as co-factors and lipids) (slide 3).
- The dog study's biological-age data (Herzig et al., GeroScience 2024): "Calorie optimization to maintain lean body mass lowers biological age". Mortality hazard ratios: age deviation 1.47 (p=0.0178), restricted diet 0.26 (p=0.0007). Read from the chart (slide 4).
- Weight and biological age, marked "Unpublished data": PhenoAge z-score rises across BMI bands from under 18 to over 40 (p<2e-16); the median difference between biological and chronological age is about 1.7 years younger after weight loss and about 1 year older after weight gain; Optifast differed from the food-based diet at week 52 (**) but not at baseline or week 26. Read from the chart (slide 5).
- Section slide: "Mitochondria are vulnerable to ageing, impacting metabolism and cell signaling" (slide 6).
- Pack shots on slide 7: Solgar Golden Prime Vitality Creatine Complex (stick packs), Solgar Cellular Energy (nicotinamide riboside chloride, Niagen), Pure Encapsulations Renual, and Pure Encapsulations NAC + Glycine powder (slide 7).
- "NAD+ precursors and natural bioactives that target mitochondrial metabolism are promising candidates to slow cellular aging", from internal research: nicotinamide and vitamin B6 for muscle stem cells (Ancel et al., JCI 2024; Hojfeldt et al., 2026); NR and NMN raise NAD+ via the microbiome, and trigonelline is "a novel NAD+ precursor, with potential benefits for muscle strength" (Christen et al., Nature Metabolism 2026; Membrez et al., Nature Metabolism 2024); thymol is a novel autophagy and mitophagy activator, and oleuropein activates mitochondrial energy metabolism through MICU (Civiletto et al., Nature Aging 2025; Gherardi et al., Cell Metabolism 2025) (slide 8).
- Muscle stem cells: a screen of 50,000 nutrients found nicotinamide and pyridoxine stimulate Pax7 and MyoD in muscle cells; in aged muscle, NAM and PN brought Pax7+ stem cells back towards young levels (about 550 against 400 cells/mm², young about 580, read from the chart) (Ancel et al., J Clin Invest 2024); serum NAM and PN decline with human skeletal muscle ageing, shown against appendicular lean mass at 60 and 80 years; the human RCT is Højfeldt et al., Science Advances 2026 (slide 9).
- NAD+ trial groups: placebo (17/16), nicotinamide (17/17), NR (16/16), NMN (15/14). Blood NAD+ rose from about 30 µM to about 75 µM on NR and about 65 µM on NMN (read from the chart). Gut effects include short-chain fatty acid production and conversion of nicotinic acid to NAD+, with a "strong sustained NAD+ increase" in whole blood via the Preiss-Handler pathway (slide 10).
- Polyphenols and other secondary metabolites are "often associated to health benefits in nutrient-dense diets"; in plants they serve pathogen defence, competition, attraction and repulsion, UV, heat and drought protection, and nitrogen storage. Example: resveratrol, quercetin and piceatannol inhibit F1 ATPase (Li et al., Journal of Future Foods 2023; Gledhill, PNAS 2007) (slide 12).
- Thymol mouse study: SAMP8 mice from 8 to 11 months of age; running distance rose over 12 weeks on thymol but not in controls, and was about double control when normalised to baseline; grip force fell in controls but not on thymol (about 0.9 against 0.6 of baseline); Pink1 protein about 1.25 times control. Read from the chart (slide 13).
- Working hypothesis: thymol and carvacrol, plant metabolites with bactericidal effects also used as food preservatives and flavourings, "target mammalian mitochondria through a conserved bactericidal mechanism"; thymol mildly lowers mitochondrial membrane potential and strongly activates mitophagy (mitophagy index about double, read from the chart) (Civiletto et al., Nature Aging 2025) (slide 14).
- Translational considerations: "Understanding the mechanism(s) is key to enable clinical evidence development"; "Biomarkers of ageing can enable discovery, serve as clinical endpoints, and provide frameworks for precision health" (slide 15).
- Nestlé Nutrition Institute's Healthy Longevity Academy, "Now launched", for healthcare professionals only, with five pillars: The Foundations, Fuel and Frame ("Powering strength, metabolic health and cognitive vitality"), Cellular Power, Cellular Renewal, and The Inner Ecosystem (slide 16).
- Nestlé Research teams in Switzerland, Beijing and Singapore; collaborators EPFL, Harvard Medical School, Clock Foundation, Università degli Studi di Milano, University of Copenhagen and Institut NeuroMyoGène. "News: we are entering a strategic partnership with Nanyang Technological University to advance research on healthy longevity", in collaboration with EDB Singapore (slide 17).
- Other talks at this summit: Lumina's Ewa Hudson cited Life Extension's Phenotypic Age blood test (lumina-new-longevity-consumer), the same PhenoAge measure Gut uses (slide 5); the retailer panel said creatine is moving from sports into healthy ageing (from-hype-to-healthspan-building-the).

takeaways.text: Calorie restriction: in a 14-year lifetime study in dogs, 25% calorie restriction against pair-fed controls gave a median life span of 13 years against 11.2, "+ 15% longer life", with better insulin sensitivity and immune function and later disease onset (Lawler et al., 2008) (slide 4).

Weight and biological age, unpublished: biological age (PhenoAge) rises with BMI, weight loss in people with obesity lowers it, and meal-replacement regimens lowered it with weight loss, against baseline at weeks 26 and 52 (read from the chart) (slide 5).

Creatine is the first of four "Examples of supplements to improve mitochondrial functions", with nicotinamide riboside, urolithin A, and N-acetylcysteine and glycine, each shown beside a Solgar or Pure Encapsulations pack (slide 7).

Muscle: nicotinamide and vitamin B6 activated muscle stem cells and enhanced regeneration in a human RCT, with 29% more activated Pax7+ cells and 37% more regenerating myofibres against placebo; the deck says there is no direct mitochondrial mechanism (slide 8) (slide 9).

NAD+: two weeks of daily nicotinamide riboside (1 g) or NMN (1 g) raised blood NAD+ against placebo; nicotinamide (0.5 g) did not. The route runs through low absorption and conversion by gut microbes (Christen et al., Nature Metabolism 2026) (slide 10).

Thymol (20 mg/kg a day) lowered biological age, improved running distance, preserved grip force and raised the mitophagy protein Pink1 in fast-ageing SAMP8 mice; his translational verdict is that more evidence in humans is needed (slide 13) (slide 15).

quotes.text: "Calorie restriction mediates benefits partially through mitochondria" (slide 6)
"No direct mitochondrial mechanism !" (slide 8)
"Can we identify natural bioactives that mimic benefits of fasting to prevent age-related decline of mitochondrial functions?" (slide 11)
"Some benefits of calorie restriction can be mimicked with natural molecules, but more evidence in humans is needed" (slide 15)

summary.Summary:
Two talks shared this slot, on one EffePharm deck. Professor Colin Selman, a biogerontologist at the University of Glasgow who lists EffePharm beside his university, opened on the science. Mitochondria work less well as animals age, and that decline is one of the hallmarks of ageing. His question was whether it can be slowed.

His answers came from animals. Turning down nutrient sensing, eating fewer calories and giving NMN, a precursor of NAD+, all preserved mitochondrial function in mice. Long-term NMN reduced frailty, and in a preprint it extended the lifespan of female mice. None of his evidence was in people.

JianJun Yu then presented UTHEVER, EffePharm's branded NMN. A trial published in 2022 is the brand's base. The new work is a small sleep trial of EffePharm's own, not yet published: 34 adults who stay up late or sleep poorly took NMN or placebo for eight weeks. Sleep quality, insomnia and fatigue scores ended lower than on placebo. Each result is labelled as within the NMN group or against placebo, and not as a treatment claim.

The talk closed on regulation. EFSA published a positive safety opinion in May 2026, and the deck expects EU novel-food approval in November 2026. EffePharm says that opens pharmacy, beauty and mainstream retail across the EU.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Selman's case, all from worms and mice: mitochondrial function falls with age, and reduced nutrient sensing, a 30% calorie cut and NMN each preserved it in mice; NMN made mitochondria more efficient without adding more of them (slide 5) (slide 7) (slide 8) (slide 9).
- Long-term NMN (about 550 mg/kg a day in drinking water from 13 months of age) is shown reducing frailty in both sexes and extending female lifespan in mice; the source is a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, and the frailty chart is labelled schematic, its values illustrative (slide 10).
- UTHEVER's published trial (Frontiers in Aging, 2022): 66 adults aged 40 to 65 randomised, 62 analysed, 300 mg a day for 60 days; the slide reports a 38% increment in NAD+ levels and 6.5% gains in walking endurance and quality of life, read from the slide image, without saying whether against placebo (slide 13).
- The sleep trial (EffePharm data on file): 34 adults aged 30 to 60, 600 mg a day or placebo for eight weeks. At day 56 the NMN group scored lower than placebo on sleep quality (PSQI, p<0.05), insomnia severity (ISI, p<0.01) and fatigue (FS-14, p<0.05); within the group the scores fell 36.61%, 48.43% and 48.15% from baseline (slide 14) (slide 15) (slide 16) (slide 17).
- Deep sleep rose 27.65 minutes (38.88%) against the NMN group's own baseline (p<0.05); no placebo comparison is shown (slide 18).
- EU novel food: filed August 2023, public consultation completed February 2025, positive EFSA safety assessment published May 2026, approval "expected" in November 2026; the US FDA sent an NDI no-objection letter in November 2025, and the UK application is in progress (slide 20) (slide 21).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: NMN is not in our range, but it is sold on cellular energy, fatigue and healthy ageing, the ground CreaWin is moving into. A retail panel at the same summit said creatine is moving from sports into longevity (from-hype-to-healthspan-building-the [19:15]).
- If EU approval lands as the deck expects, NMN can go into EU pharmacy and mainstream retail, not just cross-border e-commerce (slide 20). My reading: expect NAD+ "energy as you age" launches in EU pharmacy in 2027, competing with or stacked beside creatine; Euromonitor's talk the same morning put the NAD+ family close to a price war (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan).
- My reading: EffePharm made NAD+ felt by testing sleep and fatigue rather than biomarkers. Our healthy-ageing pitches for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea should lead the same way, on outcomes people notice.
- My reading: the deck's reporting is a model to copy. Every figure says whether it is within the group or against placebo, and each sleep slide says it is not a treatment claim (slide 15) (slide 17).
- My reading: the format, an academic on mechanism followed by the brand's human data, is one we could use in our own speaking slots.

- Living longer brings age-related disease: cardiovascular, neurodegenerative and liver disease, macular degeneration, sarcopenia, osteoporosis and osteoarthritis, cancer, type 2 diabetes and obesity, and immunosenescence (slide 3).
- Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the hallmarks of ageing (Lopez-Otin et al., 2013 and 2023), shown across humans, mice, flies and worms (slide 4).
- With age, oxygen consumption falls from about 6.9 at 4 months to 5.7 at 12 months and 4.3 at 21 months (pmol O2 per second per citrate synthase), and ATP content and ATP production fall to roughly 60% and 40% of the younger level, all read from the charts; the species is not named on the slide (Drew et al. 2003; Hempenstall et al. 2012, 2026; Morsci et al. 2016) (slide 5).

summary.Summary:
The recording holds only the last four and a half minutes of Amanda Rao's talk on pharmacokinetic testing, then one audience question. Her argument, in the part recorded: absorption studies are run on the wrong people, in the wrong conditions.

A typical pharmacokinetic study is done on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to older women on several medications. GLP-1 medicines slow food through the gut, and studies with paracetamol show lower absorption in people taking them, so they belong in absorption studies. Studies should look at responders and at high and low absorbers, and test products as people take them: with food and coffee, with missed doses and other medications, not fasted and as a single dose.

She sees research moving from single ingredients to whole formulas, and home blood tests making it easy to track blood levels in long-term trials. AI models that predict exposure need good studies to learn from.

Asked about dose, she said a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early on is easier and cheaper than five doses in a long-term trial, and that the industry may need lower doses taken for longer.
summary.Key takeaways:
- In the studies she cited, people on GLP-1 medicines absorbed paracetamol 15 to 50 percent less; absorption studies that leave them out are "not you know, collecting the right data" [00:00].
- Study populations do not match buyers: a typical pharmacokinetic study is on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to 65-year-old women on three medications, with low oestrogen and a history of antibiotics [00:00].
- Look at responders and at high and low absorbers, not only at a rise in the blood: "did 90% of people get that?" [00:00].
- Test products as they are taken: most pharmacokinetic studies are fasted and single-dose, while real users eat, drink coffee, miss doses and stack medications [00:00].
- Long-term trials should measure blood levels as well as outcomes, now that home tests are easy; some nutrients, such as iron and vitamin D, need longer studies [00:00].
- On dose, a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early is "easier and honestly cheaper" than five doses in a long-term study; she suggested lower doses for longer [05:14].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: this is how absorption evidence for ingredients will be designed and judged, and GLP-1 users are named as a population that absorbs differently [00:00].
- My reading: bioavailability claims for enhanced-absorption forms may be challenged where the study used young, fasted adults; the populations in our studies are worth checking before a pitch to a healthy-ageing brand [00:00].
- My reading: products pitched for muscle on a GLP-1 journey (protein, CreaWin) may in time need absorption data in GLP-1 users before brands rely on them [00:00].
- My reading: a multi-dose pharmacokinetic study is a cheap way to set the dose of a new ingredient before an efficacy trial [05:14].

- "So two people, one capsule, different blood levels." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
- "Your typical PK studies done on a 25-year-old." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
- "And as we know, real life is messier than the clinic." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
- "But maybe we need 10 times less for a longer period of time." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [05:14]

summary.Summary:
Ohad Manor, Vice President of Computational Precision Health at Thorne, argued that supplement shoppers suffer from too much information, not too little. His example was Lena, 47, sleeping badly and wondering about perimenopause, faced with AI answers, social media and influencers.

Personalisation is the answer, he said, but also a double-edged sword: people differ, and so do ingredients, claims and formulations. Thorne has over 250 products, so even its own shoppers struggle to choose. He sees AI as the engine that can personalise at scale, provided it is data-driven, dynamic and educational rather than a black box.

Thorne's answer is Taya, an AI adviser launched in July last year. It works only from Thorne's own products, claims, science and articles, without web access. It asks follow-up questions, narrows its recommendations, adds lifestyle advice and shares articles. By Thorne's count it held over 300,000 conversations in its first year. Manor said it ignores bestsellers and promotions.

He closed by urging supplement companies to build similar tools. Otherwise people go to ChatGPT, which does not know a company's products as its own medical and ingredient teams do.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Thorne's own survey, as Manor gave it: roughly 40% of consumers use AI for health questions, and two out of three would use an AI tool they trusted to make decisions [00:23].
- Taya is a closed system: built on foundation models, but without internet access and limited to Thorne's products, ingredients, claims and science and over 1,000 articles [00:23].
- Thorne's first-year figures for Taya, as Manor gave them: over 300,000 conversations, over 650,000 messages, over 1.2 million product and lifestyle recommendations, over 135,000 articles shared, and about 92% thumbs up [00:23].
- In his Lena example, Taya narrowed eight recommendations to two products, explained the ingredients and gave a daily routine with lifestyle tips [00:23].
- Taya recommends almost the whole portfolio, not the same five products; its top topics in year one were heart health and sports nutrition, then cognition and focus, bone and joint, and metabolism [00:23].
- His call to brands: build such tools, because ChatGPT "doesn't know everything about your products the way you know them" [00:23].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- An AI adviser on a brand's site answers only from that brand's claims and science [00:23]. My reading: the evidence and approved wording we give customers for our ingredients may end up in the knowledge base such a tool reads, so it should be clear and claim-safe.
- Shoppers find ingredient forms confusing; Manor named citrate, glycinate, bisglycinate and threonate forms of magnesium [00:23]. My reading: form-specific evidence is what lets a tool like this choose one product over another.
- Relevance medium: consumer-facing AI at a brand; it touches our ingredients only through the claims and evidence brands feed it.
summary.Quotes:
- "So the problem is not, you know, too little information. It's too much information." Speaker 2 (Ohad Manor) [00:23]
- "She doesn't care about bestsellers." Speaker 2 (Ohad Manor) [00:23]
- "Otherwise, people are going to ChatGPT, which is great." Speaker 2 (Ohad Manor) [00:23]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ohad Manor (Thorne): what ingredient evidence and claims Taya reads, and whether suppliers' data goes in.
- See the panel (from-data-to-decisions-personalizing) for Taya's limits, monitoring and conversion tracking.

summary.Summary:
Paul Spagnuolo, a food science professor at the University of Guelph and co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer of Applied Laboratory Technologies (ALT), declared his conflict of interest and explained why he built an AI tool for ingredient discovery.

For 20 years his lab has applied pharmaceutical drug discovery to food molecules, taking two products, one from avocado, from discovery to clinical trial and market. That path is long, costly and mostly fails, and the claim at the end covers only the indication studied.

AMBROSIA, an agentic AI platform built with a computational biologist, aims to shorten the discovery and validation stages. As a retroactive test they gave it the avocado molecule. He said it reached in one day the target and use his lab had taken 10 years and millions of dollars to find. ALT's slide claims the stages shrink from years to days and from millions to thousands.

He said researchers still have to validate in the lab. Finzelberg was the first partner: in less than a week AMBROSIA pointed to how its extract works, which matched Finzelberg's own research. ALT now works business to business, helping companies understand their ingredients and find new markets for them.
summary.Key takeaways:
- ALT's slide claims AMBROSIA cuts discovery and validation from "5-10 years" and millions of dollars to "5-10 days" and thousands (photo 1); Spagnuolo said it took AMBROSIA one day to reach what took his lab 10 years [20:14].
- In ALT's retroactive test on avocatin B, AMBROSIA analysed 1,284 crystal structures and found 361 potential gene targets, 99 at high confidence, with lipid metabolism and PPAR signalling among the primary pathways (photo 2); Spagnuolo said it pointed to acyl-CoA dehydrogenase and fatty acid oxidation [20:14].
- A claim covers only what was studied: a phase two result on cardiometabolic function "that's our claim", not inflammation or longevity [20:14]. ALT pitches AMBROSIA as a way to find new markets for existing ingredients (photo 3) [30:28].
- AI does not replace the lab: "you still need to flip the switch", with researchers doing the validation [20:14].
- Finzelberg, the first partner, received an answer on its extract in less than a week that matched its own research [30:28]; ALT's slide quotes Finzelberg on Menofelis, its Siberian rhubarb extract for menopause, and AMBROSIA's "multi-target profiles" (photo 4).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: AI tools that propose mechanisms and new uses change how ingredient evidence is generated, and how fast a supplier can reposition a botanical (photo 3) [30:28].
- A botanical extract supplier, Finzelberg, already uses AMBROSIA to find which compounds in its extract are active and what to study next [30:28]. My reading: a competitor can now get a mechanism map and a study plan for a botanical in days; we should know whether such maps exist for ingredients in our range.
- Spagnuolo was clear that a prediction is not evidence: lab validation and trials are still needed, and a claim covers only the indication studied [20:14]. My reading: an AI target profile could guide a study plan for one of our ingredients, but it supports no claim on its own.

- "It took my lab 10 years to go from understanding the discovery of a molecule to its applications as a fatty acid oxidation inhibitor" Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [20:14]
- "We're talking about one specific application." Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [20:14]
- "Identify new markets for existing ingredients" ALT's slide (photo 3)
