summary.Summary:
Lauren Nicolle of NutraIngredients+ chaired the last session of the day, framed as AI across the product cycle: discovery with Paul Spagnuolo of ALT, clinical validation with Jeff Chen of Radicle Science, and the consumer with Ohad Manor of Thorne.

Chen described Radicle's decentralised, in-house trials, run at home at a scale site studies cannot reach. On hallucinations, Spagnuolo said they happen all the time and ALT keeps its tool inside the scientific literature. Manor said Taya is a closed system and every message is monitored. Chen said narrow knowledge bases and checking agents cut the risk.

Chen argued that home tests, wearables and phones now let trials collect data sites never could, and that machine learning is needed to read it. He wants biomarkers, wearables and surveys combined rather than one trusted alone. Manor said Taya has limits: complicated cases need a healthcare provider, and shoppers should ask who built a tool and on what data.

All three saw true personalisation as some way off. Spagnuolo pointed to genetics and lifestyle, Chen to precision groups first and trial and error over time, Manor to levels of personalisation. Asked about small studies, Chen called for scale and real-world diversity. Stephen Daniells then closed the day.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Chen said Radicle Science has put about 100,000 people through double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials in about six years, and is running a US-government-funded mental health trial of 6,000 people with one shared placebo and 19 treatment arms [34:11].
- Guardrails against hallucination: ALT keeps AMBROSIA from going outside the literature [36:40]; Thorne monitors and scores every Taya message and sends flagged ones to regulatory and medical [37:43]; Chen said narrow knowledge bases and checking agents cut the risk [39:03].

summary.Summary:
Dr Jenna Macciochi, Director of Science & Innovation at Ancient + Brave, opened the second day's women's health session. Ancient + Brave is a UK wellness brand selling collagen and supplements for women. Her question was how the industry should innovate for women who live longer, but not healthier, lives. Women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health than men.

She set out three shifts. First, from normalised to noticed: women have learned to accept being dismissed, and the industry sells to them with "pink" reformulations, fixed age bands, borrowed evidence and fear. Second, from reproductive hormones to whole-body transitions: hormones act on the heart, bone, muscle, metabolism, sleep and brain, and perimenopause is the least studied stage. Her example was the heart: twice as many UK women die from coronary heart disease as from breast cancer. Third, from borrowed evidence to evidence built with women, since research funding and trials largely leave women out.

Her answer was Ancient + Brave's own model: placebo-controlled trials of its products with universities, blinded consumer studies, and citizen science with customers. It also funds a PhD on collagen in midlife women. She closed on four principles: dose to the evidence, design for transitions rather than age bands, test the finished product with women, and say only what the evidence supports.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Longer lives, not healthier ones: the gap between lifespan and healthy years is 2.4 years wider for women than for men across 183 countries, and women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health (slide 5).
- Women's supplements are under scrutiny for "pink" repackaging, static age bands and borrowed evidence; Which? found many menopause supplements use botanicals at doses too low to match the trials behind them. Fear (ageing as decline, hormones as a problem, hidden threats) is "a common sales tactic" (slide 9) (slide 10).
- Menopause as a whole-body transition: hormones act on brain, heart, bone, muscle, metabolism, sleep, gut, liver, immune system and skin; perimenopause is "Years of fluctuation, and the least studied". In the SWAN cohort cholesterol rose sharply around the final period, beyond what ageing alone explains (slide 12) (slide 13).
- Heart: 23,000 UK women die from coronary heart disease each year, twice as many as from breast cancer. Ancient + Brave, King's College London and Heart Research UK launch a Women's Heart Health Survey in December 2026, the first UK-wide one in 9 years and the first to add menopausal stage (slide 14) (slide 15).
- The evidence gap: under 1% of global research funding went to six female-specific conditions that carry 14% of the women's health burden, and 16.5% of 704 micronutrient studies included only men (slide 18).
- Ancient + Brave's evidence model: clinical trials ("Does it work?"), blinded consumer studies ("How does it feel?") and citizen science with its Inner Circle customers; a four-arm sleep trial of True Nightcap against placebo, with and without a wearable; and a funded Loughborough PhD on collagen and co-supplementation in midlife women (slide 19) (slide 20) (slide 22).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: Ancient + Brave sells collagen and a creatine product, True Creatine+ ("Advanced creatine formula"), pictured on the title slide beside True Collagen and True Nightcap (slide 1). Nick Stene of Euromonitor named it with IM8 as a brand winning on proof on day 1 (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). My reading: a natural CreaWin prospect; who supplies its creatine now is not known.
- Her principles include "dose to the evidence" and "test the finished product, with women", with results shared whatever they show (slide 23). My reading: a pitch to her needs the doses used in human creatine trials in women, and an offer to support a placebo-controlled study of the finished product.
- Design for transitions: muscle and bone are on her map of what hormones act on, and perimenopause is the least studied stage (slide 12) (slide 13). Stene said women heading into perimenopause are badly served, and that perimenopause still earns a premium while menopause is losing one (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). My reading: creatine and protein for muscle in perimenopause fit both talks, but the evidence has to be built in women.
- The Loughborough PhD covers collagen "and co-supplementation" in midlife women (slide 22). My reading: worth asking what is co-supplemented; a protein or creatine partner may fit.

summary.Detail:
- The brand: "a mission driven wellness brand with an award winning range of collagen" and supplements, designed to support women's health; its vision is to be the #1 wellness brand in the world, with new standards "for holistic health, sustainability and female empowerment" (slide 2).
- Research: over £400k over the next four years in independent research with Princeton Consumer Research, UEA, Cardiff and Loughborough universities; logos also show Cardiff Metropolitan and Liverpool Hope. Certification logos: B Corp, 1% for the Planet, The Climate Label, Buy Women Built, Rainforest Concern and ESG Mark. The slide's text layer also carries "£100m" with no label; it is not visible on the rendered slide (slide 3).
- The speaker: 25 years in immunology, human performance and health; former Senior Lecturer in Immunology & Biomedical Science at the University of Sussex; leads product development and clinical research at Ancient + Brave; author of three books, most recently Immune to Age (slide 4).
- Product photos: True Nightcap ("Advanced nutrient nightcap"), True Collagen (bovine collagen) and True Creatine+ ("Advanced creatine formula") on the title slide; True Magnesium+ in a photo (slide 1) (slide 7).
- Sources for the healthspan gap: Garmany and Terzic, JAMA Network Open 2024; World Economic Forum and McKinsey Health Institute 2024 (slide 5).
- What women have learned to accept: 84% said there were times they weren't listened to by healthcare professionals (nearly 100,000 respondents, England; DHSC call for evidence 2021); 56% of UK women feel their pain is ignored or dismissed, and 31% didn't want to "waste" a professional's time (Gender Pain Gap Index, Nurofen and Wellbeing of Women); 1 in 10 women who worked through menopause left a job because of their symptoms (Fawcett Society 2022) (slide 8).
- Menopause: average age 51, usually between 45 and 55; symptoms can start years earlier; more than 34 symptoms. "Women already have the ‘Pink Tax’ and now the hormone tax." Shown on the slide: the paper "What is in the bottle? An analysis of the ingredients in menopause supplements" (Sullivan, Boylan and Harper, 2026), a "Menopause gold rush" headline, and Which?, "Menopause markup", September 2026 (slide 9).
- On fear: "Fear sells answers and certainty when we should start by asking better questions", and without collective action a climate of fear persists "because it is commercially lucrative" (slide 10).
- The four transitions: puberty (bone and body composition build), pregnancy and postpartum, perimenopause, and post-menopause ("A new baseline for heart, bone and metabolism"). SWAN: Matthews et al., Journal of the American College of Cardiology 2009 (slide 13).
- Heart: up to 59% higher risk than men of an initial heart attack misdiagnosis; up to 80% of premature cardiovascular deaths are preventable. Sources include Heart Research UK, the University of Leeds (2016), the World Heart Federation (2025) and the Lancet Women and Cardiovascular Disease Commission (2021) (slide 14).
- The survey is ethically approved and designed to inform policy: when menopause is raised in an NHS Health Check, heart risk should be part of the conversation. The last UK-wide survey was Heart Research UK and Damart, 2017 (slide 15).
- England's Renewed Women's Health Strategy (April 2026) names cardiovascular disease as a priority for women and adds a menopause question to the NHS Health Check; the slide says it does not yet join the menopause question to heart health or plan how heart risk is raised in menopause care (slide 16).
- Evidence gap sources: McKinsey Health Institute 2025 (funding 2019 to 2023, 64 conditions); Science Advances 2021; Scottish Health Survey 2017. Over 80% of the micronutrient studies excluded pregnant or lactating women (slide 18).
- The Inner Circle: customers who opt in to research after three months or more on a product; over 900 survey responses in the past year. "Ingredient studies show what a compound can do. We also need to know what a product does in real lives" (slide 20).
- Citizen science runs with ARIA (myaria.health); its founder Georgina Kyriakoudes is quoted, with three participants' comments, one on the double-blind design (slide 21).
- The PhD: Ancient + Brave's first funded PhD, at Loughborough University with Dr Tom Clifford; independent academic research intended for publication; PhD researcher Chloe Errington (slide 22).
- The deck shows study designs but no results for the sleep trial, the consumer studies or the PhD (slide 19) (slide 20) (slide 22).

summary.Summary:
Serena Tongiani, Chief Portfolio Officer at Indena, the Italian botanical extracts company, argued that a healthy appearance reflects internal vitality and belongs in the longevity conversation.

She opened on the market. Nutrition Business Journal data show healthy ageing as the fastest-growing supplement category, and skin and beauty ageing among the top five concerns people address with healthy-ageing products. Botanicals can meet that need, she said, but they raise three problems: poor solubility and absorption, active content that varies with the harvest, and pesticide residues, even in organic material.

Indena's answer is a Centella asiatica extract standardised in triterpenes and formulated with sunflower lecithin on its phospholipid platform, sourced from Madagascar and grown in solar-powered greenhouses in Sardinia. In human skin cells it beat a standard extract on oxidative stress and collagen; the deck itself says this is not proof of absorption.

The centrepiece was Indena's own placebo-controlled trial in 52 women aged 45 to 60, with the manuscript submitted. After 84 days wrinkle depth at the crow's feet was 16% lower than at the start, and elasticity, firmness, skin thickness, collagen fibre density and the skin's antioxidant power improved. She closed on quality: there is no quality in a finished product without quality in its ingredients.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Market (Nutrition Business Journal, 2026): healthy ageing is the fastest-growing supplement category and the only one in double-digit growth, at 14.6% in 2025, projected to reach $2.11 billion in 2029; 51% of consumers used dietary supplements to support healthy ageing or longevity in the last 12 months (slide 5).
- Skin and beauty ageing is addressed by 40% of people using healthy-ageing products, fourth after energy and focus (49%), sleep and recovery (47%) and joint and mobility support (45%) (NBJ, January 2026, n=832; read from the chart) (slide 7) (slide 9).
- Botanicals' formulation gap, with Centella as the case: limited solubility and bioavailability, total triterpenes varying from 35.5 to 83.2 mg/g across harvest periods, and pesticide residues in trade samples including organic-certified material (slide 9).
- In human skin cells (fibroblasts) the phospholipid-formulated extract outperformed a standard extract on oxidative stress, collagen release, collagen breakdown (MMP-1) and wound closure (about 40% after 24 hours). The deck marks this "NOT PROOF OF ABSORPTION", and a footnote says clinical benefit has not been established (slide 9) (slide 14).

- Indena's frame for maximising healthspan: cellular ageing, body function and healthy appearance (slide 6). Healthy appearance "begins from within", as skin, hair and posture reflect oxidative stress and a declining ability to regenerate (slide 8).

items.title: A Bigger Sports Nutrition Landscape: Growth, Tensions and What Comes Next
items.to_check: The chair at [25:30] is unnamed by Otter (Nikki Hancocks, my reading); "Sonero", "Rocker" and "solely" are Otter's spellings of brand names; Otter gives one time per speaker turn, so most cites are [00:00].
items.added_by: Claude (from the event app's programme, screenshots from Nathan at 11:39-11:40 on 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated opened the day with a state of the market. Sports nutrition is obviously going mainstream, he said, but is it growing beyond the motivations that defined it, is it winning consumers while losing its identity, and is the market growing or are its boundaries just moving?

He answered with three rules. Growth does not guarantee value: whey protein prices have never been higher, and brands are going through a structural reset, cutting promotions, shrinking packs, reformulating, launching whey hybrids and trying to sell more higher-margin lines such as creatine and electrolytes. Relevance does not guarantee ownership: creatine is now for everyone, in gummies, chocolate and products for women, and hydration has no agreed formula and new leaders. Opportunity does not guarantee advantage: his company tracks 16,412 product listings in eight categories, and only a few products will succeed, by pulling on format, brand, dose, science and branded ingredients.

His conclusion was that the principles of sports nutrition have gone mainstream, not sports nutrition itself. Brands should think beyond the category, stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and know their right to win. Everyone has a seat at the table, but not everyone will win.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam is his example of the bigger market: Starbucks say one in seven coffees now provides 15 g of protein. A bigger market is not more of the same market [00:00].
- Brands are not just mitigating whey prices but going through a "structural reset". New products that cut whey reliance and a shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands" [00:00] (photo 6).
- More "whey hybrids" (sold as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost) launched in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes and whey plus collagen are the next pillars [00:00] (photo 9).
- Plant protein still underdelivers on taste. It should sell itself as a very good protein, not as plant [00:00] (photo 10).
- Gummies are the fastest-growing creatine format by new launches: 8.0% of creatine products, 36.2% of them added in the last six months, with "lots of conjecture about stability" [00:00] (photo 14).
- A quarter of creatine products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow; pre-workout is highest at 53% [18:50] (photo 27).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Brands want higher-margin lines than protein, and he told the room they would like to hear good solutions [00:00] (photo 6). My reading: this is the opening for CreaWin and Oxystorm.
- In creatine, branded ingredients are in 25% of products and mostly one supplier's, and he said others are racing to follow [18:50] (photo 27). My reading: this is the gap a second branded creatine pitches into, on science and story, and a stability story for CreaWin in gummies would land with brands (photo 14). The ON benchmark sets the consumer price at 25p a serve for 3 g (photo 13).
- Plant protein must sell as a very good protein, and taste is the barrier [00:00]. My reading: IsoClr: Pea should be pitched on taste and clarity first. Rocka sells fava and pea blends at EUR 1.27 to 1.65 a serve (photo 10).
- Brands now blend protein sources, including whey plus collagen in clear drinks [00:00] (photo 9). My reading: this opens room for a pea component in clear formats.
- Pre-workout has the highest branded-ingredient penetration, 53%, so it is crowded but receptive to branded actives (photo 27) (my reading, for Oxystorm). Naturalness and short ingredient lists are a prerequisite across the board [00:00] (photo 24).
summary.Quotes:
- "A really important point here is that a bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]
- "They want to sell higher value vitamins, more pre-workout, more electrolytes, more creatine, because they have a better value chain and margin structure. And so, brands would love to listen to you about some really good solutions that you have." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]
- "Creatine, which is my benchmark, one in four products uses a branded ingredient. It wouldn't take you a genius to work out where most of that comes from. There's a race for those to follow, by the way." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
- "The growth is good, and it creates opportunity. You all have a seat at the table, but it doesn't mean to say you're all going to win." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Nick Morgan (Nutrition Integrated) for the branded-ingredient penetration data by category and the creatine format split behind the slides, and why the format table counts 2,639 creatine products while the tracked-listings slide counts 3,448 [00:00], [18:50] (photo 14) (photo 23).
- "Brett" presents the whey milkshake later in the day; the whey plus collagen talk is Rousselot's (filed as whey-collagen-the-protein-power-couple) [00:00].
- Check the brands Otter heard as "Sonero" (longevity), "Rocker" (plant protein) and "solely" (protein from air), and the Sergio Ramos-backed brand [00:00], [18:50]. The slides give Rocka for the plant range (photo 10) and Centenarian for Sergio Ramos (photo 30); the longevity example on the slide is Cellaro (photo 29), which is "Sonero": his Remedy deck names Cellaro where Otter heard "Solero" (nick-morgan-longevity); the protein-from-air brand is not on a slide.
- Myprotein's coffee collaboration with Nero (photo 12) and the Malaysian coffee collaboration he mentioned [00:00].
summary.Key slides:
- (photo 6) The whey price mitigation ladder: three tactical moves, reformulation, then new products and a portfolio shift as the top priority.
- (photo 14) Creatine for all people and occasions: the format split, with gummies and "other" formats growing fastest.
- (photo 27) Branded ingredient penetration by category, from pre-workout at 53% to minerals at 17%.
- (photo 32) His four closing principles for winning in a bigger market.
summary.Detail:
- His three opening questions: is sports nutrition growing beyond the motivations that defined it, winning consumers but losing its identity, and is the market growing or are the boundaries moving [00:00] (photo 31). His three rules: growth does not guarantee value, relevance does not guarantee ownership, opportunity does not guarantee advantage [00:00].
- Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India [00:00].
- Raw whey prices on Vesper's EU index: WPI from about EUR 11/kg in January 2023 to EUR 30.5 by July 2026, WPC80 from about EUR 7 to EUR 27.6, WPC35 from about EUR 3 to EUR 4.3. The slide calls it "the strongest period of price inflation on record", with WPC80 and WPI up about fourfold on 2023 and the sharpest rise in H1 2026: "Demand continues to exceed available WPI and WPC80 production capacity, resulting in the strongest period of price inflation on record." [00:00] (photo 4)
- The brand response: fewer promotions, 1 kg packs cut to 900 g at the same price, some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00].
- Consumer prices per kilogram for priority brands in Europe, October 2025 to October 2026: clear whey up 13.6% (EUR 60.14 to 68.32), HWP/WPI 28.0% (47.73 to 61.10), whey blends 28.8% (37.56 to 48.38), whey hybrids 15.0% (35.64 to 40.97), WPC 20.8% (36.66 to 44.29). From the stage he said 15 to 25 percent [00:00] (photo 8).
- The mitigation ladder: price increases (widespread), reduced promotion (increasingly common) and pack architecture (widely adopted globally) are tactical; reformulation is strategic and brand specific; new products and a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the top priority, limited by a ground-zero revenue base, brand permission and the risk of alienating core consumers (photo 6).
- Whey milkshakes are whey plus milk; whey plus collagen is typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks. GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and protein from air are coming through but are still expensive [00:00]. "We have never seen more whey hybrids launched in the last 12 months than ever before. It is a fundamental product pillar." [00:00] The slide's examples: Bulk Daily Whey Protein ("best value protein"), Myprotein's Impact Whey Protein Milkshake (20 g protein, 2.6 g sugar, 1.2 g fat per 29 g serving), Clean Simple Eats Protein Powder + Collagen and Planta (20 g protein, 24 vitamins and minerals, 1,000 mg BCAAs) (photo 9).
- The six pillars of innovation: whey choice risks confusing consumers; communications react more than they solve; hybrid powders are gaining consistency (dairy plus plant in overt blends); caseinate is the new milkshake; plant protein still needs a taste breakthrough; the Myprotein x Nero launch signals a race for the next cafe collaboration [00:00] (photo 12).
- Plant: ranges come in and out; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time; caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00]. "What it really wants to say is we're just a really bloody good protein. That is the ideal. By differentiating yourself as being plant, typically lends people to assume it doesn't taste as good." [00:00]
- Rocka's vegan range: Pro Protein, 24 g protein, 122 kcal, 83% fava bean and pea, EUR 37.99 per 700 g (EUR 1.65 a serve); Natural Protein, 21 g, 112 kcal, 86.6% soy, fava, almond and pea, EUR 29.99 per 600 g (EUR 1.50 a serve); Protein Shake, "the tastiest vegan protein powder", 84% blend, EUR 37.99 per 900 g (EUR 1.27 a serve). Plant is moving "from an extended product proposition to a simple product attribute" (photo 10).
- The creatine benchmark is Optimum Nutrition's Micronised Creatine Powder: 3 g creatine monohydrate a serve, GBP 14.00 for 187 g unflavoured (25p a serve, EUR 0.33) and GBP 16.00 for 247 g flavoured (29p a serve), fronted by Lauren James, Chelsea and England footballer (photo 13).
- Creatine formats across 2,639 products: powder 70.1% (13.1% added in the last six months), capsule 17.0% (8.7%), gummy 8.0% (36.2%), tablet 4.2% (14.4%), effervescent 0.4% (10.0%), other 0.3% (44.4%); 378 products, 14.3% of the total, were added in six months (photo 14). "Other" (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew fastest off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [25:59]. Examples: Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate, 20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack [00:00]. Shelf prices: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65, each single (photo 16).
- Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders: 38 mg (ViDrate Boost), 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier), 750 mg (Hunter & Gather), 1,000 mg (LMNT). 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes; 8% claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).
- Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).
- Naturalness: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours, 43% include stevia. Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition, Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).
- Tracked listings (US and Europe, 16,412 across eight spaces): creatine 3,448 (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), magnesium 2,833 (+15%), collagen 2,648, energy and focus 2,153, pre-workout 1,869, sleep and mood 1,626, electrolyte 1,487, longevity 348 (+20% new). From the stage: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium, over 2,500 collagen. "Only a few will be really successful" [00:00] (photo 23).
- Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%. The slide adds that minerals in general are "needing to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).
- Longevity takes three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life). Example: Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing [18:50] (photo 29).
- Longevity and athlete-backed brands compete for the same consumer: Sergio Ramos links sport to longevity through Centenarian ("Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better."), with normal sports products framed as living better today. The competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).
- Brands should engage with gut and microbiome, longevity and GLP-1, but stay true to the industry's DNA; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].
- The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

A quarter of creatine products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow; pre-workout is highest at 53% [18:50] (photo 27).

quotes.text: "A really important point here is that a bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]

"They want to sell higher value vitamins, more pre-workout, more electrolytes, more creatine, because they have a better value chain and margin structure. And so, brands would love to listen to you about some really good solutions that you have." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]

"Creatine, which is my benchmark, one in four products uses a branded ingredient. It wouldn't take you a genius to work out where most of that comes from. There's a race for those to follow, by the way." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
"The growth is good, and it creates opportunity. You all have a seat at the table, but it doesn't mean to say you're all going to win." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]

followups: Ask Nick Morgan (Nutrition Integrated) for the branded-ingredient penetration data by category and the creatine format split behind the slides, and why the format table counts 2,639 creatine products while the tracked-listings slide counts 3,448 [00:00], [18:50] (photo 14) (photo 23).
"Brett" presents the whey milkshake later in the day; the whey plus collagen talk is Rousselot's (filed as whey-collagen-the-protein-power-couple) [00:00].

Check the brands Otter heard as "Sonero" (longevity), "Rocker" (plant protein) and "solely" (protein from air), and the Sergio Ramos-backed brand [00:00], [18:50]. The slides give Rocka for the plant range (photo 10) and Centenarian for Sergio Ramos (photo 30); the longevity example on the slide is Cellaro (photo 29), which is "Sonero": his Remedy deck names Cellaro where Otter heard "Solero" (nick-morgan-longevity); the protein-from-air brand is not on a slide.
Myprotein's coffee collaboration with Nero (photo 12) and the Malaysian coffee collaboration he mentioned [00:00].

key_slides.caption: The whey price mitigation ladder: three tactical moves, reformulation, then new products and a portfolio shift as the top priority.
Creatine for all people and occasions: the format split, with gummies and "other" formats growing fastest.
Branded ingredient penetration by category, from pre-workout at 53% to minerals at 17%.
His four closing principles for winning in a bigger market.

detail.text: His three opening questions: is sports nutrition growing beyond the motivations that defined it, winning consumers but losing its identity, and is the market growing or are the boundaries moving [00:00] (photo 31). His three rules: growth does not guarantee value, relevance does not guarantee ownership, opportunity does not guarantee advantage [00:00].
Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India [00:00].

Raw whey prices on Vesper's EU index: WPI from about EUR 11/kg in January 2023 to EUR 30.5 by July 2026, WPC80 from about EUR 7 to EUR 27.6, WPC35 from about EUR 3 to EUR 4.3. The slide calls it "the strongest period of price inflation on record", with WPC80 and WPI up about fourfold on 2023 and the sharpest rise in H1 2026: "Demand continues to exceed available WPI and WPC80 production capacity, resulting in the strongest period of price inflation on record." [00:00] (photo 4)

The brand response: fewer promotions, 1 kg packs cut to 900 g at the same price, some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00].

Consumer prices per kilogram for priority brands in Europe, October 2025 to October 2026: clear whey up 13.6% (EUR 60.14 to 68.32), HWP/WPI 28.0% (47.73 to 61.10), whey blends 28.8% (37.56 to 48.38), whey hybrids 15.0% (35.64 to 40.97), WPC 20.8% (36.66 to 44.29). From the stage he said 15 to 25 percent [00:00] (photo 8).

The mitigation ladder: price increases (widespread), reduced promotion (increasingly common) and pack architecture (widely adopted globally) are tactical; reformulation is strategic and brand specific; new products and a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the top priority, limited by a ground-zero revenue base, brand permission and the risk of alienating core consumers (photo 6).

Whey milkshakes are whey plus milk; whey plus collagen is typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks. GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and protein from air are coming through but are still expensive [00:00]. "We have never seen more whey hybrids launched in the last 12 months than ever before. It is a fundamental product pillar." [00:00] The slide's examples: Bulk Daily Whey Protein ("best value protein"), Myprotein's Impact Whey Protein Milkshake (20 g protein, 2.6 g sugar, 1.2 g fat per 29 g serving), Clean Simple Eats Protein Powder + Collagen and Planta (20 g protein, 24 vitamins and minerals, 1,000 mg BCAAs) (photo 9).

The six pillars of innovation: whey choice risks confusing consumers; communications react more than they solve; hybrid powders are gaining consistency (dairy plus plant in overt blends); caseinate is the new milkshake; plant protein still needs a taste breakthrough; the Myprotein x Nero launch signals a race for the next cafe collaboration [00:00] (photo 12).

Plant: ranges come in and out; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time; caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00]. "What it really wants to say is we're just a really bloody good protein. That is the ideal. By differentiating yourself as being plant, typically lends people to assume it doesn't taste as good." [00:00]

Rocka's vegan range: Pro Protein, 24 g protein, 122 kcal, 83% fava bean and pea, EUR 37.99 per 700 g (EUR 1.65 a serve); Natural Protein, 21 g, 112 kcal, 86.6% soy, fava, almond and pea, EUR 29.99 per 600 g (EUR 1.50 a serve); Protein Shake, "the tastiest vegan protein powder", 84% blend, EUR 37.99 per 900 g (EUR 1.27 a serve). Plant is moving "from an extended product proposition to a simple product attribute" (photo 10).

The creatine benchmark is Optimum Nutrition's Micronised Creatine Powder: 3 g creatine monohydrate a serve, GBP 14.00 for 187 g unflavoured (25p a serve, EUR 0.33) and GBP 16.00 for 247 g flavoured (29p a serve), fronted by Lauren James, Chelsea and England footballer (photo 13).

Creatine formats across 2,639 products: powder 70.1% (13.1% added in the last six months), capsule 17.0% (8.7%), gummy 8.0% (36.2%), tablet 4.2% (14.4%), effervescent 0.4% (10.0%), other 0.3% (44.4%); 378 products, 14.3% of the total, were added in six months (photo 14). "Other" (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew fastest off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [25:59]. Examples: Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate, 20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose (photo 14) (photo 15).

Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack [00:00]. Shelf prices: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65, each single (photo 16).

Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders: 38 mg (ViDrate Boost), 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier), 750 mg (Hunter & Gather), 1,000 mg (LMNT). 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes; 8% claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).

Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).

Naturalness: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours, 43% include stevia. Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition, Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).

Tracked listings (US and Europe, 16,412 across eight spaces): creatine 3,448 (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), magnesium 2,833 (+15%), collagen 2,648, energy and focus 2,153, pre-workout 1,869, sleep and mood 1,626, electrolyte 1,487, longevity 348 (+20% new). From the stage: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium, over 2,500 collagen. "Only a few will be really successful" [00:00] (photo 23).

Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%. The slide adds that minerals in general are "needing to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).

Longevity takes three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life). Example: Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing [18:50] (photo 29).

Longevity and athlete-backed brands compete for the same consumer: Sergio Ramos links sport to longevity through Centenarian ("Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better."), with normal sports products framed as living better today. The competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).

Brands should engage with gut and microbiome, longevity and GLP-1, but stay true to the industry's DNA; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].

The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

items.title: Unfiltered: An Insider's View of the Whey Protein Market

speakers.name: Alan Johnstone
speakers.role: Owner (as introduced; formerly Arla Foods Ingredients)

summary.Summary:
Alan Johnstone, who has spent most of the last decades selling whey protein, most recently at Arla Foods Ingredients, and now runs Nutrilution, explained why whey prices hit records this year and what buyers should do about it.

His answer starts with milk. Whey protein comes from cheese, and cheese production grows only about one and a half percent a year, while demand for whey protein grows by 10% or more: sports nutrition, GLP-1 users, protein in everyday food, and clear whey. Filtration plants are expensive and take years to build, and producers have put the whey they have into isolate, so concentrate was short when brands had just switched to it.

Prices then swing further than supply and demand alone would explain, because buyers stock up when prices rise and wait when they fall. That is happening now: concentrate is falling fast, isolate is correcting, and the proteins brands moved into are rising.

His advice was plain. Do not try to time the bottom. Keep buying steadily if today's price lets you make money. And accept that whey will stay expensive, because the supply limit is structural.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The core constraint: cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, while whey protein demand grows over 10%. He called it the most important conclusion of the talk [00:16] (photo 7) (slide 5).
- Producers chose isolate. Over five years WPI grew 15.0% a year and WPC80 1.5%; clear WPI is now about a quarter of all isolate (photo 9) (slide 8).
- Between 25 August and 4 November 2026, WPC80 fell 40.7% to €16.00/kg and WPI 20.3% to €25.50/kg, while MPC85 rose 13.5% to €15.80/kg (photo 18) (slide 12).
- New capacity will not close the gap: he forecast WPI at 7 to 11% a year and WPC80 at 4 to 7% to 2030, and both cannot reach the top of their range [00:16] (photo 11) (slide 9).
- Mainstream buyers choose on taste and texture, not protein source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good [00:16].
- For buyers: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20) (slide 13)
summary.For Vita Actives:
- The structural case for non-dairy protein comes from a whey insider: supply is capped by cheese and he expects whey to stay expensive [00:16]. My reading: this is the opening for IsoClr: Pea.
- He also set the bar. Mainstream consumers care about taste and texture, not source [00:16]. My reading: a clear pea isolate has to win on taste and clarity before it wins on supply.
- Clear whey is almost all WPI, where supply is tightest (photo 9). My reading: a clear pea isolate is positioned exactly there.
- Brands have just reformulated and are reviewing protein blends while WPC80 falls (photo 18). My reading: now is the time to be in front of formulators, before WPC80 settles.
summary.Quotes:
- "...certainly the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source. I think what people always care about is taste and texture. And whey protein is delicious." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "...if WPI is growing 11% a year, then WPC 80 has to be more like four because there's not enough whey." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "So over the last few weeks, WPC80 has been falling pretty hard. WPI still expensive, but definitely correcting." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "...whey protein will be expensive. It should be expensive. It's the best protein source for so many uses. It's got a structural supply restriction, and the amount of protein is not really going away." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Talk to Alan Johnstone (Nutrilution) about his price series and the capacity lists; he invited conversations on sourcing strategy [00:16] (slide 14).
- His price series is Vesper's; check whether we have access, or want it (slide 2).
- Check the Euromonitor figure he cited for sports nutrition growth, 10% a year; his slide says 8 to 10% and names its source only as the global sports nutrition market, 2024 [00:16] (slide 3).
summary.Key slides:
- (photo 7) Supply bottlenecks: cheese production +1.5% a year against whey protein demand of 10%+.
- (photo 9) Five years of supply growth: WPI the growth engine, clear WPI a quarter of all isolate.
- (photo 18) The last ten weeks: WPC80 and WPI falling while MPC85 rises to meet WPC80.
- (photo 20) Where prices go from here, with his three takeaways for buyers.
summary.Detail:
- His full deck arrived after the talk (files/alan-johnstone-whey-market-deck.pdf, 14 pages). Slide numbers here are the file's pages; the slides print their own numbers, which run behind from page 6 because some slides have a page per build. The deck confirms every labelled figure read from the photos; only the chart readings below moved.
- Prices this year, as he said them: WPI went from around €7/kg in 2023 to over €30/kg; WPC80 held around €12/kg, then rose to €28/kg in about six weeks. WPC80 was the bigger risk for brands because they had already moved their sourcing into it [00:16].
- His monthly chart differs from the spoken WPC80 figures. It peaks at about €27.4/kg in June and July 2026, not €28, and the rise from about €12.5 in November 2025 takes about seven months, steepest from about €17.7 in March to €25.4 in May; all read from the chart (slide 2). The WPI figures agree: a low of about €7.4 in June 2023 and a peak of about €31.8 in August 2026, read from the chart (slide 2).
- The monthly chart (Vesper VPI, EU monthly prices in €/kg, December 2019 to October 2026), read from the chart: WPC80 between €4.5 and €5.6 through 2020, a peak of about €12.2 in April 2022, a low of about €4.7 in May 2023, about €12 through 2025, the 2026 peak of about €27.4, and about €18.9 in October 2026; WPI about €8 in early 2020, a peak of about €18.0 in spring 2022, the 2023 low of about €7.4, about €22 in March 2025, the 2026 peak of about €31.8, and about €28.1 in October 2026 (slide 2). The photo reading had put the 2026 peaks at about €26 to 27 (WPC80) and €31 (WPI), and the October points at about €18 and €27 (photo 2). The slide headline: "Record highs this summer (WPC80 up roughly 6x since 2020, WPI near €32/kg), now correcting" (photo 2) (slide 2).
- Another speaker's view of the same price: Tess Plaquet (Rousselot, whey-collagen-the-protein-power-couple) showed WPC80 at US$5.7k a tonne in June 2023 and US$31.7k in June 2026 (US$5.70 and US$31.70 a kilogram), with Mintel and Vesper as her slide's sources. His series is Vesper's EU price in euros a kilogram: about €5.2 in June 2023 and €27.4 in June 2026, read from the chart (slide 2), and €27.00 in the week of 25 August 2026 (slide 12). The two differ in currency and unit; both show close to a sixfold rise.
- Demand drivers: traditional sports nutrition at 10% a year on Euromonitor, which he thinks underestimates it; GLP-1 users as new demand; protein going mainstream (Starbucks, Papa John's, Dunkin'); and clear whey, which barely existed five years ago and is almost all whey [00:16].
- The demand slide: the 2024 global sports nutrition market splits 48% protein powders, 26% protein bars, 17% non-protein and 9% protein RTD, growing 8 to 10% a year; clear whey SKUs are up 35% a year; 12% of US adults take a GLP-1 medication, with protein spend up 20% (KFF 2025, BCG 2026) (photo 3) (slide 3).
- Milk by weight: water 87.3%, lactose 4.7%, fat 3.9%, casein 2.8%, minerals 0.7%, whey protein 0.6% [00:16] (photo 4) (slide 4).
- The route from milk: cheese keeps the casein and fat; liquid whey goes through ultrafiltration and drying to WPC (35 to 80% protein), microfiltration or ion exchange to WPI (90% or more), then acidification or hydrolysis to clear or hydrolysed WPI. Sweet whey powder (about 12% protein), permeate, lactose, demineralised whey (D70, D90 for infant nutrition) and whey cream are the other outlets for the same whey [00:16] (photo 4) (slide 4).
- Three bottlenecks: factories ("CAPEX intensive, less flexible than people expect, takes years to start commercial production"), liquid whey, and by-products, "a major influencer of producer value". Making WPC80 leaves permeate and lactose, which are easy to sell; WPI makers must also sell a fatty protein stream, shown on the slide as whey cream (Procream or WFC) [00:16] (photo 6) (photo 7) (slide 5) (slide 6).
- Global production: WPC80 334,000 t in 2020 and 360,000 t in 2025; WPI 80,494 t and 161,800 t (40,450 t clear, 121,350 t standard); total 414,494 t and 521,800 t, up 26% (4.7% a year). Clear WPI at 40,450 t is, he said, the top of the estimate range; standard WPI grew 8.6% a year, below the category [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 9) (slide 7) (slide 8).
- Announced US capacity (McCully Consulting, approximate; WPC80 converted from million pounds): 24,400 t of WPC80 and 7,500 t of WPI in 2026, 41,600 t and 20,300 t in 2027, 45,900 t and 22,900 t in 2028; each block on the chart is one company. UK, EU and Oceania: FrieslandCampina (WPI), Fonterra (speciality) and Polmlek (WPC, WPI) in 2026; Tirlán (WPC, WPI, clear) and Liprovit (WPI) in 2027; Arla's mozzarella plant in 2028. He said the European list is incomplete [00:16] (photo 11) (slide 9).
- The buying cycle, using COVID as the example: longer lead times, more stock, rising demand, buyers competing, rising prices and an incentive to buy early; then the reverse, with the 2022 peak as logistics freed up and buyers destocked, and the 2023 trough as buyers waited with stocks too low [00:16] (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15) (slide 10) (slide 11).
- Now: new US plants planned three or four years ago are commissioning; isolate, WPC35 and sweet whey powder are better uses of whey, so WPC80 output should fall; substitutes (MPC85, MPI, caseins, plant proteins) are rising, and WPC80 and milk protein "should never meet" [00:16].
- Weekly Vesper prices, 25 August to 4 November 2026: WPC80 €27.00 to €16.00; WPI €32.00 to €25.50; MPC85 €13.92 to €15.80. On 4 November WPC80 was still €0.20 above MPC85 (photo 16) (photo 18) (slide 12). Read from the chart, WPC80 held about €27 for two weeks, then fell every week, to about €19 by 14 October; MPC85 was about €16 from 7 October (slide 12).
- Forces for the next move. WPC80, up: strong other derivatives, rising alternatives, long-term protein demand; down: high inventories, powerful momentum, demand destruction. WPI, up: smaller share of brand costs, healthy inventories on both sides, harder to replace; down: demand destruction, production increases due (photo 16) (slide 12).
- Where prices go: "structurally rising but volatile"; the correction "may overshoot below trend" before demand pulls prices back up. The slide's line is the average of EU WPC80 and WPI (Vesper, monthly to October 2026, lightly smoothed), and it says the trend and forward path are "directional, not a forecast" (photo 19) (slide 13).
- He quoted Keynes, that markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent, so WPC80 and MPC85 touching does not mean they part at once, "but it can't go on forever" [00:16].
- Nutrilution sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16]. Contact on the closing slide: alan@nutrilution.com (slide 14).

Making WPC80 leaves permeate and lactose, which are easy to sell; WPI makers must also sell a fatty protein stream, shown on the slide as whey cream (Procream or WFC) [00:16] (photo 6) (photo 7) (slide 5) (slide 6).

Global production: WPC80 334,000 t in 2020 and 360,000 t in 2025; WPI 80,494 t and 161,800 t (40,450 t clear, 121,350 t standard); total 414,494 t and 521,800 t, up 26% (4.7% a year). Clear WPI at 40,450 t is, he said, the top of the estimate range; standard WPI grew 8.6% a year, below the category [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 9) (slide 7) (slide 8).

Announced US capacity (McCully Consulting, approximate; WPC80 converted from million pounds): 24,400 t of WPC80 and 7,500 t of WPI in 2026, 41,600 t and 20,300 t in 2027, 45,900 t and 22,900 t in 2028; each block on the chart is one company. UK, EU and Oceania: FrieslandCampina (WPI), Fonterra (speciality) and Polmlek (WPC, WPI) in 2026; Tirlán (WPC, WPI, clear) and Liprovit (WPI) in 2027; Arla's mozzarella plant in 2028. He said the European list is incomplete [00:16] (photo 11) (slide 9).

The buying cycle, using COVID as the example: longer lead times, more stock, rising demand, buyers competing, rising prices and an incentive to buy early; then the reverse, with the 2022 peak as logistics freed up and buyers destocked, and the 2023 trough as buyers waited with stocks too low [00:16] (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15) (slide 10) (slide 11).

Now: new US plants planned three or four years ago are commissioning; isolate, WPC35 and sweet whey powder are better uses of whey, so WPC80 output should fall; substitutes (MPC85, MPI, caseins, plant proteins) are rising, and WPC80 and milk protein "should never meet" [00:16].

Weekly Vesper prices, 25 August to 4 November 2026: WPC80 €27.00 to €16.00; WPI €32.00 to €25.50; MPC85 €13.92 to €15.80. On 4 November WPC80 was still €0.20 above MPC85 (photo 16) (photo 18) (slide 12). Read from the chart, WPC80 held about €27 for two weeks, then fell every week, to about €19 by 14 October; MPC85 was about €16 from 7 October (slide 12).

Forces for the next move. WPC80, up: strong other derivatives, rising alternatives, long-term protein demand; down: high inventories, powerful momentum, demand destruction. WPI, up: smaller share of brand costs, healthy inventories on both sides, harder to replace; down: demand destruction, production increases due (photo 16) (slide 12).

Where prices go: "structurally rising but volatile"; the correction "may overshoot below trend" before demand pulls prices back up. The slide's line is the average of EU WPC80 and WPI (Vesper, monthly to October 2026, lightly smoothed), and it says the trend and forward path are "directional, not a forecast" (photo 19) (slide 13).
He quoted Keynes, that markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent, so WPC80 and MPC85 touching does not mean they part at once, "but it can't go on forever" [00:16].

Nutrilution sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16]. Contact on the closing slide: alan@nutrilution.com (slide 14).

summary.Summary:
Nikki Hancocks of NutraIngredients chaired a panel on how brands build communities online while regulators watch. She opened with a report of more than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers, with supplements the most frequent subject.

The panel agreed that social content works when it educates or entertains rather than sells. Sinead Gibbons said almost none of Tonic Health's content is about its products; its supermarket swap videos have built 1.9 million followers. Julian Harvie said AG1 learned that talking about its trials and testing did not land, so it keeps the science further down the funnel and practises restraint; Clearcast rejected three versions of its TV advert's opening line. Dan Richardson, a nutritionist in professional sport, said athletes want the headline backed by research, that brands slip by using buzzwords whose meaning differs from the research, and that athletes are the most impressionable audience of all.

Luca Bucchini, speaking for ESSNA, set out the rules and the failures he sees most: undisclosed ads, and marketing strategies built around non-compliance. Brands carry most of the responsibility for what their influencers claim. On AI, Julian's rule is that every idea begins and ends with a human; Luca expects regulators to act as people take nutrition advice from AI.
summary.Key takeaways:
- More than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers were counted in a recent report, with supplements the most frequent subject [00:01].
- Tonic runs itself as "a media business that happens to sell vitamins": 99% of its content is not about its products, and it has 1.9 million followers and about 70 million views a month [01:00], [03:24].
- AG1 found that talking about trials and third-party testing did not land: "people didn't care". Too much evidence fails at the top of the funnel; the science sits mid-funnel [04:17], [18:30].
- Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version of you" and "a slightly better version of you" before approving "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" Julian's lesson: "creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication" [18:30].
- Brands bear most responsibility for their influencers' health claims in most jurisdictions; the answer is training, contracts and briefing [28:27].
- Athletes are "probably the most impressionable group": they believe a claim of "up to 10% better performance" applies to them personally [32:33].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Our customers' marketing teams are under claims pressure from the ASA, Clearcast and the claims regulation, and the panel's answer was education that does not sell: "what is creatine, how does it work" is exactly what AG1 makes with its experts [22:46].
- My reading: a branded ingredient earns its place by giving brands substantiated, claim-safe education they can publish, in the headline-plus-evidence form Dan described, not by giving them stronger claims [06:30].
- For CreaWin, Dan's food-first framing and his athlete stories show creatine is already a mainstay for athletes and nutritionists [24:22], [32:33]. My reading: our creatine content should be calm and educational, and wording we supply to brands must survive an ASA review.
- Brands carry the liability for what influencers say [28:27]. My reading: they will want suppliers' claims referenced and hedged exactly.
- Relevance medium: marketing and regulation, adjacent to our ingredients.
summary.Quotes:
- "...99% of our content is not about our product, which a lot of people on our board and you know investors constantly question every day." Speaker 2 (Sinead Gibbons) [03:24]
- "...we talk a lot about restraint being its own version of power in our space, where so many businesses oversell and underdeliver, and we we actively pursue the opposite dynamic." Speaker 3 (Julian Harvie) [18:30]
- "The first is that it's not when a brand occasionally oversteps, but where there is a marketing strategy, it builds around non-compliance." Luca Buccini (ESSNA) [11:59]
- "I think athletes probably one of the most impressionable audiences because it's all about a competitive edge and advantage." Speaker 4 (Dan Richardson) [32:33]

- Find the NutraIngredients report on the more than 1,000 misleading influencer posts [00:01].
- Luca Bucchini (ESSNA): the upcoming digital act he named (Otter: "Digital Finance Act"), and ESSNA's position on influencer responsibility [09:45], [28:27].
- Dan Richardson (DRN Nutrition Group) works across professional sport and academies and is food first on creatine; a possible contact on how clubs see creatine and collagen [24:22], [32:33].
- Tonic Health's AI compliance review and AG1's "Dropping Hours" series as examples of compliant education content [14:35], [04:17].
summary.Detail:
- Tonic's flagship content is the "Unsponsored Truth": its founder gives simple supermarket swaps. Clips are 20 to 30 seconds, three posts a day; people come to social "to be educated or to be entertained" [01:00], [03:24].
- Tonic posts 900 pieces of content a month across four channels with one 22-year-old social media manager and a freelance editor. After the ASA pulled up a profile cover for its magnesium drink ("...she wrote on the social cover the best sleep supplement in the market, and now we don't have that claim"), every piece now goes through an AI compliance agent [14:35].
- Tonic never deletes a challenged post: it changes the caption, answers the comments, sends voice notes and makes response videos, because "trust is really built in those small moments" [14:35].
- Julian: on social, people "come to be educated or entertained", and education must be hyper relevant to the person; "Too much evidence doesn't work." AG1's US campaign "WTF is NSF" and its "Dropping Hours" series humanise the science without selling [04:17].
- AG1 cannot associate healthcare professionals, dietitians or doctors directly with the brand, so it uses them for pure education ("what is creatine? Like, how does it work?", "why is magnesium important?") and hopes the credibility transfers [22:46].
- Dan: athletes want the headline, backed by the research. The common slip is swapping dull research words for buzzwords whose connotations differ, often "genuine accidental misleading"; "what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area" [06:30], [08:33].
- Dan is food first: on a creatine company's podcast he said not everybody should take creatine until the baseline of nutrition is fixed, and the company objected [24:22].
- A 35-year-old EFL player with 200-plus appearances bought a supplement off TikTok Shop; athletes think they are the subject of the research papers [32:33].
- Luca's rules: the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules, and a new digital act whose text is not yet known (Otter: "Digital Finance Act") [09:45].
- Luca's recurring failures: undisclosed ads, no training or allocated responsibility with creators, strategies built around non-compliance, and following a non-compliant discourse [11:59].
- Provocation without a solution is fearmongering: Tonic will not post a call-out unless it gives the healthier swap [30:18].
- AI: Julian's hard rule is that "...the idea has to begin and end with a human being"; AI scales the middle, and he found human copy still better by some margin [35:43]. items.title: Fuelling female performance: Separating Science from Myth in Women's Sports Nutrition

summary.Summary:
Dr Emily Jevons, a registered nutritionist who specialises in sports nutrition, nutrition education and disordered eating, asked how much of women's sports nutrition is science and how much is myth.

She began with the evidence base. Only 6% of sport and exercise science publications study women alone. Even when women are included, their hormonal status is rarely verified properly. Women are not one population either: adolescents, contraceptive users, pregnant and postpartum women and women in menopause all differ, and the last groups are almost absent from research.

On the menstrual cycle she was clear. Most studies find no effect of cycle phase on performance; effects are small and individual variation is large. Popular advice to train hard early in the cycle and switch to pilates later is not backed by the evidence. Carbohydrate needs follow the training session, not the phase. Energy availability comes first; in theory, protein needs may rise in the luteal phase.

She then turned to the women's health aisle, where demand is outpacing evidence, and asked whether it is pink washing or progress. Her answer for industry: use ingredients with evidence for the outcome claimed, at trial doses, fully disclosed and batch-tested; claim honestly; design with women; and fund female-specific trials, publishing null results too.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The evidence gap: of 5,261 publications with 12,511,386 participants, 63% studied males and females, 31% males only and 6% females only (Cowley et al., 2021) (slide 4).
- Even when women are included, 14% of performance supplement studies defined menstrual status and about 0.5% verified it with best-practice methods; female participation rose from about 39% (2011-13) to about 44% (2021-23) (Smith et al., 2022; Ose et al., 2025) (slide 6).
- The cycle and performance: 13 of 16 studies found no effect on anaerobic performance and 14 of 22 none on aerobic performance; no influence of phase on strength or training adaptations, "BUT motivation could be impactful" (Carmichael et al., 2021; Colenso-Semple et al., 2023). A review found the evidence does not warrant general guidance on changing exercise across the cycle (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 15) (slide 16).
- Nutrition: carbohydrate targets are per kg of body mass and apply to both sexes, with no evidence for phase-specific targets; energy intake tends to rise about 170 kcal a day in the luteal phase. The primary focus is adequate energy intake and optimal energy availability (ISSN position stand, Sims et al., 2023) (slide 18) (slide 19).
- Protein: high-quality protein as close to the start and/or end of exercise as possible at 0.3-0.4 g/kg body weight, aiming for the upper end in the luteal phase "due to the catabolic actions of progesterone" (Sims et al., 2023) (slide 20).
- Building better products: include only ingredients with evidence for the outcome claimed, "e.g. creatine 3–5 g/day alongside strength training for midlife muscle and strength"; use trial doses, list every dose, batch-test for athletes (e.g. Informed Sport); use authorised claims; co-design with women and fund female-specific studies (slide 23).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: her one named example of an evidence-based ingredient for women was creatine, 3-5 g a day alongside strength training for midlife muscle and strength (slide 23). My reading: this is the CreaWin case for women in a nutritionist's own words, and it rests on trials, so our material should lead with trial doses and references.
- Women's creatine products are already on the shelf. Her slides show Zooki Creatine+ for Women (5 g creatine, "extra support for energy, cognition and hormonal balance") and Marchon Women's Formula (5 g creatine, 4 g myo-inositol, 8 g marine collagen), read from the pack shots, under "Cycle syncing, myth or evidence based?" and "Pink washing or progress?"; she gave no verdict on each product (slide 11) (slide 21). My reading: "hormonal balance" is the kind of claim she warns against (slide 23); a brand that wants her kind of approval needs trial-dose creatine and honest claims, which is where CreaWin should sit.
- Protein: 0.3-0.4 g/kg around exercise (slide 20). My reading: about 18-24 g a serving for a 60 kg woman, a dose a clear pea protein drink (IsoClr: Pea) can carry.
- Her industry list asks for female-specific trials with verified menstrual status, research on the product not just the ingredient, and published null results (slide 24). My reading: a CreaWin study in active women designed that way would answer her directly, and she asks for nutritionists to be involved "from day one" (slide 23).
- James Morton (SiS) said the same at 11:20: fuel for the work, not the menstrual cycle (fuelling-the-female-runner-from-paper). SiS is among the logos on her "Who am I?" slide (slide 2).
summary.Quotes:
- "Hormones treated as noise: the cycle was seen as a confounder to avoid rather than a variable to study." (slide 5)
- "Carbohydrate needs are driven by the training session, not the cycle phase." (slide 18)
- "Demand is outpacing evidence" (slide 22)
- "Women's products should be built on evidence, not trends." (slide 25)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm the end time, track, her organisation and role as billed, and the programme title.
- Talk to Emily Jevons (contact details on slides 1 and 26) about what a CreaWin study in active or midlife women should look like; she named creatine 3-5 g a day as her evidence-based example (slide 23).
- Find the papers: Cowley et al. 2021, Smith et al. 2022, Ose et al. 2025, McNulty et al. 2020, Carmichael et al. 2021, Colenso-Semple et al. 2023, the ISSN female athlete position stand (Sims et al. 2023) and the UCL 2026 review of menopause supplements.
- Find out who supplies the creatine in Zooki Creatine+ for Women and Marchon Women's Formula (slide 11) (slide 21).
summary.Detail:
- Why research leaned on men: the "70 kg male" became the reference participant; hormones were treated as noise; testing women properly means verifying phase with hormone measures across several phases; contraception variety makes uniform groups harder; product claims were built on male evidence, "This is where industry can now lead" (slide 5).
- Women aren't one population: adolescents; menstruating women with a natural cycle; women on hormonal contraception, which suppresses endogenous hormones and may be used to manage conditions such as endometriosis; pregnancy and postpartum, a one to two year period; peri- and menopause, diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months without menstruation. "Lots of individual variation across all phases" (slide 7). The hormone curves across the lifespan are marked "Illustrative – not to scale" (slide 8).
- About 50% of elite athletes use hormonal contraception (Martin et al. 2018); 77% of non-users report negative cycle symptoms, mostly on days 1-2 of bleeding; peri- and postmenopausal athletes are almost absent from research; adolescents, pregnancy and postpartum have even less data; findings in one group can't simply be applied to another (slide 9).
- She asked the room "Who is your target audience?" before the cycle-syncing section (slide 10). The cycle-syncing slide also shows an SiS Run Fuel gel and Fast and Female (slide 11).
- Physiology: the 28-day cycle is an average, not a rule; the follicular phase is the more variable; the luteal phase lasts about 12-15 days after ovulation; the LH surge is not exactly day 14; stress, sleep, body weight, training load and life context all affect the pattern (slide 12). "Every woman will experience the menstrual cycle differently" (slide 13).
- Proposed mechanisms. Muscle activation: in theory oestrogen raises excitability and progesterone "may lower strength outcomes in the luteal phase". Muscle and tendon stiffness: oestrogen may change collagen synthesis, but "Most research states this increase is not great enough to have an effect". Thermoregulation: a sufficient warm-up nulled any luteal advantage; higher body temperature could hurt endurance. Metabolism: trends disappear at higher intensities or when fed; exercise intensity and nutrition status appear "to be more influential than menstrual cycle phase" (slide 14).
- One study found peak power higher in the ovulatory phase, but motivation to train was also greatest then; intermittent endurance is more likely to be affected than continuous endurance (slide 15).
- What social media says (crossed out on the slide): train hard early, pilates and walking later. What the review says: performance "might be reduced by a small amount" in the early phase, with large personal differences (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 16). Her conclusion: a personalised approach based on each woman's response (slide 17).
- Resting metabolic rate may rise slightly in the luteal phase, but studies are inconsistent and mostly low quality; combined pill users do not show these fluctuations (slide 18).
- Protein: oestrogen is anabolic and progesterone catabolic, so in theory an athletic woman might need more protein in the luteal phase, but rising metabolic rate and appetite are already likely to raise her intake (slide 20).
- The women's health aisle: UK menopause supplements projected to grow from £42m (2020) to £100m by 2028 (GenM/Kantar); Holland & Barrett women's health sales up 22% year on year; a UCL 2026 review found half of UK menopause supplements had no vitamin D and only 24% contained calcium; "hormone balance" stacks (DIM, inositol, vitex, ashwagandha) are booming online (slide 22).
- Packs on the "Pink washing or progress?" slide, read from the pack shots: Wassen Prime Protect 50+ Women, Hairburst Womens 35+ Hair Vitamins (with added collagen), Viviscal, Swedish Collagen Collagen Deluxe (12,500 mg hydrolysed marine collagen), Novomins Women's Bio-Balance Gummies and Zooki Creatine+ for Women (slide 21).
- The four rules in full: Justify (no trending "oestrogen balance" ingredients without evidence in active women); Dose and Disclose (no proprietary blends at token doses, untested for banned substances); Claim honestly (no "balances your hormones" or "cycle-synced" without trials; say what isn't yet known); Co-design (not "a pink tub on the same formula") (slide 23).
- What industry can do: fund female-specific trials rather than adding women to male designs; verify menstrual status with best-practice methods, not day-counting; educate on who the product is for; research the product, not just the ingredient; publish null results (slide 24).
- Take-home messages: more high-quality research across the lifespan; cycle effects small, individual variation large, energy availability first; products built on evidence; industry can fund, design and report better research (slide 25).
- Her "Who am I?" slide carries logos including SiS, British Cycling, IRONMAN, Swim with Jazz, Feisty Women's Performance, fuel/HQ, David Lloyd Clubs, Fast and Female, Team Picnic PostNL and the University of Chester; it does not say what each relationship is (slide 2).

She asked the room "Who is your target audience?" before the cycle-syncing section (slide 10). The cycle-syncing slide also shows an SiS Run Fuel gel and Fast and Female (slide 11).

Physiology: the 28-day cycle is an average, not a rule; the follicular phase is the more variable; the luteal phase lasts about 12-15 days after ovulation; the LH surge is not exactly day 14; stress, sleep, body weight, training load and life context all affect the pattern (slide 12). "Every woman will experience the menstrual cycle differently" (slide 13).

Proposed mechanisms. Muscle activation: in theory oestrogen raises excitability and progesterone "may lower strength outcomes in the luteal phase". Muscle and tendon stiffness: oestrogen may change collagen synthesis, but "Most research states this increase is not great enough to have an effect". Thermoregulation: a sufficient warm-up nulled any luteal advantage; higher body temperature could hurt endurance. Metabolism: trends disappear at higher intensities or when fed; exercise intensity and nutrition status appear "to be more influential than menstrual cycle phase" (slide 14).
One study found peak power higher in the ovulatory phase, but motivation to train was also greatest then; intermittent endurance is more likely to be affected than continuous endurance (slide 15).

What social media says (crossed out on the slide): train hard early, pilates and walking later. What the review says: performance "might be reduced by a small amount" in the early phase, with large personal differences (McNulty et al., 2020) (slide 16). Her conclusion: a personalised approach based on each woman's response (slide 17).
Resting metabolic rate may rise slightly in the luteal phase, but studies are inconsistent and mostly low quality; combined pill users do not show these fluctuations (slide 18).

Protein: oestrogen is anabolic and progesterone catabolic, so in theory an athletic woman might need more protein in the luteal phase, but rising metabolic rate and appetite are already likely to raise her intake (slide 20).

The women's health aisle: UK menopause supplements projected to grow from £42m (2020) to £100m by 2028 (GenM/Kantar); Holland & Barrett women's health sales up 22% year on year; a UCL 2026 review found half of UK menopause supplements had no vitamin D and only 24% contained calcium; "hormone balance" stacks (DIM, inositol, vitex, ashwagandha) are booming online (slide 22).

Packs on the "Pink washing or progress?" slide, read from the pack shots: Wassen Prime Protect 50+ Women, Hairburst Womens 35+ Hair Vitamins (with added collagen), Viviscal, Swedish Collagen Collagen Deluxe (12,500 mg hydrolysed marine collagen), Novomins Women's Bio-Balance Gummies and Zooki Creatine+ for Women (slide 21).

The four rules in full: Justify (no trending "oestrogen balance" ingredients without evidence in active women); Dose and Disclose (no proprietary blends at token doses, untested for banned substances); Claim honestly (no "balances your hormones" or "cycle-synced" without trials; say what isn't yet known); Co-design (not "a pink tub on the same formula") (slide 23).

What industry can do: fund female-specific trials rather than adding women to male designs; verify menstrual status with best-practice methods, not day-counting; educate on who the product is for; research the product, not just the ingredient; publish null results (slide 24).

Take-home messages: more high-quality research across the lifespan; cycle effects small, individual variation large, energy availability first; products built on evidence; industry can fund, design and report better research (slide 25).

Her "Who am I?" slide carries logos including SiS, British Cycling, IRONMAN, Swim with Jazz, Feisty Women's Performance, fuel/HQ, David Lloyd Clubs, Fast and Female, Team Picnic PostNL and the University of Chester; it does not say what each relationship is (slide 2).

summary.Summary:
James Morton of Science in Sport asked whether women need to fuel differently from men when they run. His answer: the barrier is knowledge, not biology.

He started with glycogen. In a 2021 study of recreational runners, women began with less muscle glycogen than men but finished equally depleted. The gap came from dosing per kilogram of body weight: given the same absolute carbohydrate, women store about the same.

He then showed an England Athletics study of elite runners fed 60, 90 or 120 g of carbohydrate an hour over two hours near race pace. At 120 g the switch from carbohydrate to fat never came, in men or in women. Both sexes oxidised the extra carbohydrate equally well, and running economy improved by two to 3%. Women reported more gut symptoms, so tolerance may differ slightly, but oxidation does not.

From this he drew a framework that sets carbohydrate by intensity and duration, up to 120 g an hour for a marathon, and described SiS's partnership with Nike's After Dark Tour as an education programme rather than a product launch. His conclusion: female runners do not know the numbers and have lived with under-fuelling. Treat the female athlete as an athlete first, and fuel for the work, not the menstrual cycle.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished similarly depleted. The gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius, comes from dosing per kilogram, and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
- At 120 g of carbohydrate an hour, the crossover from carbohydrate to fat was completely prevented over two hours, in both sexes; at 60 g it came after about an hour [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Men and women oxidise carbohydrate taken during exercise at comparable rates, rising with dose (120 > 90 > 60 g); at 120 g some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took [00:00] (photo 7).
- Running economy improved by two to 3% at 120 g an hour, against the 4% Nike claimed for the Vaporfly; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00] (photo 9).
- Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; individual variation warrants personalised fuelling [00:00] (photo 9).
- The biggest barrier is educational, in a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent; he does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle [00:00] (photo 20).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Nothing in the talk touches our ingredients. No protein, creatine or pre-workout was mentioned from the stage; the only protein on a slide is 25 g (including 5 g collagen) in the two Run Recovery drinks of the Nike x SiS range, source not stated (photo 19).
- The value is customer insight. SiS builds its pitch on its own trials (England Athletics, Nike), published papers and a one-slide framework, and its chief science voice is openly sceptical of claims he sees on social media [00:00] (photo 12). My reading: a brand like this expects a supplier to bring trial data and a one-slide rule of thumb, not a benefit list; CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea material should meet that standard.
- Gut tolerance (more symptoms in women at high intakes, a runner skipping gels on an unhappy stomach) is adjacent to the digestibility story for a clear pea protein (photo 15) (my reading).
- The clear recovery drinks carry 25 g protein in a clear format for women runners, which is the format IsoClr: Pea is made for (photo 19) (my reading).
- Relevance low: carbohydrate fuelling, outside our range.
