- (photo 7) Peak oxidation of ingested carbohydrate rises with dose and is the same in men and women.

summary.Detail:
- The 2021 study (Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise): recreational runners with muscle biopsies before and after three sessions, on 6 g per kg carbohydrate on the day, a 10-mile run at lactate threshold, 8 x 800 m and 3 x 10 minutes [00:00].
- Given the same absolute carbohydrate, "there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage", even if women then take eight or nine grams per kilogram. His hedge: for a given relative intake women "may present with slightly less absolute glycogen" [00:00].
- The elite study: men with marathon bests about 2:20, women about 2:40. 8 g per kg carbohydrate on day one, a 2 g per kg breakfast on day two, then 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint (simulated race pace) and 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold. The 60 g an hour condition was maltodextrin only; 90 and 120 g were 1:1 maltodextrin and fructose [00:00] (photo 2). The male data is Ravikanti et al. (2025), Journal of Applied Physiology; the female data is under revision [00:00].
- Crossover: at 60 g an hour, after about 60 minutes (the slides show about 60 to 75 minutes in both sexes); 90 g shifted it right; 120 g prevented it for the full two hours. Men's carbohydrate oxidation on 120 g held at about 3.0 to 3.2 g a minute from 45 to 105 minutes [00:00] (photo 3) (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Exogenous oxidation (carbon-13): about 1 g a minute at 60 g an hour, close to 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g, and at 120 g "some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported in literature". Peak means read from the chart: men about 1.0, 1.5 and 1.8 g a minute at 60, 90 and 120 g; women about 1.0, 1.45 and 1.75; seven to eight participants a group [00:00] (photo 7).
- The conclusion slide: "Female trained runners can oxidise exogenous CHO at comparable rates to male runners. Furthermore, in both sexes, 120 g/h maintains whole body CHO oxidation, CHO dependency and reduces the oxygen cost of running (i.e. improves running economy) compared with traditional CHO guidelines of 60-90 g/h. However, individual variations in rates of exogenous CHO oxidation and gastrointestinal symptoms warrant CHO personalisation strategies." (photo 9)
- Women may differ slightly in their ability to tolerate carbohydrate at those intensities; there is "definitely not a difference" in their ability to digest and oxidise it [00:00].
- The fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].
- The framework in full (Morton et al. 2026, Journal of Nutrition) plots intensity (zones 1 to 5; moderate under 2 mmol/L, heavy 2 to 4, severe over 4) against duration: under an hour, 0 g, 0 to 30 g or 30 to 60 g single source for HIT (mouth rinse, drinks, gels); one to two hours, 30 to 60 g single source, 60 to 90 g single or dual source for soccer, 90 g dual source for a half marathon (drinks, gels, chews); two to three hours, 60 to 90 g single or dual, 90 to 120 g dual, 120 g dual source for a marathon (drinks, gels, chews, bars); beyond three hours cycling stages, beyond six ultra (photo 10) (photo 12).
- The barriers: female marathoners "do not know the numbers" (psychological capability; participant 18 took her first gel at 7 or 8 miles and went by what others do), and tolerating carbohydrate in a race can be a barrier (physical capability; participant 13 aimed for about 80 g an hour, felt her stomach "was not happy" in the heat and skipped her last two gels). Like men, female runners need to practise fuelling in training (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Nike's After Dark Tour runs women's night races in seven cities. SiS partnered on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00]. The Sydney 21K race pack sells at $40.00 ("Fuel your night"): eight packs of Run Fuel Endurance energy gels (3 x 60 ml), Run Hydro+ electrolyte powder (4.3 g), a Run Fuel Endurance energy chew (50 g) and Run Recovery Endurance powder (73 g) (photo 17) (photo 18).
- The Nike x SiS After Dark range, "designed for her", laid out for 10K and half marathon: Run Fuel Isotonic gel (22 g single-source carbohydrate; before and during), Run Fuel Endurance gel (40 g dual source; during), Run Fuel Endurance chew (40 g dual source, 1:0.8 glucose to fructose; before and during), Run Hydro+ sugar-free electrolytes (350 mg sodium; before, during and after), Run Recovery (25 g single-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) and Run Recovery Endurance (40 g dual-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) (photo 19).
- The closing slide: "The biggest barrier to fuelling the female runner is not likely a biological limitation i.e. their gut or their muscles. Rather, it is lack of knowledge and awareness of the guidelines (i.e. educational) and the associated physiological and performance benefits, especially when considering a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent. Fuelling is less about hormones and tailoring to the menstrual cycle, put simply, it is about fuelling for the work required." (photo 20) From the stage he added that he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling at all, and treats a female athlete as an athlete first [00:00].
- Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]. Women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure: "I'd rather be in the approximately right count than the precisely wrong count." [23:48] Dual source is needed at 90 and 120 g, above about 90 minutes, but not below, and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].

items.title: Whey & Collagen: The Protein Power Couple

speakers.name: Tess Plaquet
speakers.role: Technical sport manager (as she introduced herself)

items.to_check: Sponsored slot (Rousselot by Darling Ingredients logo on the programme). Otter produced no summary and labelled the speaker "Speaker unknown"; the recording ends mid-sentence in her closing invitation to the roundtables, so any Q&A is missing; which market the US dollar WPC80 price on slide 3 is for.

summary.Summary:
Tess Plaquet, technical sport manager at Rousselot, argued that brands should stop asking when whey prices will fall and work around them by blending whey with collagen.

She began with the market. Whey launches keep growing, and she said the forces behind whey prices, from GLP-1 users and China to whey being a cheese by-product and rising energy and labour costs, mean high prices are here to stay. Brands can raise prices, shrink packs or reformulate; she called smarter formulation with protein blends the most elegant answer. Launches combining whey and collagen are growing at 17.44% a year, and collagen comes from four animal sources with far steadier prices.

She then made the case that the two proteins complement rather than compete: whey builds and repairs muscle, while Rousselot's Peptan collagen peptides support tendons, joints and bone. Her evidence was Rousselot's own studies. The central one gave 22 men either 45 g of whey or 25 g of whey plus 20 g of Peptan for three weeks of training, and recovery and performance were similar in both groups. Studies of Peptan on its own reported less muscle soreness, fewer blood endotoxins after a run, better knee comfort and better sleep.

The recording ends as she invites the room to Rousselot's roundtables.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Brands have three responses to whey costs: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and a way to stand out on shelf [00:10] (slide 5).
- Launches combining whey and collagen grew at 17.44% a year from 2023 to 2026 to date, led by snacks, cereals and energy bars (39.7%) and nutritional and meal replacement drinks (36.4%); her example, Optimum Nutrition's clear whey isolate with collagen, has 10 g of each [00:10] (slide 6).
- Collagen supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish, and its historical prices fluctuate far less than whey's [00:10].
- Whey and collagen are "no competitors": whey for muscle, Peptan (rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline) for ligaments, tendons, joints and bone [00:10] (slide 8).
- In 22 men over three weeks of training, 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan a day gave the same recovery and performance as 45 g whey; the slide says such blends "may provide broader support across the musculoskeletal system" [00:10] (slide 9).
- 2 × 10 g Peptan a day with vitamin C, for a week before 150 drop jumps and two days after, gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo; the slide marks the soreness result as a likely benefit and the recovery result as significant [00:10] (slide 10).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Rousselot sells into the same brand problem we do, with a different answer: replace part of the whey with collagen, backed by a head-to-head showing no loss of recovery or performance at 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan [00:10]. My reading: IsoClr: Pea competes for the same "smarter formulation" slot in a brand's protein review, and our pitch should match hers in form: the supply argument first, then evidence that a blend performs.
- We have no head-to-head of this kind for pea; that is the gap (my reading).
- Her collagen supply story (four animal sources, little volatility) is the kind of supply-security argument a plant protein can make more strongly (my reading).
- Nick Morgan named whey plus collagen clear drinks earlier; a clear pea plus collagen format is a possible combination rather than a competition (my reading).
- The health claims here come from Rousselot's own studies, with her hedges; none are ours. Relevance high: protein blends and whey pricing.
summary.Quotes:
- "So people should no longer ask when will whey prices go down, but what can we do to work around this?" Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
- "...there are more and more launches of products combining whey and collagen, so steady increase over the last couple of years, and yeah, actually an average growth rate of 17.5 percent almost." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
- "...these two are no competitors; these two already complementary, and when you add in both, you can have extra additional health benefits." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
- "So actually, the athletes, the recovery was the same, the performance was the same, but you also have more support in your movement system..." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Find the papers the deck cites: Robberechts et al. 2023 (IJSNEM), Clifford et al. 2019, Taylor et al. 2022, Jiang et al. 2014 and Thomas et al. 2023. Slide 10 gives Clifford et al. the DOI that slide 8 gives Aussieker et al. 2025, so check which paper the soreness figures come from (slide 8) (slide 10).
- Ask Rousselot which market the WPC80 price on slide 3 is for (slide 3).
- Question for us: what head-to-head data would show a pea isolate replacing part of the whey without loss of performance? (my reading).
summary.Detail:
- Her deck arrived after the talk (files/rousselot-whey-collagen-deck.pdf, 23 pages). Slides 17 to 23 come after the closing "Thank you" slide and are not in the recording (see the last bullet).
- Whey launches: food and beverage supplement launches featuring whey grew 7.53% a year from 2023 to 2025 (she said seven and a half percent), from about 18,600 in 2023 to about 19,800 in 2024 and 21,600 in 2025, read from the chart [00:10] (slide 3).
- The "8.7" she gave as the biggest growth yet is, on the slide, the 2024 to 2025 rise of +8.73% in the average price of those launches: US$3.17 per 100 g in 2023, US$3.32 in 2024, US$3.61 in 2025 and US$3.78 in 2026 to date [00:10] (slide 3).
- WPC80 price: she said "in 2023 the price of a ton of whey protein concentrate of 80% was 5.7 k, whereas in 2026 it's almost 32 k. So really, in just three years' time, it's almost a sixfold" [00:10]. summary.Summary:
Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients talked with Ollie Marchon, founder of the UK brand Marchon, and Liam Holmes, its head of product, about what the rise of the everyday athlete means for sports nutrition.

Ollie described three kinds of consumer: those inspired by training, who want habits and to feel better; those driven by it, who measure progress and time their nutrients; and those who live by it, planning the whole day around training. Most people on Marchon's training app train at 6 in the morning, which changes what they need. Liam argued for situational formats, such as carbohydrate in a pre-workout for people who cannot eat first.

Ollie said awareness of supplements is high but understanding lags, so education, honest positioning and effective doses matter more than hype. Creatine shows how this works: decades of research and podcast voices did the selling, and it built the daily supplement habit. Liam sees creatine as here to stay and moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers, the challenge is stability in water, gummies and other formats. Claims are a regulatory nightmare, so Marchon adds ingredients to products already in people's routines.

Asked where the category goes in five years, Liam answered: formats that improve compliance.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Three segments of everyday athlete: "inspired by" (habits, feeling better, food first), "driven by" (measured progress, nutrient timing around training) and "live by" (optimisers who plan the whole 24 hours around training) [00:54].
- Most of their 8,000 daily training-app users train at 6:00 in the morning, so Marchon put carbohydrate into a pre-workout for people who will not eat toast or porridge first [00:54], [04:00].
- Awareness is high but understanding lags: gym-goers talk confidently about products they saw in an ad without knowing why, so "education is really critical at this stage" [05:29].
- Liam: creatine is "here to stay" and the research is moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers the challenge is format, meaning stability in water, gummies and other formats [08:24].
- When Marchon surveyed its gym members, the number one struggle was still hitting their daily protein requirement [16:50].
- Five years out, Liam's bet is "formats that improve compliance": gummies, jellies, powders, RTDs, and convenience [22:11].

summary.Summary:
Mark Evans, a senior scientist at Holland & Barrett, asked whether polyphenols earn their place in sports nutrition. He began with a quiz. Protein, creatine and caffeine each have a known dose and timing. Polyphenols have general guidance too, but it leaves a question: milligrams of what?

Polyphenols are several thousand compounds, not one thing. The same figure on a label can mean a whole extract, a subclass or a single compound. They work less as antioxidants than as signals. Of the five ways they act, only raising blood flow through nitric oxide shows up consistently in people. Of the four best-studied sources, blackcurrant has the strongest evidence for performance and cherry for recovery.

His lesson came from outside polyphenols. Beetroot nitrate and a broccoli sprout extract built awareness by teaching a simple rule of use, not a mechanism. Brands are starting to name anthocyanins, and he asked whether consumers will learn the word.

His answer: for some polyphenols, yes. Cherry at over 1,000 mg a day for recovery and blackcurrant at about 300 mg before exercise are reasonably settled. The industry now has to standardise and declare what is in the product, fund better trials and communicate dose and timing.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The dose problem: guidance from fruit-polyphenol studies is about 300 mg 1 to 2 hours before exercise for performance and over 1,000 mg a day for at least 3 days around hard exercise for recovery, but the slide asks "mg of what?" (slide 3). A label figure can mean total polyphenols, a subclass or one compound; his three questions for any ingredient are which compound, how much and measured how (slide 5).
- Mechanism: blood levels are too low for polyphenols to act as direct antioxidants; they act as signals. Of five mechanisms, only increased blood flow (nitric oxide) is rated "consistent" in humans; the others are rated limited, mostly animal, inconsistent or mostly lab (slide 6).
- The big four: blackcurrant has the strongest evidence for performance and cherry for recovery; pomegranate (performance) and turmeric (recovery) are equivocal; 3 of the 4 share anthocyanins as a main polyphenol (slide 7).
- The lesson from nitrate and Nomio: make the dose and timing the message, and let credible users do the teaching. Beetroot nitrate became "one shot, 2–3 hours before and/or for 1 week prior to competition" (slide 11).
- A layered label: "Rich in polyphenols" on the front for awareness, "X mg anthocyanins per serving, standardised and batch tested" on the back for credibility (slide 12).
- His three asks of the industry: standardise and declare, fund the right trials (trained athletes, women, blood levels, real outcomes) and communicate dose and timing (slide 13).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: polyphenols are outside our range, but a Holland & Barrett scientist set out how he judges a sports ingredient: a declared, standardised dose, the right trials and a simple rule of use (slide 5) (slide 13). My reading: that is the bar CreaWin, IsoClr: Pea and Oxystorm will be held to at that retailer.
- Oxystorm: his model of success is dietary nitrate, sold as a standardised dose with a timing rule (slide 11), and the one polyphenol effect he rates consistent in humans is blood flow through nitric oxide (slide 6). My reading: lead Oxystorm, a nitrate-rich amaranth extract, with its nitrate dose and when to take it, not its mechanism.
- Stacking for pre-workout: blackcurrant's performance guidance is about 300 mg 1 to 2 hours before exercise (slide 13); nitrate's rule is 2 to 3 hours before (slide 11). My reading: an anthocyanin plus Oxystorm pre-workout fits one timing window, but no trial of the pair was shown.
- CreaWin and recovery: creatine is his example of an ingredient with a clear dose and timing, 3 to 5 g a day, daily and ongoing (slide 2). Cherry for recovery is over 1,000 mg a day for at least 3 days before and after hard exercise (slide 13). My reading: a daily recovery formula with CreaWin and tart cherry fits one routine; again, no combined evidence was shown.
summary.Quotes:
- "mg of what?" (slide 3)
- "Strong vascular, weak sport" (slide 8)
- "Neither led with mechanism. Both gave people a simple rule and a reason to trust it." (slide 11)
- "For some polyphenols, yes. Now the industry needs to prove it, and explain it." (slide 13)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Read Howatson and Clifford (2026), Experimental Physiology, doi:10.1113/EP093724, the review behind most of the deck, and Bowtell and Kelly (2019), Sports Medicine 49(Suppl 1):S3–S23.
- Ask Mark Evans what Holland & Barrett expects a supplier to declare for a standardised sports ingredient, and whether nitrate products are judged the same way.
- Ask for the final deck: the file has a placeholder for a second brand example on slide 12.
- Confirm whether Nathan attended and what was said in questions; only a 35-second clip was recorded.
summary.Detail:
- The quiz's reference doses: protein about 0.3 g/kg per meal (20 to 40 g) and about 1.6 g/kg a day for muscle gain, every 3 to 4 hours; creatine 3 to 5 g a day (or 20 g a day for 5 to 7 days to load), about 4 weeks to saturate muscle without loading; caffeine 3 to 6 mg/kg about 60 minutes before exercise (slide 2).
- Worked examples of the guidance: Montmorency cherry 600 mg twice daily for at least 3 days before and during recovery; pomegranate about 620 mg twice daily for 7 days before and after. Chronic dosing over 1 to 6 weeks showed no clear advantage over a single acute dose for performance. The source review (Bowtell and Kelly, 2019) appeared in a supplement sponsored by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (slide 3).
- The four classes: flavonoids (anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols, flavonols such as quercetin, flavanones; the best active-nutrition evidence), phenolic acids, stilbenes (resveratrol) and lignans. Curcuminoids from turmeric do not sit neatly in any class (slide 4).

items.title: Fuel the Frame: Carbohydrate, recovery and the forgotten tissue
items.to_check: Her role (the deck gives only "PhD, RD, FFSEM"); the organisation's exact name (the programme says Sports Ireland Institute, the deck only an instituteofsport.ie address; my reading, Sport Ireland Institute). summary.Summary:
Dr Sharon Madigan (PhD, RD, FFSEM) started from the slide everyone knows: 1 to 1.2 g of carbohydrate per kg per hour for rapid recovery in the first four hours after exercise. That is correct, she said, but nowhere near the whole story.

Her case is that carbohydrate is a signal, not just fuel. When it is available, the body treats it as safe to invest in bone, iron handling, hormones, immunity and sleep. When it is short, those are switched off to protect muscle output. A glycogen debt shows up as heavy legs the next day. The other costs build silently for weeks, until they appear as a bone stress injury, low ferritin or menstrual dysfunction.

Bone, the forgotten tissue, responds to every session in the same window used to fuel muscle. Carbohydrate during running blunts a marker of bone breakdown, and enough energy overall can still leave bone at risk if carbohydrate is low. Back-loading food into the evening, training low and cutting weight carry the same hidden costs, and low carbohydrate also amplifies the hormone that blocks iron absorption after exercise.

She closed on the limits. Most bone-marker studies are in men and measure hours or weeks, not fractures, and the dose and timing that protect bone are not yet defined.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Carbohydrate is "a Signal, Not Just a Substrate": its availability is "an electrical green light" telling the body it is metabolically safe to invest in bone remodelling, iron handling and endocrine function (slide 3) (slide 4).
- Quick against quiet costs: a glycogen deficit shows as a flat session and heavy legs, usually fixed within a day of good fuelling; bone, iron and hormones give no immediate signal, and by the time a bone stress injury, low ferritin or menstrual dysfunction appears the debt has been building for weeks (slide 5).
- Bone markers: carbohydrate during running significantly reduces the acute rise in the resorption marker CTX, and carbohydrate with protein after exercise alters bone turnover markers favourably; about 3.5 weeks of a ketogenic diet in race walkers raised resorption and suppressed formation, with incomplete recovery once carbohydrate was restored. The slide notes these are acute responses over hours, mostly in men (Sale et al., 2015) (slide 8).
- The hidden risk zone: short-term carbohydrate restriction suppresses bone formation more than low energy availability does, so energy intake alone will not flag bone risk and practitioners must screen for carbohydrate availability (Heikura et al., 2020; Fensham et al., 2022) (slide 10).
- Timing: even with an identical daily total, within-day energy deficiency is linked to unfavourable hormonal profiles in female and male athletes (Fahrenholtz et al., 2018); "Daily totals cannot save a back-loaded schedule" (slide 12) (slide 20).
- Iron: a hard endurance session triggers an IL-6 spike and hepcidin rises over 3-6 hours; low carbohydrate availability amplifies this, "functionally blocking iron absorption", so iron-rich meals and supplements should be timed around carbohydrate-restored windows (slide 13).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: none of our ingredients was named, but the recovery window she redefines includes carbohydrate with protein, which she shows altering bone turnover markers favourably after exercise (slide 8). My reading: a carbohydrate-plus-clear-protein recovery drink (IsoClr: Pea) has a bone and recovery story beyond muscle, but only as education; her own caveat is that the data are acute markers, mostly in men (slide 8) (slide 19).
- Women's needs: the quiet costs she names (bone stress injury, low ferritin, menstrual dysfunction) are female-athlete concerns, and she lists athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction among the absolute contraindications for low-carbohydrate protocols (slide 5) (slide 16). My reading: products for active women should not lean on low-carb positioning.
- Two speakers, two emphases. Emily Jevons put adequate energy intake first (ISSN position stand) (fuelling-female-performance); Madigan argues that adequate overall energy "is insufficient to protect the system" if carbohydrate availability is chronically restricted (slide 9). My reading: the views add up rather than conflict.
- James Morton's figures (up to 120 g of carbohydrate an hour) are for fuelling during exercise (fuelling-the-female-runner-from-paper); Madigan's 1-1.2 g/kg/h is for recovery after it (slide 2). Different windows, not different advice.
- Creatine and collagen were not mentioned.
summary.Quotes:
- "Most bone-marker studies are in men; menstrual status adds complexity." (slide 19)
- "We measure markers over hours and weeks, not fractures over years." (slide 19)
- "How much carbohydrate, and when, is needed to protect bone isn't yet defined." (slide 19)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm her role and the institute's exact name (slide 21 gives an instituteofsport.ie address).
- Find the papers: Sale et al. 2015 and the Townsend paper on slide 8, Heikura et al. 2020, Fensham et al. 2022, Lodge et al. 2023, Fahrenholtz et al. 2018.
- Open question: has anyone tested carbohydrate with a plant protein, rather than the protein in the slide 8 studies, on bone turnover markers after exercise, and in women?
summary.Detail:
- The deck's subtitle: "Clinical Insights on Carbohydrates as a Systemic Survival Signal" (slide 1). Every slide except 19 is an image; the text below is read from the slide images.
- The traditional view treats carbohydrate as "gas in the tank" to refill muscle glycogen when the next session is close (slide 2). Her paradigm shift: from substrate to signal ("Governor of systemic safety"); from muscle and liver to bone, endocrine, immune and iron handling; from flat sessions tomorrow to stress injuries and hormonal dysfunction next month; from daily totals to intra-day timing (slide 4).
- Glycogen: under 8 hours to the next session, start early and feed often, speed being the main variable; over 24 hours, total carbohydrate over the day matters more than precise timing. Glucose-fructose blends restore liver glycogen more effectively than glucose alone (Burke et al., 2011; Fuchs et al., 2019) (slide 6).
- "Bone responds to every single session": exercise shifts bone turnover in the hours afterwards, the same window used to fuel muscle (slide 7).
- On slide 8, β-CTX reflects existing bone being broken down and P1NP new bone being laid down; the footnote's second reference is cut off after "Townse" (slide 8).
- The blind spot: low energy availability is measured to prevent the Female Athlete Triad and RED-S, but low carbohydrate availability is a compounding variable. Read from the chart: the low-energy bar is mostly carbohydrate, the low-carb high-fat bar is tall with a thin carbohydrate layer; the bars carry no values (slide 9).
- Lodge et al. (2023) note that low carbohydrate availability "operates as an independent risk factor" within RED-S, overlapping on glycogen stores, bone health (stress injuries), menstrual function and immunity (slide 11).
- Within-day fuelling, read from the chart: targeted fuelling spreads intake across the day with short deficits; back-loaded fuelling eats little around training and catches up in the evening, with long, deep deficits. The curves are illustrative, without values (slide 12).
- The switchboard: when carbohydrate drops, power stays with heart, lungs and muscle output, and is cut to bone formation, iron handling, hormonal reproduction and immune defence; this also drives immune disturbance in heavy blocks and disrupts sleep onset and quality (slide 14).
- Her diagnostic matrix rates targeted fuelling optimal or protected on every line; back-loaded fuelling sub-optimal, with P1NP suppressed, β-CTX elevated and hormones and iron disrupted; train-low variable or compromised, with P1NP highly suppressed and β-CTX highly elevated (slide 15).
- Train low "heavily suppresses bone formation and increases injury risk without consistent performance benefits in elite racing"; repeated weight cuts mean repeated exposure to low carbohydrate availability over a season. Absolute contraindications for low-carbohydrate protocols: adolescent athletes, athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction, and athletes with a history of bone stress injuries (slide 16).
- Two more quiet costs: carbohydrate availability influences immune disturbance after prolonged heavy exercise (high risk in heavy blocks, major competitions and travel; Walsh, 2019), and evening carbohydrate influences sleep onset and quality (high risk with late training and evening competitions; Halson, 2014) (slide 17).
- Making weight: carbohydrate is cut before the weigh-in to reduce glycogen, water and gut content, followed by a panicked refeed limited by gut tolerance (slide 18).
- Where evidence runs thin: female athletes (mostly male bone-marker studies), adolescents (peak bone mass being built, little direct data), outcomes (markers, not fractures) and dose and timing (slide 19).
- Her four pillars: protect more than glycogen; fuel recovery early to avoid the within-day deficit; treat low carbohydrate availability as an independent bone-health risk even when calories look adequate; periodise with intent and keep adolescent, low-energy and previously injured athletes off train-low protocols (slide 20).

items.to_check: The name of the chair (Speaker 2); which countries make up the European sample of 352 (the deck says only "Europe"); what question slide 16 asked (it repeats slide 14's subtitle); the basis of the 11% by 2031 forecast, which is spoken only, not in the deck.

summary.Summary:
Morgan Griffiths, Commercial Lead at Lumina Intelligence, argued that GLP-1 drugs, bad news for many food and drink brands, are an opportunity for active nutrition.

He started with scale. In the UK, almost 27% of people, about 18.4 million, are taking, have taken or are considering a GLP-1. A summer survey found similar use in Italy, France, Germany and Spain.

He then described the users. They are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: most are women, Gen X or Millennial and better off. They are already health-minded and happy to pay more for quality. Most European users spend the same or more on food and drink, and most have increased their supplement use. Proteins lead their supplement list; creatine ranked higher than he expected.

He saw three openings: side effects, access to nutrition (protein, nutrients, muscle loss) and lapsed users. Users are confident of keeping the weight off, but a BMJ study he showed found weight returns almost four times faster after the drugs than after diet and exercise. Huel, Cambridge Nutrition's PortionIQ and Boots are already moving, and Lumina forecasts that UK use will keep growing to 2031.
summary.Key takeaways:
- In the UK, 6.1% currently use GLP-1s, 5.7% have used them and 15.1% are considering them: almost 27% of the population, c.18.4 million people (slide 8) [00:08].
- Current UK users are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: 56% female, 63% Gen X or Millennial, 63% ABC1 (slide 10), and 74% happy to pay more for quality against a 70% average (slide 11).
- Among European current users (n=352), 57% increased their supplement use, 88% including no change. Proteins lead at 51%; creatine is at 27%, above HMB at 15% (slide 13). He had said "near 60%" and "near 90%", and creatine was "maybe slightly higher" than expected [00:08].
- The most common challenges on the drugs: fear of weight regain 30%, side effects 29%, cost 29%, reduced food enjoyment 27%, maintaining nutrition 22%, muscle loss concerns 22% and difficulty consuming enough protein 19% (slide 14).
- 78% of users are confident of keeping the weight off (94% including neutral), yet the BMJ study on his slide found regain almost four times faster after stopping the drugs than after diet and physical activity changes (slide 15, read from the slide image).
- Putting GLP-1 on pack is "a kind of a health claim", so retailer support such as Boots' GLP-1 bays matters [00:08] (slide 17).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Proteins top European GLP-1 users' supplement list at 51%, and 27% take creatine (slide 13). My reading: a direct opening for IsoClr: Pea in low-volume, high-protein products, and for CreaWin.
- Muscle loss concerns (22%) and difficulty consuming enough protein (19%) sit in Lumina's "access to nutrition" group, and lapsed users are a group of their own (slide 14). My reading: muscle-retention products (protein plus creatine) for people coming off the drugs are a concept to put to customers.
- His benchmark set leads on protein: Huel lite at 25 g, PortionIQ at 20 g and 21 g, and a Myprotein clear protein in Boots' GLP-1 display (slide 17, read from the slide image). My reading: a clear protein already sits on the GLP-1 shelf, which fits IsoClr: Pea's clear format.
- He said brands are careful with GLP-1 wording on pack and lean on retailer support [00:08]. My reading: supplier support should be evidence on muscle and protein, not GLP-1 wording.
- The European data cover our customers' markets (slide 12) [00:08]. Relevance high: GLP-1 nutrition and market structure.
summary.Quotes:
- "I guess creatine maybe slightly higher than than you might have thought" Speaker 1 (Morgan Griffiths) [00:08]
- "GLP-1 is unique because your behavior changes, but you do not have to change your behavior." Speaker 1 (Morgan Griffiths) [00:08]
- "Our data forecasts in the UK alone, it's going to grow to around 11% by 2031." Speaker 1 (Morgan Griffiths) [00:08]
- "Will you spot the impact before your competitors?" (slide 18)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Morgan Griffiths (Commercial Lead, Lumina Intelligence) which countries make up the European sample of 352, what question slide 16 asked, and for the GLP-1 Navigator sample data (slide 12) (slide 16) (slide 19).
- Read the BMJ study behind the press release on weight regain (slide 15).
- Look at Huel lite, PortionIQ and Boots' GLP-1 display as the benchmark set, and at which proteins they use (slide 17).
summary.Detail:
- The deck is titled "GLP-Won", with the subtitle "The opportunities for the European nutrition & supplements industry" (slide 1).
- The context charts: UK population from 50.6 million in 1950 to 68.4 million (Macrotrends); UK adults living with obesity from 5.8% to 27.4% (WHO Global Health Observatory, BMI 30 or over); UK food, drink and catering spend from £54.5bn in 1985 to £328.5bn in 2025 (Defra) (slide 2) (slide 3) (slide 4). He spoke of a calories line [00:08]; the deck's second line is the obesity rate (slide 5).
- The US chart (Gallup National Health and Well-Being Index, published 28 October 2025) runs from 26.5 in 2009 to a peak of 39.9 in 2022 and 37.0 in 2025, with 2021 circled beside a Wegovy pen (slide 6) (slide 7, read from the chart). He called it US obesity prevalence and said semaglutide had "a pretty much kind of immediate impact" [00:08]. The slides do not label the measure.
- Sources: the UK figures come from Lumina's GLP-1 Navigator and GLP-1 Out of Home Tracking, 24 weeks ending 5 July 2026 (slide 8). The European figures come from Lumina's Global Longevity Study, Europe GLP-1 current users, n=352 (slide 12). The deck does not name the countries; he said the summer study covered Italy, France, Germany and Spain, with the US further ahead [00:08].
- The 18.4 million equals everyone born since 2000, the UK's Netflix subscribers, or the 12th largest country in Europe, larger than the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Greece, Portugal or Czechia (slide 8). The considering figure jumped "by about two thirds, a third to a half" when the pill was introduced [00:08].
- Current users (6.1%) outnumber vegans and vegetarians combined (5.7%), yet food and drink teams invest more in vegan innovation (slide 9) [00:08].

speakers.organisation: Centre for Nutraceuticals, University of Westminster
speakers.role: Director and Founder; Professor of Translational Physiology

summary.Summary:
Professor Gulrez Zariwala, founder and director of the Centre for Nutraceuticals at the University of Westminster, asked which supplements aimed at GLP-1 and appetite have science behind them.

He began with the biology. Gut hormones such as GLP-1 and PYY signal fullness, and ghrelin signals hunger. Earlier obesity drugs that acted on the brain carried psychiatric risks, which turned the field to gut hormones. GLP-1 drugs bring dramatic weight loss, but about 40% of the weight lost is lean body mass.

The boom in GLP-1 supplements, he said, has brought lawsuits, regulatory clampdowns and lower consumer confidence. He then went through the candidates. Proteins have an undisputed effect on GLP-1 release. Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have plausible mechanisms but modest effects and few human studies. His centre's own trials, both still unpublished, found that potato protein raised GLP-1 comparably to whey protein isolate, and that Phynova's mulberry leaf extract, Reducose, raised post-meal GLP-1 by 140% and cut appetite by 23% against placebo.

His conclusion: supplements may fill a gap for current or lapsed users, but none can match a drug, so expectations need managing. Products with strong scientific substantiation stand out, and GLP-1 use creates demand for micronutrients, protein, fibre and probiotics.
summary.Key takeaways:
- GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of "between five to 15%" [00:15]; his table gives 3.6% for liraglutide, 11.4% for semaglutide and 15.0% for tirzepatide (slide 17).
- Up to 50% of users have GI symptoms and about 40% of the weight reduction comes from lean body mass (slide 20). He said muscle loss "can lead to sarcopenia" [00:15]; his slide lists sarcopenia with "insufficient evidence" (slide 20, read from the slide image).
- Proteins have an "undisputed effect" on GLP-1 secretion; high-protein meals trigger GLP-1 and PYY, and the effect depends on the amino acid profile, such as leucine [00:15] (slide 23).
- Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have mechanisms but "mild to modest" effects and few human studies; berberine "does not directly bind to or activate GLP-1 receptors" [00:15] (slide 25) (slide 26).
- In his centre's APPETITE trial (12 participants; porridge alone, with potato protein or with whey protein), both proteins gave a comparable, significant increase in GLP-1 secretion (slide 28) (slide 30).
- In the SATISPHY trial of Reducose (40 participants), post-meal GLP-1 rose 140% and appetite fell 23% against placebo, with "a marked reduction in appetite as well as food noise"; both trials are unpublished, manuscripts in progress (slide 31) (slide 33).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- A plant protein matched whey protein isolate on GLP-1 in his trial; that was potato protein, not pea, and whey raised GIP more than potato did (slide 30). My reading: this opens a satiety angle for IsoClr: Pea, but only with our own data, and his centre runs exactly this protocol for industry partners [00:15].
- Lean mass is about 40% of the weight lost on the drugs (slide 20), and protein is the one supplement class he called validated on both satiety and muscle [00:15]. My reading: protein for GLP-1 users is a pitch with science behind it; CreaWin's place there would rest on its muscle evidence, which he did not discuss.
- His protein slide shows Applied Nutrition's "GLP1 Friendly" range, including Complete Protein and an Energy + Creatine product (slide 23, read from the slide image). My reading: a UK sports brand already pairs protein and creatine with GLP-1 positioning; worth a look as a customer.
- His warning on overclaiming (lawsuits, clampdowns, an FDA warning letter) fits EU claims rules [00:15] (slide 22). My reading: we should not let customers imply GLP-1 effects for our ingredients.
- Relevance high: GLP-1 nutrition and protein.

summary.Detail:
- He is Prof M. Gulrez Zariwala, Director and Founder of the Centre for Nutraceuticals and Professor of Translational Physiology at the University of Westminster (slide 1). The centre is at 115 New Cavendish Street, London (slide 29), on the fourth floor of the building by the BT Tower (Otter: "BD Tower") [00:15] (slide 2).
- The centre aims to bridge industry and academia and to be a source of trustworthy, scientifically validated information (slide 2). Its model runs from formulation through cell studies (Caco-2, MIN-6, SH-SY5Y) to clinical studies, including head-to-head comparisons (slide 4). Its counts: 6 funded projects, 2 products developed, 7 clinical trials, 6 pipeline contract or collaborative projects, 30+ publications, 25+ student placements (slide 7, read from the slide image).
- Partner logos include Phynova, Gencor, Avebe, Agropur, GNC, Nelsons, Pharmako, Axonova, Issa Group and several universities and governments (slide 6, read from the slide image). The deck does not say whose potato protein APPETITE used; Avebe makes potato protein (my reading).
- His papers on the research slide are mostly on iron, curcumin and nanocarriers, plus a mouth-rinse study in runners (slide 5, read from the slide image).
- Obesity: he put US incidence at 40% and parts of South America and Africa at 35 to 40% [00:15]; the map uses WHO 2022 data (slide 8). Obesity is a BMI of 30 or more (slide 9).
- Treatments: diet is the most desirable but often unsustainable; bariatric surgery gives durable loss of about 25% to 30%; drugs are long-term, often lifelong, and usually prescribed at a BMI of 27 or more (slide 10).
- Drug history: most obesity drugs were withdrawn; rimonabant ("rimonaban" in Otter) was withdrawn in Europe in 2009 for suicidal thoughts and depression (slide 11). In one year of trial data, psychiatric disorders affected 6.7% on 20 mg against 3.2% on placebo (slide 12, read from the slide image).
- Gut hormones: ghrelin signals hunger; GLP-1, PYY, oxyntomodulin, GIP and cholecystokinin signal fullness (slide 14). He said PYY is the more potent anorexigenic hormone, but GLP-1 drugs came first for commercial and clinical reasons [00:15]. GLP-1 is rapidly degraded by DPP-4 (slide 15).
- Exendin-4 came from Gila monster venom; exenatide (Byetta, Amylin) was its synthetic, injectable version (slide 16). Otter heard "BioTuff" and "Emilin". The chart notes GLP-1 drug sales of $22 billion in 2022 (slide 16, read from the chart).
- Consumerisation: online weight-loss services advertise "Less Strict Than NHS Criteria", a qualifying BMI from 25 and plans from £64 for the first month (slide 18, read from the slide image). He cited digital pharmacies, cosmetic pressures and lower costs [00:15].
- Sport: GLP-1 drugs found to reduce inflammation, micro-dosing to lose weight and enhance performance, and a WADA monitoring programme; he said they are not banned but on the watch list [00:15] (slide 19).
- His slide puts protein at about 50%, multivitamins about 50% and probiotics about 30% among supplements taken with or after the drugs, citing Lumina Intelligence (slide 19). Lumina's own deck in the 16:00 talk (glp-won-market-opportunities-for-the) gives proteins 51%, multivitamins 48% and probiotics 37%; the two differ on probiotics.
- Other side effects: nausea and vomiting, loss of facial fat pads and collagen breakdown [00:15], shown as "Ozempic face" (slide 20, read from the slide image).
- The boom: Expo West photos of a "GLP-1 Companion" supplement, Metabolaid's "GLP-1 Inducer", "GLP-1 friendly vegan chicken & waffles" and a "GLP-1 Boost" stand (slide 21, read from the slide image). He dated it to Expo West last year [00:15].
- Substantiation: press headlines "As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors and regulators raise flags" (20 October 2026) and "Unverified GLP-1-Related Claims Flood Food, Supplement Markets" (13 July 2026), and an FDA warning letter (Veronvy, 10 December 2024) (slide 22, read from the slide image). He spoke of "some high-profile lawsuits" [00:15]; the slide shows no lawsuit.
- Proteins: a 2015 study of high protein against high carbohydrate and high fat meals showed a significant post-meal rise in GLP-1 and PYY [00:15]. The slide's charts show both hormones highest after the protein meal (slide 23, read from the chart); its reference is incomplete.
- OEA is an agonist of PPAR-α and binds GPR-119 on L-cells. Formulated OEA, TRPTI™ (Otter: "tripty"), was "shown to enhance meal-stimulated total GLP-1 and GIP in a dose-dependent manner" (slide 24). On the chart, the 300 mg line rises above placebo after breakfast and before lunch, and the 150 mg line stays below zero (slide 24, read from the chart). Reference: doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2026.1879799.
- Berberine works mainly through AMPK; low oral bioavailability means high doses, such as 500 mg three times a day. Cinnamon has a mild effect through the gut's TRPA1 receptors ("trip A1" in Otter) (slide 25).
- Bitter compounds such as quercetin and berberine "may increase GLP-1 secretion" through bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs) in the gut (slide 26).
- His earlier paper: Tiekou Lorinczova et al. (2021), Nutrients 13(7), doi.org/10.3390/nu13072157, comparing whey, rice and potato protein isolates (slide 27). Its abstract, on the slide: nine healthy men, single-blind triple crossover; whey raised insulin more than potato at 30 minutes; no significant difference in average appetite; both plant proteins gave a lower insulin response and better glucose maintenance than whey (slide 27, read from the slide image). He called it "quite a complex quadruple crossover study" [00:15]; the abstract says triple crossover, so the two differ.
- APPETITE design: 12 participants; porridge alone or with potato or whey protein; overnight fast; blood samples, appetite and palatability scales; an ad libitum lunch; ethics ETH2223-1377 (slide 28). It recruited healthy men aged 18 to 50, paid £100 (slide 29, read from the slide image). He said the breakfasts were isocaloric and isovolumic, blood was drawn every 30 minutes, and it was an unfunded PhD project [00:15].
- APPETITE results: whey was above control at 120 and 180 minutes and potato at 180 minutes (p ≤ 0.05). On GIP, whey was above potato at 30 minutes (p ≤ 0.05) and at 60 and 120 minutes (p ≤ 0.01) (slide 30, read from the chart). He said whey raised GIP significantly at 60 minutes, the first nutraceutical with a similar trend to the dual drugs, "not to the same magnitude" [00:15]; the slide's GIP marks compare whey with potato, not with control.
- SATISPHY design: 40 participants (12 men, 28 women; mean age 31.2, BMI 24.6); placebo, mulberry leaf extract, and mulberry leaf extract with a citrus-fruit supplement; appetite scales to 180 minutes, blood from 15 to 180 minutes, and a food noise questionnaire 24 hours later; ethics ETH2526-0070 (slide 31) (slide 32, read from the slide image). He described the third arm as Reducose with two other compounds, from "one of the leading U.S. GLP-1 brands" [00:15]. Otter heard Reducose as "Redicools" and Phynova as "Finova".
- SATISPHY results: "MLE supplementation improves glycaemic response and significantly enhances post-meal GLP-1 secretion"; +140% and -23% against placebo (slide 33). The slide does not say which arm or time point. He said GLP-1 rose significantly at 180 minutes and food noise fell over 24 hours, "19 with one and 21 with the other" [00:15]; the deck gives no food noise figure.
- The study finished last month and was due to be submitted the following week; two follow-on studies are planned for 2027-28 if the partner supports them [00:15].
- Conclusions slide: "Nutraceutical approaches may provide safer alternatives for specific populations"; "No supplement product can provide the magnitude of response seen with GLP-1 drugs"; GLP-1 use creates demand for companion products (slide 34). Spoken, supplements "may fill a gap" for current or lapsed users [00:15].

Treatments: diet is the most desirable but often unsustainable; bariatric surgery gives durable loss of about 25% to 30%; drugs are long-term, often lifelong, and usually prescribed at a BMI of 27 or more (slide 10).

Drug history: most obesity drugs were withdrawn; rimonabant ("rimonaban" in Otter) was withdrawn in Europe in 2009 for suicidal thoughts and depression (slide 11). In one year of trial data, psychiatric disorders affected 6.7% on 20 mg against 3.2% on placebo (slide 12, read from the slide image).

Gut hormones: ghrelin signals hunger; GLP-1, PYY, oxyntomodulin, GIP and cholecystokinin signal fullness (slide 14). He said PYY is the more potent anorexigenic hormone, but GLP-1 drugs came first for commercial and clinical reasons [00:15]. GLP-1 is rapidly degraded by DPP-4 (slide 15).

Exendin-4 came from Gila monster venom; exenatide (Byetta, Amylin) was its synthetic, injectable version (slide 16). Otter heard "BioTuff" and "Emilin". The chart notes GLP-1 drug sales of $22 billion in 2022 (slide 16, read from the chart).

Consumerisation: online weight-loss services advertise "Less Strict Than NHS Criteria", a qualifying BMI from 25 and plans from £64 for the first month (slide 18, read from the slide image). He cited digital pharmacies, cosmetic pressures and lower costs [00:15].

Sport: GLP-1 drugs found to reduce inflammation, micro-dosing to lose weight and enhance performance, and a WADA monitoring programme; he said they are not banned but on the watch list [00:15] (slide 19).

His slide puts protein at about 50%, multivitamins about 50% and probiotics about 30% among supplements taken with or after the drugs, citing Lumina Intelligence (slide 19). Lumina's own deck in the 16:00 talk (glp-won-market-opportunities-for-the) gives proteins 51%, multivitamins 48% and probiotics 37%; the two differ on probiotics.
Other side effects: nausea and vomiting, loss of facial fat pads and collagen breakdown [00:15], shown as "Ozempic face" (slide 20, read from the slide image).

The boom: Expo West photos of a "GLP-1 Companion" supplement, Metabolaid's "GLP-1 Inducer", "GLP-1 friendly vegan chicken & waffles" and a "GLP-1 Boost" stand (slide 21, read from the slide image). He dated it to Expo West last year [00:15].

Substantiation: press headlines "As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors and regulators raise flags" (20 October 2026) and "Unverified GLP-1-Related Claims Flood Food, Supplement Markets" (13 July 2026), and an FDA warning letter (Veronvy, 10 December 2024) (slide 22, read from the slide image). He spoke of "some high-profile lawsuits" [00:15]; the slide shows no lawsuit.

Proteins: a 2015 study of high protein against high carbohydrate and high fat meals showed a significant post-meal rise in GLP-1 and PYY [00:15]. The slide's charts show both hormones highest after the protein meal (slide 23, read from the chart); its reference is incomplete.

OEA is an agonist of PPAR-α and binds GPR-119 on L-cells. Formulated OEA, TRPTI™ (Otter: "tripty"), was "shown to enhance meal-stimulated total GLP-1 and GIP in a dose-dependent manner" (slide 24). On the chart, the 300 mg line rises above placebo after breakfast and before lunch, and the 150 mg line stays below zero (slide 24, read from the chart). Reference: doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2026.1879799.

Berberine works mainly through AMPK; low oral bioavailability means high doses, such as 500 mg three times a day. Cinnamon has a mild effect through the gut's TRPA1 receptors ("trip A1" in Otter) (slide 25).
Bitter compounds such as quercetin and berberine "may increase GLP-1 secretion" through bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs) in the gut (slide 26).

His earlier paper: Tiekou Lorinczova et al. (2021), Nutrients 13(7), doi.org/10.3390/nu13072157, comparing whey, rice and potato protein isolates (slide 27). Its abstract, on the slide: nine healthy men, single-blind triple crossover; whey raised insulin more than potato at 30 minutes; no significant difference in average appetite; both plant proteins gave a lower insulin response and better glucose maintenance than whey (slide 27, read from the slide image). He called it "quite a complex quadruple crossover study" [00:15]; the abstract says triple crossover, so the two differ.

APPETITE design: 12 participants; porridge alone or with potato or whey protein; overnight fast; blood samples, appetite and palatability scales; an ad libitum lunch; ethics ETH2223-1377 (slide 28). It recruited healthy men aged 18 to 50, paid £100 (slide 29, read from the slide image). He said the breakfasts were isocaloric and isovolumic, blood was drawn every 30 minutes, and it was an unfunded PhD project [00:15].

APPETITE results: whey was above control at 120 and 180 minutes and potato at 180 minutes (p ≤ 0.05). On GIP, whey was above potato at 30 minutes (p ≤ 0.05) and at 60 and 120 minutes (p ≤ 0.01) (slide 30, read from the chart). He said whey raised GIP significantly at 60 minutes, the first nutraceutical with a similar trend to the dual drugs, "not to the same magnitude" [00:15]; the slide's GIP marks compare whey with potato, not with control.

SATISPHY design: 40 participants (12 men, 28 women; mean age 31.2, BMI 24.6); placebo, mulberry leaf extract, and mulberry leaf extract with a citrus-fruit supplement; appetite scales to 180 minutes, blood from 15 to 180 minutes, and a food noise questionnaire 24 hours later; ethics ETH2526-0070 (slide 31) (slide 32, read from the slide image). He described the third arm as Reducose with two other compounds, from "one of the leading U.S. GLP-1 brands" [00:15]. Otter heard Reducose as "Redicools" and Phynova as "Finova".

SATISPHY results: "MLE supplementation improves glycaemic response and significantly enhances post-meal GLP-1 secretion"; +140% and -23% against placebo (slide 33). The slide does not say which arm or time point. He said GLP-1 rose significantly at 180 minutes and food noise fell over 24 hours, "19 with one and 21 with the other" [00:15]; the deck gives no food noise figure.
The study finished last month and was due to be submitted the following week; two follow-on studies are planned for 2027-28 if the partner supports them [00:15].

Conclusions slide: "Nutraceutical approaches may provide safer alternatives for specific populations"; "No supplement product can provide the magnitude of response seen with GLP-1 drugs"; GLP-1 use creates demand for companion products (slide 34). Spoken, supplements "may fill a gap" for current or lapsed users [00:15].

No slide is marked Confidential. The title slide is marked "©University of Westminster 2026", and the two trial results are marked "Unpublished data – manuscript in progress" (slide 1) (slide 30) (slide 33).

summary.Summary:
The day's last panel asked what GLP-1 means for sports and active nutrition beyond the boom. It brought together Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated, Brett Hamer, product director at Myprotein, and Ed Tooley, a performance nutritionist.

They agreed that GLP-1 is speeding up trends that already existed rather than creating new ones, and that few brands put GLP-1 on pack: Myprotein sells need-state bundles, and retailer bays such as Boots' let brands be present without the wording. Brett said clear protein, and clear protein with collagen, is selling very well to this consumer, while plant protein has not taken off; Nick put that down to taste. Nick called creatine almost a tier one ingredient, now bought by women, older consumers and people managing their weight.

They differed in where they looked. Ed's concern was nutrition: people who simply eat less risk missing protein, carbohydrate and micronutrients, so he puts protein first. Brett and Nick looked at products: both would launch protein with fibre, and Nick named low-volume clear protein with fibre and products for people coming off the drugs as the gaps. For the next disruptor, Brett named people coming off the drugs, Ed education between on and off, and Nick AI.

The recording ends with the host's close of the day.

- Brett: clear protein is "performing extremely well" in retail, and clear protein plus collagen is "just a sweet spot for this this consumer", with retail launches coming [35:09], [43:51].

items.title: From Longevity to Peakspan: The Role of Krill Oil in Healthy Aging
ingredients: krill oil (Superba Krill, Superba2, Superba Boost)
items.to_check: The speaker (the deck names none; its file name carries the initials MJ; my reading, probably Matt, called "Max", who spoke on the fish oil shortage and "my presentation earlier" in the closing panel), the date and time, and whether Nathan saw the talk; slides only, no recording.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's upload, 23 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Aker BioMarine pitched its Superba Krill oil to Remedy's contract manufacturers as an ingredient for healthy ageing. Its frame is "Peakspan": not how long we live, or how long we avoid disease, but how long we stay close to our personal best. Consumers put it in plainer words: maintaining mobility, keeping physically active and keeping an active mind.

The deck opens on the market. Europe's longevity supplement market is put at $0.50 billion in 2025, rising to $1.23 billion by 2035. It then names seven areas that come under pressure with age, from muscle and joints to heart and skin, and gives trial evidence for krill oil in five of them.

The muscle evidence leads: in 102 adults over 65 taking 4 g a day for six months, strength rose against placebo. A weight-loss trial showed more of the weight lost coming from fat and less from muscle. Knee pain, triglycerides and skin follow.

It closes with three product concepts built on two of its ingredients, labelled as positioning directions, not approved claims, and a projection that fish oil supply falls short of demand from 2027.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The frame: lifespan is how long we live, healthspan how long we avoid disease, "Peakspan" how long we stay close to our personal best; consumers rank mobility, staying active and an active mind as the top three aspects of healthy ageing (Innova survey, 11 countries) (slide 4).
- Muscle: in a six-month randomised, double-blind trial of 102 adults aged 65+ on 4 g a day (University of Glasgow), knee extension strength rose 9%, grip strength 11% and muscle thickness 3.5% against placebo (slide 7).
- Weight loss: in a 12-week trial (52 randomised, 41 completed, BMI over 25, alternate-day fasting), both groups lost about 4.5 kg, but 96% of the weight lost was fat on krill oil against 73% on placebo; fat-free mass fell 0.2 kg against 1.2 kg (slide 9).
- Joints: knee pain fell 18% against 13% on placebo (p=0.04) in 235 adults aged 40 to 65 with mild-to-moderate knee osteoarthritis; the deck cites a TGA assessed-listed knee claim in Australia (slide 8).
- Supply: Aker's own projection has fish oil demand overtaking supply from about 2027, with a gap of 0.16 million tonnes by 2031 and aquaculture taking most of the demand (slide 13).
- The three concepts (Peak, Renew, Strength) run on two products, Superba2 and Superba Boost, and are "positioning directions, not approved on-pack claims" (slide 12).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: krill oil is outside our range, but it is pitched on strength in over-65s and on keeping muscle during weight loss, the same healthy-ageing muscle brief as CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea (slide 7) (slide 9).
- My reading: a stacking partner rather than a rival; its "Strength" concept (muscle and mobility) could sit beside creatine or protein in one routine (slide 12).
- My reading: the only EU-authorised claim the deck cites is for EPA and DHA and the heart (slide 10); the rest rests on trials, the same position our ingredients are in when pitched for healthy ageing.
- The fish oil projection matches the panel's warning that aquaculture is buying up supply and shelves will feel it by next summer (panel-evidence-regulation-ai). My reading: supply continuity is a selling point buyers are listening for now.
summary.Quotes:
- "How long we stay close to our personal best." (slide 4)
- "Maintaining strength matters only if people can keep moving" (slide 8)
- "Concepts are positioning directions, not approved on-pack claims." (slide 12)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm the speaker, the date and whether Nathan attended (the panel's Matt, "Max", is the likely speaker).
- Ask Aker BioMarine whether krill oil has been tested with creatine or protein, and for the papers behind slides 7 to 9.
- Ask for the source and update of the fish oil projection, and Aker's view of krill supply against it.
summary.Detail:
- Market (Future Market Insights 2025): EU longevity supplements $0.50 billion in 2025 to $1.23 billion in 2035, 9.4% a year, 146% in total; largest markets Germany, France, the UK and the Netherlands. The slide warns this definition is narrower than NBJ's US "Healthy Aging" category (slide 3).
- Other figures on the market slide: 60% of consumers in the UK, Germany, the US and China rate healthy ageing a top or very important priority (McKinsey 2025, n over 9,000); 22% of the world aged 60 or over by 2050 (WHO); "cellular health" claims up 135% across 32 countries in the first half of 2024 (Euromonitor) (slide 3).
- The seven areas: cellular health, muscle, joints, heart, metabolism, skin, and brain and eyes. Muscle: 3 to 5% of muscle mass is lost every decade from the 40s, and strength declines faster than mass; osteoarthritis and chronic pain are the main reasons adults over 55 stop being active (slide 5).
- Muscle trial: Alkhedhairi et al., Clinical Nutrition 2022. The grip gain is described as comparable to the difference across a 10-year age gap (65 against 55) (slide 7).
- Joints: Stonehouse et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition 2022; in the high-CRP subgroup knee pain fell 27% against 7% (p<0.001). A 12-week pilot in 40 adults over 60 with hip, knee or lower-back pain (Superba Boost, 4 g a day) showed improvement in 67% against 40%; the slide calls it a feasibility study, not powered for efficacy (Tamargo et al., 2026) (slide 8).
- Weight loss: Alblaji et al., Obesity 2025. Grip strength fell 0.2 kg against 0.9 kg, chair-rise performance improved against no change, and the omega-3 index rose from 5.5% to 8.2% against 5.5% to 5.3%; blood pressure, TNF-alpha and CRP also improved against placebo (slide 9).
- Heart: in 520 adults with severe hypertriglyceridaemia at 164 centres, 4 g a day for 26 weeks lowered triglycerides 33.5% against 20.8% on placebo, and 37.4% against 16.1% in those already on statins, without raising LDL (Mozaffarian et al., JAMA Network Open 2022); two meta-analyses cited (slide 10).
- Skin: Superba Boost at 1 g and 2 g improved hydration, barrier function and elasticity against placebo, dose-dependently (Handeland and Wakeman, Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology 2024) (slide 11).
- Fish oil model assumptions: aquaculture demand and supplement demand each growing 3% a year, pet food 4%, and a 5% shortfall in each El Niño dip (2023, 2026, 2029). The slide is marked "Confidential" by Aker (slide 13).
- Slide 2 is blank in the PDF, probably a video in the original.

summary.Summary:
Martina Pavlová, CEO of the Czech contract manufacturer FAVEA, asked how a nutraceutical business keeps its credibility and its clients' trust while AI speeds everything up. By expertise she means understanding, not the amount of information a company holds.

She opened with a test: which of two real enquiries to Favea, a year apart, was written with AI? Then she introduced Favea: two certified sites in the Czech Republic, 210 products in active manufacture, its own Combicaps capsule technology, and ready-to-go products from a heart-health capsule to chewable and sparkling probiotic tablets.

Back to the test. The human enquiry, from September 2025, spotted that zinc and iron in the sender's own formula could not be combined, admitted she had not known, and asked for a meeting. The AI-written one, from 2026, asked for a catalogue, prices at five pack sizes, minimum orders, samples, lead times and certificates, all at once. Her verdict: perfect form is not understanding.

Her answer: critical thinking filters the flood of information down to its essence. Without it, speed rises and understanding falls. Understanding starts with wanting to understand, then questioning the assumption and adapting; inertia is the enemy. At Favea that means validating enquiries, verifying sources and quality through expertise. Her tip for Monday: when a perfect email arrives, pick up the phone.

- Expertise is understanding, not the amount of information held; it lives where people and processes inside a company meet customers, change and credible sources outside it (slide 12) (slide 13).
- Information floods in from seminars, conferences and AI; critical thinking (verifying sources and context) filters it to the essence, and without the filter speed rises and understanding falls (slide 17).

items.title: The gym & beyond: Creatine’s new buyers … and what they want
items.to_check: The date, time and room (the deck gives none) and Nathan's role as billed; slides only, no recording, so questions from the floor are not captured.

summary.Summary:
Nathan Gray of Vita Actives told Remedy's contract manufacturers who is now buying creatine and what they want. Creatine launches grew 61.9% in the first eight months of 2026 against the same months of 2025, three times the average ingredient's growth over 2022 to 2025.

His four lessons came from launch data. First, creatine's benefits are moving beyond performance: hydration, brain and mood, energy and women-specific claims are rising, and launches in the supplements aisle outside sports nutrition are growing fastest. Second, combinations now grow faster than creatine on its own, with electrolytes, HMB, collagen, magnesium and citicoline as partners. Third, consumers want flavours and formats they enjoy: two in three launches were flavoured by 2025, and bars and chewables grow fastest. Fourth, new buyers expect proof of quality, and independent testing found that 18 of 88 creatine gummies failed their label claim.

Price follows the move. A kilogram of creatine sells at a retail median of €73 as plain powder and €275 in formats such as gummies.

He closed on CreaWin: a specification inside EFSA's residue limits, a certificate with every batch, stock in Europe, and concepts in fast-melt sticks, chewable tablets and fruit chews. His message: plain creatine is a commodity, and benefits, combinations, flavour and format are where the growth is.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Creatine launches rose 61.9% in January to August 2026 against January to August 2025; over 2022 to 2025 they grew +35.6% against +11.1% for the average ingredient (Innova Market Insights; Vita Actives analysis) (slide 2).
- Retail price per kg of creatine, medians: €73 plain unflavoured powder, €87 flavoured powder (1.19×), €222 combination powder (3.03×), €275 formats such as gummies (3.76×) (slide 2).
- Beyond performance: pack claims on creatine launches, 2025 to 2026, hydration +107.1%, health and wellness +78.2%, brain and mood +61.5%, energy and stamina +60.0%, women-specific +400.0% (base below 10); creatine launches in the supplements aisle outside sports nutrition +194.7%; the EU-authorised claim for strength with training in adults over 55 is rarely used on pack (slide 3).
- Combinations grew 134.0% in 2026 against 52.7% for creatine on its own; the fastest partners are electrolytes +101.2% (hydration), magnesium +138.9% (sleep and overnight recovery), collagen +80.0% (recovery, skin and joints), and HMB and citicoline from a base below 10 (slide 4).
- Flavoured launches rose from 38.4% to 66.6% of creatine launches from 2022 to 2025, yet 82% of products on the shelf are still a single unflavoured SKU; in 2026 bars grew +260.0%, chewables +250.0%, powder +62.4% and gummies +29.5% (slide 5).
- Quality: 18 of 88 creatine gummies failed their label claim in independent testing and 10 contained no creatine (ABENUTRI 2024); in the only published market survey, half of commercial creatine failed at least one EFSA limit (Moret et al., 2011) (slide 6) (slide 7).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: this is our own CreaWin pitch to CDMOs, and four other Remedy sessions echo or test it.
- Formats, echoed: Tantus showed a creatine chewable tablet developed with Solabia, 3 g of creatine with a hesperidin-based ingredient, "Chew it, don't shake it" (tantus-longevity-concepts), and Solabia said heat in gummies turns creatine into creatinine, so the tablet is cold-pressed (solabia-launches). That backs Lesson 3 and the low-moisture point (slide 5) (slide 8). My reading: their 3 g a tablet against our 1.5 g concept is worth checking.
- Combinations, echoed and tested: Solabia said briefs now ask for 3 to 5 g of creatine with 5 to 10 g of collagen and botanicals in one soluble format (solabia-launches), which matches Lesson 2 (slide 4); but Alex Glover of Holland & Barrett warned on the panel against "throwing the kitchen sink" (panel-evidence-regulation-ai). - Price, on another measure: Nick Morgan put creatine at a median €0.47 a serving in capsules and tablets and MitoQ's longevity creatine with citicoline at €1.60, 3.41 times as much (nick-morgan-longevity). items.title: Healthy Ageing Reimagined
items.to_check: The recording holds only the last six minutes; the slides (added 23 Nov 2026) give the billed title and the five parts. His role and the room are unconfirmed.

summary.Summary:
Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated talked through how longevity is sold, from his own database of products. The recording catches only his last six minutes; his slides give the whole talk in five parts.

Healthy ageing, healthspan and longevity are different things: function and wellbeing, years in good health, and years of life. Brands either try to alter the biology of ageing, optimise how people feel as they age, or fit longevity to one group such as ageing athletes or women through menopause. On the page they sell energy and vitality, not science: the hallmarks of ageing appear on only one product page in eleven.

Brands sell a system, not a product: Cellaro's three products for morning, evening and a monthly reset. And longevity is one of the most expensive categories per serving. Creatine sells at a median of €0.47 a serving in capsules and tablets, while MitoQ's longevity creatine sells at €1.60, more than three times as much.

He closed on where the category is going: new formats, longevity claims moving into hydration, and longevity told as a performance story through sports nutrition.
summary.Key takeaways:
- On 265 product pages assessed, energy and vitality is the most common message (83.8%), while the hallmarks of ageing are named on 9.1% and placed in lead copy on 4.2% (slide 5); spoken as about 300 products, 9% and 4% [00:00].
- Price: median price per serving in capsules and tablets is €0.47 for creatine (518 products) against €1.35 for longevity (194) and €1.36 for NAD (28), read from the chart (slide 7); spoken as "around about 50 cents" for creatine [00:00].

items.title: Nuritas: AI-discovered plant peptides and the PeptiStrong trials
items.to_check: Miguel's surname (Otter heard "Miguel Push"; the deck does not give it), the billed title (the deck is titled "AI-Discovered Plant Peptides: The Next Frontier in Longevity & Healthy Aging") and the room are unconfirmed.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Miguel, business developer, and Brian Keogh, chief scientific officer, presented Nuritas, a Dublin R&D company that uses its own AI platform to find bioactive plant peptides. The AI starts from a mechanism of action or a consumer need and returns candidate peptides for lab and animal testing.

Keogh then made the case for PeptiStrong, a fava bean (Vicia faba) protein hydrolysate. The speaker says its peptides build muscle through mTOR, protect it from breakdown and calm inflammation through NF-κB. In mice it cut the muscle lost when the hind legs were unloaded by 54.3%. Three published human trials followed. After immobilisation, strength came back to baseline against a milk protein control. After a damaging exercise bout, strength recovered faster and fatigue was lower than with placebo. In untrained men and women, strength rose faster, with more bone mineral content as an unexpected finding.

His conclusion was that PeptiStrong boosts protein rather than competing with it. His slides add cell data with leucine and HMB, and ask whether it can augment creatine.

Miguel closed on the commercial side. EU on-pack claims rest on protein claims, with brand callouts beside them. PeptiSleep, a sleep peptide, is next. Vivatis Pharma and Tantus are partners, with a prototype PeptiStrong tablet shown.
summary.Key takeaways:
- PeptiStrong is a Vicia faba (fava bean) protein hydrolysate; the speaker says it works three ways: building muscle (mTOR), protecting it from breakdown (ubiquitination) and calming inflammation (NF-κB) [03:56] (slide 8).
- Immobilisation trial (Weijzen et al. 2023, The Journal of Nutrition; men aged 18-35, 20 g a day): muscle size changed the same as with milk protein concentrate, which was the control, not a placebo. Leg press strength recovered to 103% of baseline against 68% with milk protein, and muscle protein synthesis in recovery was about four times higher (read from the chart) [03:56] (slide 10).
- Strength recovery trial (Kerr et al. 2023, Nutrients; men aged 30-45, 2.4 g a day for 17 days, muscle damage on day 14): peak torque was higher than placebo at 72 hours (p=0.025), with 36% less fatigue at 48 hours and 47% less at 72 hours (read from the chart) [03:56] (slide 11).
- Strength and endurance trial (Mohan et al., BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health; men and women aged 19-40, 2.4 g a day for 56 days): leg extension 1RM higher at day 28 and day 56, endurance higher at day 56, bone mineral content up ("a serendipitous finding"), and 51.85% against 14.29% on placebo rated their health above 95 [03:56] (slide 12).
- Nuritas positions PeptiStrong as a booster of protein and a partner for leucine, HMB and creatine: "we're not competing with protein". The leucine and HMB data are from muscle cells; the creatine case is in vitro data for each ingredient on its own [03:56] (slides 13, 14).
- EU claims are protein claims ("source of protein" needs at least 12% of energy from protein), with US structure and function claims and brand callouts beside them; Vivatis Pharma and Tantus show a prototype PeptiStrong tablet with Nuritas [13:50] (slides 15, 17).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Nuritas sells PeptiStrong as an add-on to protein and creatine, not a replacement [03:56], and gives a whole slide to "Can PeptiStrong augment the effects of creatine?" (slide 13). My reading: a stacking partner for CreaWin in a recovery formula, not a competitor. The combination itself is untested on the slides, so any joint pitch would rest on each ingredient's own evidence.
- A plant peptide beside a clear pea protein isolate is a coherent vegan story for IsoClr: Pea (my reading). The deck's EU claims are the generic protein claims, which IsoClr: Pea can carry too (slide 15).
- When a customer quotes the trials: the headline immobilisation strength result is against milk protein concentrate at 20 g a day, while the two later trials used 2.4 g a day against placebo (slides 10, 11, 12). The mouse slide compares against casein (slide 9).
- The last slide shows a wall of about 60 brand logos with no caption, sports names among them (C4, Applied Nutrition, Jacked Factory, Force Factor, Yamamoto Nutrition, Sponser, Nutrishop, Xendurance) (slide 18). My reading: probably brands that use Nuritas ingredients; the slide does not say. Sports brands open to a peptide add-on are CreaWin prospects.
- Relevance stays high. The deck confirms the muscle and protein focus, makes the creatine pairing explicit and names the Polish CDMOs formulating with Nuritas (Vivatis Pharma, Tantus) (slides 13, 17).
summary.Quotes:
- "So we're not competing with protein. We're boosting protein, and that protein can be augmented to your diet or come from your diet." Speaker 3 (Brian Keogh) [03:56]
- "Now our control here is not a true placebo. Our control is milk protein concentration. So if you will, the gold standard of of protein." Speaker 3 (Brian Keogh) [03:56]
- "...so in theory, we could add to the benefit of creatine. Creating increases ATP. If you can train harder, if you can put more energy into it, you might get more damage to your muscles. Peptidron can help with that." Speaker 3 (Brian Keogh) [03:56]
- "Creatine and PeptiStrong fuel muscle through different routes. Together, they cover more ground." (slide 13)
