- Confirm Miguel's surname (Otter: "Miguel Push"); the deck does not give it.
- Get the three papers on the slides (Weijzen et al. 2023; Kerr et al. 2023; Mohan et al.) and find the mouse unloading paper, which the deck does not reference.
- Ask Nuritas whether creatine and PeptiStrong have been tested together, in cells or in people; the slide shows each on its own.
- Ask which brands on the logo wall use PeptiStrong; the sports brands are CreaWin prospects.
- Who at Tantus and at Vivatis Pharma (Joanna, surname heard as "Snader") handles Nuritas, where the Peptide Bite prototype stands, and which other Polish CDMOs they are talking to.
- Try the PeptiSleep sample from the sampling bag.
summary.Detail:
- The deck is titled "AI-Discovered Plant Peptides: The Next Frontier in Longevity & Healthy Aging", "Nuritas Company Overview | Nutrafood Poland", Gdańsk, 22 October 2026. Nuritas marks its title slide and the PeptiSleep slide "Confidential" (slides 1, 16).
- Nuritas is an R&D company in Dublin; its own AI goes from a mechanism, consumer need or pathway to peptide candidates, then in vitro and in vivo [00:20]. The name is Nutrition + Veritas (slide 3).
- Discovery time differs between the two sources. Miguel said about two years on average from first hypothesis to result [00:20]; the slide headline says "What Once Took Decades Now Happens in Months" (slide 2).
- Target areas on the slide: sleep support, muscle strength and recovery, cognitive performance, and metabolic and overall wellness (slide 2). A peptide is defined as a chain of 2 to 50 amino acids (slide 4).
- The three things Miguel asked the audience to remember: artificial intelligence, a plant-based source, and the bioactivity of peptides [00:20].
- Potential effects listed: better glucose uptake, lower cortisol, more muscle protein synthesis, less inflammation [03:56] (slide 5).
- The 17% figure is worded differently. Keogh said that if we keep our muscles healthy "we get a 17% decrease in all-cause mortality" [03:56]; the slide says the 17% decrease is "associated with increasing muscle mass", citing "Sarcopenia: an emerging geriatric giant" (amjournal.co.uk) (slide 7).
- The same slide says muscle loss starts at age 30, skeletal muscle is up to 35% of body weight, and the usual sports actives (dairy protein, BCAAs, creatine, HMB) "typically target one pathway" (slide 7).
- Mouse hind-limb unloading (C57BL/6 mice, 650 mg/kg/day of PeptiStrong or casein for 18 days): the control lost 33.4% of soleus weight and PeptiStrong reduced that loss by 54.3%; the slide headline says "more effectively than milk protein" (slide 9). The recording has about 50% ("prevent rather 50% of that loss") [03:56]; the slide figure is exact. Circulating IL-6 was 60% lower than the control (read from the chart) (slide 9).
- Immobilisation trial design: supplement from day -2, leg immobilised to day 7, recovery to day 21, with a D2O tracer, muscle biopsies and 1RM tests (slide 10). Creatine kinase was higher with milk protein than PeptiStrong after recovery, p=0.045 (read from the chart) (slide 10).
- Reference: Weijzen, M.E., Holwerda, A.M., Jetten, G.H., Houben, L.H., Kerr, A., Davis, H., Keogh, B., Khaldi, N., Verdijk, L.B. and van Loon, L.J., 2023. "Vicia Faba peptide network supplementation does not differ from milk protein in modulating changes in muscle size during short-term immobilization and subsequent remobilization, but increases muscle protein synthesis rates during remobilization in healthy young men." The Journal of Nutrition (slide 10). The Netherlands group Otter heard as "Luke Van Noon" [03:56] is Luc J.C. van Loon's.
- The sexes differ between the two sources. Keogh said the first trial was in males only and every trial since includes men and women [03:56]; the slides show both the immobilisation trial and the strength recovery trial were in men (slides 10, 11).
- Strength recovery trial: Keogh said 14 days' supplementation before the damage, done in a Dublin sports clinic in a trained population [03:56]. The slide shows 17 days in all, with the muscle injury on day 14 and peak torque tested again two and three days later (slide 11). The chart marks gaps of 43% at 48 hours and 148% at 72 hours against placebo (read from the chart) (slide 11).
- In the same trial, myostatin rose after the damage with placebo but stayed near baseline with PeptiStrong, and irisin rose right after the damage then returned to normal (read from the chart) (slide 11). Reference: Kerr, Alish, et al. "Improved Strength Recovery and Reduced Fatigue with Suppressed Plasma Myostatin Following Supplementation of a Vicia faba Hydrolysate, in a Healthy Male Population." Nutrients 15.4 (2023): 986 (slide 11).
- Both later trials give the dose as "2.4g PeptiStrong or MCC daily"; the MCC arm is labelled placebo in the charts (read from the slide image) (slides 11, 12).
- Strength and endurance trial: Keogh said it was run with KGK, a CRO in Canada, in gym-familiar but untrained people on a supervised, progressive programme, with DEXA [03:56]. KGK is not named on the slide (slide 12). Reference: Mohan, Niamh Máire, Nora Khaldi, Brian Keogh and Andy Franklyn Miller, "Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the effect on human strength and endurance after resistance training and supplementation of Vicia faba protein hydrolysate compared with placebo", BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health (slide 12).
- In that trial, repetitions to exhaustion at 80% of 1RM rose by about 4.5 against about 2.3 on placebo at day 56 (read from the chart). FSTL-1 and fractalkine were higher and GDF-15 lower with PeptiStrong (read from the chart) (slide 12). Keogh linked the GDF-15 fall to the training load [03:56].
- IL-6 moved in opposite directions on two slides: lower than the control in mice (slide 9), and a higher fold change than placebo in the strength and endurance trial (read from the chart) (slide 12).
- The creatine slide: creatine monohydrate gives ATP through the phosphocreatine system; PeptiStrong increases muscle protein synthesis through mTOR, "Elevates OxPhos-produced ATP in vitro", acts independently of leucine signalling and "Reduces myostatin production post-exercise" (slide 13).
- Its ATP charts are in vitro and show each ingredient on its own: total ATP production rose from about 700 pmol/min untreated to about 1,000 with 2 mM creatine and about 950 with 50 µg/ml PeptiStrong (read from the chart) (slide 13). A "Combined product" column lists benefits such as "Improves max strength and power output", with no combination data on the slide (slide 13). Keogh argued the creatine case "in theory" [03:56].
- Leucine and HMB: Keogh said a dose of each that does nothing on its own, added to a dose of PeptiStrong that does nothing on its own, boosts the effect of both [03:56]. The slide shows this as mTOR signalling (phospho-S6) in young and aged muscle cells. It adds that leucine transporters SLC7A5 and SLC3A2 are "markedly reduced in aged muscle cells", and that blocking leucine transport suppresses leucine's effect while PeptiStrong's signalling is maintained (slide 14).
- Claims slide. EU: "PeptiStrong is a source of protein", "Protein contributes to a growth in muscle mass", "Protein contributes to the maintenance of muscle". US structure and function claims include "Increases muscle strength recovery rate after exercise" and "Clinically studied to combat muscular fatigue after exercise". Brand callouts include "Patented plant-based peptides" and "AI-discovered ingredient" (slide 15).
- The "clouds" the regulatory manager has been "creatively defining" [13:50] are most likely the slide's "Brand callouts" (my reading) (slide 15).
- Nuritas has a library of more than 9 million peptides [13:50]. The sleep peptide is PeptiSleep, "Natural Plant Peptides For Your Deepest Sleep Yet" (slide 16); Miguel called it non-hormonal, with a peripheral mechanism, formulated by Vivatis and handed out in the sampling bag [13:50]. The chair called it "Pepsi sleep" [16:11].
- Vivatis Pharma's "Day & Night Sticks": a Koncentra "Rise 'n Shine" stick (lemon, 4 g, "With caffeine alternative") and a PeptiSleep "Relax 'n dream" stick (berries, 4 g, "With Melatonin & plant-based peptides"), as written on the pack visuals (read from the slide image) (slide 17). The stick lists melatonin; Miguel's "no hormonal" was said of the peptide [13:50].
- The same slide shows "Peptide Bite", a prototype from Nuritas, Tantus and Vivatis Pharma: a daily tablet with PeptiStrong for "an active, healthy-ageing lifestyle", 20 tablets, one a day, marked "Concept visual · not for sale", with a QR code for samples (read from the slide image) (slide 17). Miguel said Nuritas is developing a product with Tantus and has been active in Poland for six months [13:50].
- The last slide names five Nuritas ingredients: PeptiStrong, PeptiYouth, PeptiSleep, PeptiProtect and PeptiPump. Its product display is an illustration with partly unreadable labels, including tubs labelled creatine and one "Creatine + Peptide" (read from the slide image) (slide 18).

The sexes differ between the two sources. Keogh said the first trial was in males only and every trial since includes men and women [03:56]; the slides show both the immobilisation trial and the strength recovery trial were in men (slides 10, 11).

Strength recovery trial: Keogh said 14 days' supplementation before the damage, done in a Dublin sports clinic in a trained population [03:56]. The slide shows 17 days in all, with the muscle injury on day 14 and peak torque tested again two and three days later (slide 11). The chart marks gaps of 43% at 48 hours and 148% at 72 hours against placebo (read from the chart) (slide 11).

In the same trial, myostatin rose after the damage with placebo but stayed near baseline with PeptiStrong, and irisin rose right after the damage then returned to normal (read from the chart) (slide 11). Reference: Kerr, Alish, et al. "Improved Strength Recovery and Reduced Fatigue with Suppressed Plasma Myostatin Following Supplementation of a Vicia faba Hydrolysate, in a Healthy Male Population." Nutrients 15.4 (2023): 986 (slide 11).
Both later trials give the dose as "2.4g PeptiStrong or MCC daily"; the MCC arm is labelled placebo in the charts (read from the slide image) (slides 11, 12).

Strength and endurance trial: Keogh said it was run with KGK, a CRO in Canada, in gym-familiar but untrained people on a supervised, progressive programme, with DEXA [03:56]. KGK is not named on the slide (slide 12). Reference: Mohan, Niamh Máire, Nora Khaldi, Brian Keogh and Andy Franklyn Miller, "Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the effect on human strength and endurance after resistance training and supplementation of Vicia faba protein hydrolysate compared with placebo", BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health (slide 12).

In that trial, repetitions to exhaustion at 80% of 1RM rose by about 4.5 against about 2.3 on placebo at day 56 (read from the chart). FSTL-1 and fractalkine were higher and GDF-15 lower with PeptiStrong (read from the chart) (slide 12). Keogh linked the GDF-15 fall to the training load [03:56].
IL-6 moved in opposite directions on two slides: lower than the control in mice (slide 9), and a higher fold change than placebo in the strength and endurance trial (read from the chart) (slide 12).

The creatine slide: creatine monohydrate gives ATP through the phosphocreatine system; PeptiStrong increases muscle protein synthesis through mTOR, "Elevates OxPhos-produced ATP in vitro", acts independently of leucine signalling and "Reduces myostatin production post-exercise" (slide 13).

Its ATP charts are in vitro and show each ingredient on its own: total ATP production rose from about 700 pmol/min untreated to about 1,000 with 2 mM creatine and about 950 with 50 µg/ml PeptiStrong (read from the chart) (slide 13). A "Combined product" column lists benefits such as "Improves max strength and power output", with no combination data on the slide (slide 13). Keogh argued the creatine case "in theory" [03:56].

Leucine and HMB: Keogh said a dose of each that does nothing on its own, added to a dose of PeptiStrong that does nothing on its own, boosts the effect of both [03:56]. The slide shows this as mTOR signalling (phospho-S6) in young and aged muscle cells. It adds that leucine transporters SLC7A5 and SLC3A2 are "markedly reduced in aged muscle cells", and that blocking leucine transport suppresses leucine's effect while PeptiStrong's signalling is maintained (slide 14).

Claims slide. EU: "PeptiStrong is a source of protein", "Protein contributes to a growth in muscle mass", "Protein contributes to the maintenance of muscle". US structure and function claims include "Increases muscle strength recovery rate after exercise" and "Clinically studied to combat muscular fatigue after exercise". Brand callouts include "Patented plant-based peptides" and "AI-discovered ingredient" (slide 15).
The "clouds" the regulatory manager has been "creatively defining" [13:50] are most likely the slide's "Brand callouts" (my reading) (slide 15).

Nuritas has a library of more than 9 million peptides [13:50]. The sleep peptide is PeptiSleep, "Natural Plant Peptides For Your Deepest Sleep Yet" (slide 16); Miguel called it non-hormonal, with a peripheral mechanism, formulated by Vivatis and handed out in the sampling bag [13:50]. The chair called it "Pepsi sleep" [16:11].

Vivatis Pharma's "Day & Night Sticks": a Koncentra "Rise 'n Shine" stick (lemon, 4 g, "With caffeine alternative") and a PeptiSleep "Relax 'n dream" stick (berries, 4 g, "With Melatonin & plant-based peptides"), as written on the pack visuals (read from the slide image) (slide 17). The stick lists melatonin; Miguel's "no hormonal" was said of the peptide [13:50].

The same slide shows "Peptide Bite", a prototype from Nuritas, Tantus and Vivatis Pharma: a daily tablet with PeptiStrong for "an active, healthy-ageing lifestyle", 20 tablets, one a day, marked "Concept visual · not for sale", with a QR code for samples (read from the slide image) (slide 17). Miguel said Nuritas is developing a product with Tantus and has been active in Poland for six months [13:50].

The last slide names five Nuritas ingredients: PeptiStrong, PeptiYouth, PeptiSleep, PeptiProtect and PeptiPump. Its product display is an illustration with partly unreadable labels, including tubs labelled creatine and one "Creatine + Peptide" (read from the slide image) (slide 18).

items.title: Kaneka: Ubiquinol, the active form of coenzyme Q10
items.to_check: Billed title, Oliver Romanow's role and the room are unconfirmed; the slides (added 23 Nov 2026) give neither.

summary.Summary:
Oliver Romanow of Kaneka presented Kaneka Ubiquinol, the reduced and active form of coenzyme Q10, which Kaneka makes in Japan by yeast fermentation. His question was why a brand should use ubiquinol rather than ordinary Q10.

His argument began with conversion. The enzymes that turn Q10 into ubiquinol decline with age, he said, so giving the active form directly gets round that. He showed blood levels after 28 days in which 90 mg of ubiquinol matched 300 mg of Q10, while higher Q10 doses added little. He then listed the benefits Kaneka claims, from heart and energy to fertility, cognition and menopause, which the deck says rest on more than 100 studies.

He closed on Kaneka as a supplier: 100 mg a day for most people and 300 mg to restore or boost energy and for fertility; a pure grade for softgels and gummies and a stabilised grade for tablets, bars, shots, sticks and gels; a long list of certifications; and a Belgian warehouse for short lead times in Europe.

The deck leans on sport more than the talk did. It sets out a loading protocol before marathons and triathlons, counts 16 energy and sports studies, and shows a partnership with Borussia Dortmund's women's team.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Ubiquinol is the reduced, active form of CoQ10. The speaker said the converting enzyme diaphorase is no longer available from about 30 [00:00]; the slide shows NQO1 activity falling 88% between 15 and 60 years (slide 2).
- Blood levels after 28 days, read from the chart: 90 mg of ubiquinol about 2.8 µg/ml against about 2.7 for 300 mg of oxidised CoQ10; 300 mg of ubiquinol about 7.3 against about 3.2 for 900 mg of CoQ10 (slide 9). Spoken as equivalent at 90 against 300 mg [00:00].
- Dose: 100 mg a day (to 200 mg for one month) to maintain energy levels; 300 mg to restore or boost energy and for fertility support (slide 11). Spoken, 300 mg is also for statin users and people under stress [00:00]; the slide names neither.
- Sport: "Ubiquinol loading", every day for seven days before events such as marathons and triathlons and five days after, sits under the 300 mg dose (slide 11). The Energy and Sports block counts 16 studies, on energy and fatigue, oxidative stress, inflammation and muscle recovery (slide 13).
- Formats: pure ubiquinol for softgels, liquid-filled hard capsules, gummies and beadlets; "ultra stabilized" ubiquinol for tablets, capsules, bars, shots, sticks, gels, gums and coffee or tea capsules (slide 12). Spoken as "a microencapsule form" [00:00].
- Claimed evidence base: 100+ studies, 80+ patents, 45+ years of research; heart health 23 studies, healthy ageing and cognition 23, fertility 18, energy and sports 16, women and beauty from within 4 (slide 13).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Ubiquinol is outside our range and this was a product pitch. The deck adds sport detail but names no creatine, protein or muscle-building claim, so relevance stays low.
- Kaneka is pitching ubiquinol into sports nutrition: a loading protocol for endurance events, muscle recovery among its sports study areas, running and cycling imagery, and a women's football partnership (slides 1, 11, 13, 16). My reading: it will sit beside creatine in energy and healthy-ageing active products, not against CreaWin; an energy stack with CreaWin is a possible pitch angle.
- Its stabilised grade targets the formats our sports customers use: bars, shots, sticks and gels (slide 12). My reading: a reminder that CDMOs want an ingredient grade matched to the dosage form.
- The MTick "Menopause Friendly" mark and the GenM partnership are how Kaneka signals women's-health suitability (slide 16). My reading: worth knowing if we pitch CreaWin to menopause or women's-health brands.
summary.Quotes:
- "You just have to eat 60 avocados or 3.5 kilograms of beef every day to get the daily doses of Ubiquinol." Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "...if you take 300 milligrams of Q10, you have equivalent ubiquinol in the blood level when taking 90 milligrams of ubiquinol." Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "Superiority of Ubiquinol: at lower dose, better accumulation (dose effect)" (slide 9)
- "We as Kanika say 100 milligram a day for normal person is good enough." Speaker 1 [00:00]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Oliver Romanow's role at Kaneka (the slides do not give it).
- Read Hosoe et al. 2007 and Ikematsu et al. 2006 to see how the two blood-level studies compare.
- Which of the 16 energy and sports studies cover muscle recovery or performance, at what dose; relevant to an energy stack with CreaWin.
- The source of the mitochondrial CoQ10 chart on slide 9, which the slide does not cite.
summary.Detail:
- He opened on Nick Morgan's product coding, which he said placed CoQ10 second among longevity ingredients [00:00].
- Conversion: Q10 is activated by DT-diaphorase (NQO1) and thioredoxin reductase, using NADPH (slide 2). NQO1 activity is 100% at 15 years, about 55% at 30 and about 12% at 60, read from the chart (Shih et al., 2007) (slide 2). The speaker said the enzyme is not available from maybe 30 [00:00]; the slide shows a decline, not an absence, so the two differ.
- Also on conversion: 30-50% of people have reduced capacity to convert Q10 due to genetic polymorphism (Kelsey et al., 1997); a high glycaemia level (fasting plasma glucose 5.6-6.9 mmol/L) reduces Q10 activation by 50% (Lim et al., 2006) (slide 2).
- Blood-level chart, all three pairs read from the chart: 90 mg ubiquinol about 2.8 against 300 mg CoQ10 about 2.7; 150 mg about 3.8 against 600 mg about 3.1; 300 mg about 7.3 against 900 mg about 3.2 µg/ml, plasma level after 28 days (slide 9). The ubiquinol bars cite Hosoe K. et al., 2007 and the CoQ10 bars Ikematsu H. et al., 2006 (slide 9). My reading: two studies set side by side, not one head-to-head trial.
- The speaker said the body cannot convert Q10 doses above 300 mg [00:00]; the chart shows CoQ10 plasma levels rising little from 300 to 900 mg (slide 9).
- In "mitochondrial and CoQ10 deficient subjects", mitochondrial total CoQ10 was about 95 ng/mg protein on placebo, about 85 on CoQ10 and about 225 on ubiquinol, read from the chart; the slide gives no source (slide 9).
- Antioxidant: the slide says ubiquinol exceeds vitamin E and C antioxidant activity, with a bar marked "+30%", in vitro (Cervellati et al., Helv. Chim. Acta, 2016) (slide 4). The speaker said it supports "the intake of vitamin C or vitamin E up to 30%" [00:00]; the two differ.
- "Triple action": a cofactor for cellular energy production, an antioxidant protecting mitochondria against reactive oxygen species, and a contributor to the biogenesis of mitochondria (slide 3).
- At the cellular level, Kaneka Ubiquinol increased SIRT-1 and PGC-1α ("the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis") mRNA against placebo, p<0.05 (Pérez-Sánchez et al., 2017) (slide 6). Read from the chart, on a broken axis: about +180 for SIRT-1 and about +700 for PGC-1α relative expression (slide 6).
- A slide on mitochondrial dysfunction lists conditions by organ, including skeletal muscle weakness, fatigue and myopathy (Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine); the slide says ubiquinol "helps to protect against mitochondrial dysfunction" (slide 7).
- Ageing: ubiquinol level at 80 against 20 years is 42.9% in the heart, 51.7% in the lungs, 65.3% in the kidneys and 83.0% in the liver; at 40 it is 68.2% in the heart, 72.6% in the kidneys and 93.5% in the liver (Kalén et al., Lipids, 1989) (slide 10). Spoken: the heart needs ubiquinol most, hence "the heart vitamin" [00:00].
- Consumer survey: over 100 consumers aged 50+ took 100 mg a day for 28 days; 7 in 10 would recommend it to a friend and 8 in 10 felt an improvement in overall health (slide 10).
- Food equivalent of 100 mg a day: 10 kg of broccoli, 1.6 kg of sardines or 3 kg of beef (slide 11). Spoken as 60 avocados or 3.5 kg of beef [00:00]; the beef figures differ.
- Claimed areas, the speaker's: immune support, energy performance, healthspan against lifespan, mitochondrial health, heart, male and female reproductive health, cognition, menopause (slide 5).
- Study sub-areas: heart (cardiac and endothelial function, glycaemic control, blood pressure); healthy ageing (brain health, cognitive function, fatigue, migraine); women (PMS, menopause, skin turnover and hydration); fertility (sperm quality, ovarian function, oocyte quality, oxidative stress) (slide 13). The five blocks add to 84 studies against the headline 100+ (slide 13).
- Supplier: maker of Kaneka Ubiquinol since 2007, by "ultrapure, natural yeast fermentation", with pharmaceutical-grade manufacturing practices; stability tested in tablets, softgels, capsules, liquid, powder and gummies (slide 15).
- Certifications shown: TGA, GMP, GRAS, HACCP, NDI, OSHMS, halal, kosher, non-GMO, non-animal origin, ISO 14001 (printed "140001") and ISO 22000 (slide 15). Spoken: halal is the latest [00:00].
- Awards shown: NutraIngredients Asia Awards winner 2026 (Ingredient of the Year: Healthspan) and 2024 (Healthy Ageing), finalist 2025 (women's health); Vitafoods Europe Innovation Awards 2026 (most innovative consumer-ready nutraceutical finished product); Natural Health Products NZ 2025 marketing winner; a 2025 Tmall Global marketing innovation award; CMA raw material supplier award 2024 (slide 16).
- "MTIC certified" in the recording is MTick® certified, "Menopause Friendly", with Kaneka an "Official GenM Partner, supporting women's health through the menopause transition" (slide 16). The speaker placed it in the UK and called it "female-friendly" [00:00]; the slide does not name a country.
- Kaneka Ubiquinol is a "Proud Partner" of BVB Frauen, Borussia Dortmund's women's team (slide 16).
- Europe is served from a warehouse in Belgium for short lead times [00:00]; the slides do not mention it.
- The deck carries no "Confidential" marking.

items.title: Aquanova NovaSol micellar delivery, then Balchem OptiMSM
items.to_check: The billed title of the OptiMSM talk, the spelling Lena Leder or Leda, the room, what the Q in NovaSOL Q stands for (slide 2 does not say), and the end of the OptiMSM talk (the recording stops at 12:53, a few minutes in) are unconfirmed; the Aquanova deck has no slides for Balchem.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Two short talks in one recording.

Torsten Seck, director of sales and marketing at Aquanova, asked how delivery technology can turn a hard-to-use, fat-soluble ingredient into a market-ready, differentiated product. His answer was NovaSOL, a micellar technology. The native ingredient sits in a tiny micelle with a fat-loving core and a water-loving shell, so it dissolves in water and passes stomach acid. Processing is physical, with no chemical change, and each formula is unique to its ingredient. The result is a liquid concentrate ready for capsules, shots and combinations. His examples were Favea's cap-in-cap product, NeuroFlex PD, and the US longevity brand Nugevia, which built three products on the same micellar resveratrol. His conclusion: NovaSOL is a bridge between delivery science and differentiated finished products.

Lena Leder, senior manager nutrition science at Balchem, then began on OptiMSM. She set it in Balchem's 33 active research projects, then described MSM as a source of sulfur and methyl groups which, she said, has shown effects on joint and skin health and exercise recovery. The recording ends about three minutes into her talk, before the data.
summary.Key takeaways:
- NovaSOL is a micelle encapsulation technology: the active ingredient is the core, a food-grade liquid emulsification system the shell; it is water-soluble and made by physical processing only, with no chemical modification (slide 3) (slide 4) [00:18].
- Each NovaSOL formula is unique to its ingredient; it is a water-free liquid concentrate for capsules and shots, and different NovaSOL formulations can be combined in capsules (slide 3) (slide 5).
- Nugevia, a US direct-to-consumer brand, launched three combination products on Jotrol micellar resveratrol: MND with NovaSOL Curcumin, PWR with NovaSOL Q and GLO with NovaSOL Astaxanthin, in vegetarian SeaGel softgels, positioned in longevity (slide 7).
- MSM is 34% sulfur by weight, a source of sulfur and methyl groups; supplementation "has shown" effects on joint and skin health and exercise recovery, the speaker said [10:40].
- Balchem has 33 active research projects; methylfolate is a new ingredient it hopes to bring to Europe soon [09:04].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Neither technology touches our ingredients directly, but both show what our customers' manufacturers are buying.
- Micellar delivery is a format play: it lets a capsule or shot maker differentiate on bioavailability rather than on the ingredient, and the cap-in-cap and three-product Nugevia examples are the finished-product systems Nick Morgan described (slide 6) (slide 7). My reading: delivery technology is where a CDMO earns its margin, so when we pitch creatine or clear pea protein to a Polish contract manufacturer, "which format can you make it work in" will come before price.
- Nugevia's PWR pack reads "Muscle Recovery", and Balchem positions OptiMSM on exercise recovery (slide 7) [10:40]. My reading: recovery is being sold in softgels and combination products, not only in powders.
- Relevance stays medium: the deck corrects names and adds detail, but brings no new link to our range.
summary.Quotes:
- "A Novasol formulation is a water-free, homogeneous liquid active ingredient concentrate." Speaker 2 (Torsten Seck) [00:18]
- "During our processing, we not chemically modify the ingredient; it's just carefully controlled physical processing parameters, which help to create the micelles around the ingredient" Speaker 2 (Torsten Seck) [00:18]
- "...we have 33 active projects, ongoing research projects in Balkam, and that is over all over the whole portfolio." Speaker 3 [09:04]
- "MSM provides multiple advantages, so it is a source of sulfur, a source of methyl groups, and supplementation has shown that it has an effect on joint and skin health, and that it's supporting exercise recovery." Speaker 3 [10:40]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Torsten Seck (Aquanova) invited questions after the talk; his contact details are on slide 9 [00:18].
- Lena Leder's spelling (Otter also "Leda") and Balchem's OptiMSM exercise-recovery papers, which the recording missed.
- Favea's NeuroFlex PD cap-in-cap sample (Martina and "Pabla" at Favea's table).
- Which Polish CDMOs run NovaSOL liquids and shots: the deck names only Favea, for cap-in-cap, and no shot maker.
summary.Detail:
- Attendance: "250" at this edition, as the organiser had announced [00:18].
- The Aquanova deck is titled "From Lipophilic Actives to Versatile Dosage Forms: The NovaSOL® Technology Platform", Remedy NutraFood CDMO Conference, Gdańsk, 22 October 2026 (slide 1).
- The speaker is Torsten Seck, Director Sales & Marketing, Aquanova AG, Darmstadt (slide 9). Otter heard "Toshton Sack" and the host said "Austin" [00:00] [08:32].
- The slides correct names the recording garbled: NeuroFlex PD (heard "Nourreflex PD"), COMBICAPS (heard "Comic Caps"), Nugevia (heard "GVR"), MND, PWR and GLO (heard "Mind", "Q Power" and "Glow"), and Jotrol (heard "Jotron") (slide 6) (slide 7) [00:18].
- The native ingredient can start as a liquid or a powder. The ready products are NovaSOL Curcumin, NovaSOL Astaxanthin and NovaSOL Q; the slide does not say what Q stands for, and the spoken word was heard as "cuten" (slide 2) [00:18].
- NovaSOL "Mimics nature´s architecture (biomimetic)": the body makes micelles itself, inefficiently, he said (slide 4) [00:18]. A badge on the title slide reads "patented NovaSOL® micellization, made by AQUANOVA AG in germany", read from the image (slide 1).
- He said the micelle also protects the ingredient from stomach acid; the slides do not say this [00:18].
- Further properties: proprietary recipes and processing IP, the FSSC 22000 quality standard, sustainable use of resources, and "Human trials & comprehensive research" as scientific evidence (slide 5). With enhanced bioavailability "you might need less" of the ingredient per finished dose, the speaker said [00:18]. No trial is named in the talk or the deck.
- NeuroFlex PD uses Favea's COMBICAPS cap-in-cap: inner capsule size 3, outer size 00, NovaSOL Curcumin in the outer capsule (slide 6). Samples were at Favea's table [00:18].
- Cap-in-cap benefits on the slide: separation of ingredients, reduced risk of interactions, greater formulation flexibility, targeted ingredient placement, combination of different dosage forms, and a premium, differentiated dosage form. He spoke of four of the six (slide 6) [00:18].

items.title: Martin Bauer: RhoSera, cultivated Rhodiola rosea against anabolic resistance
items.to_check: The billed title in the programme, Ralf Spreemann's role (the deck gives none), the room, and the Polish sites he named (Otter: "Martin Bovatska", "Vita Chiche", "Klenkari Phyto Farm", "Europlant Group" in "Posnan") are unconfirmed; the deck (files/martin-bauer-rhosera-beyond-protein.pdf, titled "RhoSera Beyond Protein") does not settle them.

summary.Summary:
Dr Ralf Spreemann of MartinBauer Nutraceuticals, a new unit of the family-owned Nature Network, introduced RhoSera, an extract of cultivated Rhodiola rosea for the ageing muscle. His question was what goes "beyond protein" for older people.

His case started with anabolic resistance. Ageing muscle responds less to protein and training, and he said hardly any ingredient addresses that gap. Wild rhodiola is overharvested, adulterated and now needs trade permits. So the group has spent decades breeding its own elite lines, grown in Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands. The cultivated root carries several times more of some compounds than wild material. In human muscle cells it switched on two stem-cell markers that wild material did not.

The human trial put 140 inactive adults aged 55 to 75 on training and protein, with RhoSera or placebo on top. Muscle soreness fell by about half on RhoSera, far more than on placebo. Strength, balance and fatigue also improved. He called them the best results of his career with a botanical. The trial is not yet published.

He closed with a typical dose of 250 to 350 mg and a regulatory note. Rhodiola has no authorised EFSA claim, so brands pair it with magnesium or B vitamins for fatigue claims.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The gap he names is anabolic resistance: ageing muscle "responds less to protein and training", so protein advice rises from 0.8 to 1.2 g, and "hardly any ingredient" addresses it (slide 3) [00:00].
- Wild Rhodiola rosea is overharvested and adulterated with non-rosea species. Rhodiola spp. has been in CITES Appendix II since February 2023, so roots and extracts traded across borders need CITES documents (slide 4). He said it was listed "as an endangered species"; the slide says CITES Appendix II, which differs [00:00].
- In primary human muscle cells only the cultivated extract raised Pax7 and MyoD, the muscle stem-cell markers; wild harvest had no effect. Published as Iannuzzo et al., Antioxidants 2024;13:1000 (slide 8) [00:00].
- Trial: 12 weeks, 140 inactive adults aged 55 to 75, RhoSera 400 mg a day or placebo, both arms on the same training programme plus 60 g protein a day (slide 9). He described it as double-blind and placebo-controlled [00:00].
- Muscle soreness (DOMS) fell 46.3% in men and 51.7% in women, against 18.1% and 10.6% on placebo (slide 9, read from the chart); p = 0.004 and p < 0.001. He rounded these to 46%, 52%, 18% and 11% [00:00]. The data are "on file" and the manuscript is "in preparation" (slide 9).
- No authorised EFSA claim for rhodiola. On-hold areas (stress, physical and mental performance) are usable if substantiated, per national rules; pair with magnesium or B vitamins for authorised fatigue claims (slide 11) [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- This is the most direct talk for us. RhoSera is pitched "beyond protein": its closing slide says protein builds muscle and RhoSera tells it to (slide 10). Both trial arms got 60 g protein a day (slide 9). My reading: a stacking partner for IsoClr: Pea and CreaWin in healthy-ageing and active-nutrition products, not a substitute, and the framing of protein plus an enabler is one our customers will hear again.
- The soreness and performance figures are the speaker's, from a trial not yet published (data on file, manuscript in preparation). The slide itself says they "do not constitute a registered health claim" (slide 9). Carry them with that caveat.
- His point that a brand needs a secure, cultivated, traceable supply and a clean regulatory story is one we can make for creatine too (my reading).
- The group offers "science to shelf" to brand owners, formulators and CDMOs, including the RhoSera brand and logo (slide 11): a botanicals supplier selling to the same CDMOs we want to reach.
- Relevance stays high: muscle, protein utilisation and active nutrition for the over-55s. The deck confirms protein was given to both arms.
summary.Quotes:
- "...there is hardly any ingredient on the market which is really trying to fill this gap by enabling a muscle cell to utilize protein more efficiently, and that was our motivation." Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "I'm in this business now 31 years, and it was the best results I've ever seen with a botanical." Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "The marker does not predict the effect." (slide 7)
- "You don't have EFSA claims. You have only on old claims, or you can borrow claims like magnesia, or for magnesium, or for instance, vitamin B, to claim loss on fatigue." Speaker 1 [00:00]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ralf Spreemann's role at MartinBauer Nutraceuticals (not on the slides).
- Ask for the clinical study summary they offer (slide 11) and the trial manuscript when published; check registration CTRI/2025/04/083930 for the primary endpoint.
- Read Iannuzzo et al., Antioxidants 2024;13:1000, on the cell work.
- The Polish sites he named and who they supply (the deck does not name them).
- Whether RhoSera has been combined with creatine or a pea protein in a finished product.
summary.Detail:
- The Nature Network: privately owned, fourth generation. MartinBauer (founded 1930, "the vanguard of botanical solutions": cultivation and sourcing, big in tea and RTD drinks), Finzelberg ("the experts in botanical efficacy": extracts for pharma and supplements; he said 1875 and that he came from there) and PhytoLab (third-party lab: reference substances, contaminants) (slide 2) [00:00].
- Group figures: 90+ years, 30+ manufacturing sites and sales units, 4,300+ employees, 650+ million euro consolidated revenue (slide 2). Otter heard "over 30 here in Poland"; the slide's 30+ is the group's sites and sales units, which differs [00:00]. The deck names no Polish sites.
- The ageing population: people aged 60+ rise from 1.0 billion in 2020 to 2.1 billion in 2050, and from 12% of the world's population in 2015 to 22% in 2050 (WHO/UN; slide 3, read from the chart). He said "probably over 2 billion" by 2050 [00:00].
- 10 to 27% of people aged 60+ live with sarcopenia, depending on the definition (Petermann-Rocha et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2022) (slide 3).
- RhodioFarm cultivation: own fields in Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands; young plants raised in Germany; a 3-year cycle; K.I.A. standard, "no chemical pesticides as a rule, none in the 6 months before harvest"; a PA avoidance programme and full batch traceability (slide 5). He said "Central Europe", three to four years to harvest and that farmers may not use pesticides; the slide's 3 years and pesticide wording differ [00:00].
- Cultivation history: 242 accessions collected 25+ years ago; 210 were true R. rosea (32 were not) and 143 survived cultivation (67 failed in the field); only 6 to 11% met single targets (root biomass, rosavin and salidroside, reproducibility) and none met all; about 1% entered breeding; today 3 elite lines (slide 6). He said "over 10 years" to reach the three elite lines; the slide says "decades of selective breeding followed", which differs [00:00].
- Cultivated against wild, by HRMS peak area: rhodiolin 4.8 times, quercetin glycoside 3.6 times, rhodiocyanoside A 3.4 times (Iannuzzo et al. 2024) (slide 7). He said a "four to five-fold concentration" of the precursors; the slide's range is 3.4 to 4.8 times [00:00]. Otter's "rhodiolene, glycosyl, rhodiocyanide A" are these compounds.
- The "salidroside paradox": the wild extract had 1.4% salidroside and RhoSera 0.8%, yet only RhoSera switched on Pax7 and MyoD (slide 7).
- Cell work: primary human myoblasts, 48 hours, 30 µg/mL (slide 8). Pax7 rose about 1.5-fold and MyoD about 2.3-fold over untreated with the cultivated extract; myogenin did not change (slide 8, read from the chart). The clinical tests to date on rhodiola used wild material, he said [00:00].
- He said the cultivated extract also triggers folate and polyamine pathways, so spermidine, spermine and putrescine are made in the cell [00:00]. The slide gives an estimated 2.5-fold "dose advantage" on folate and polyamine pathways against wild extract, "calculated from metabolite ratios, in vitro" (slide 8). He said wild material concentrated 2.5 times shows similar effects in cells [00:00].
- Trial population: slight muscle loss but no sarcopenia, considered healthy [00:00]. Registered as CTRI/2025/04/083930. No serious adverse events (slide 9).
- Other results, as % change from baseline to week 12 in each arm (slide 9): chair stand +36 to +40% against +9 to +14% on placebo; single-leg balance with eyes closed +35 to +48% against +3 to +18%; handgrip in women +13% against +5%; bench press in men +13% against +6%; all significant against placebo. Fatigue fell and social engagement and quality of life rose, significant in men and women; sleep quality improved significantly in women. He also named leg press as improved "statistically highly significant" [00:00]; the slide does not show it.
- Formulation: 250 to 350 mg a day typical in finished products; the study used 400 mg (slide 11). Hydro-ethanolic (70%) extract on maltodextrin; vegan, non-GMO, caffeine-free, preservative-free (slide 11).
- Formats: the slide lists capsules, soft-gels, tablets, instant powders and beverages (slide 11). He named tablets, capsules, bars and V caps, and called beverages a challenge because rhodiola is very bitter [00:00].
- Supply: "100% EU grown", zero wild sourcing, "CITES-compliant by design" (slides 10, 11). Otter's "100% cytosy compliance" is CITES [00:00].
- Support offered: a clinical study summary (data on file), the RhoSera ingredient brand and logo, regulatory guidance and formulation support from their NPD team (slide 11).
- RhoSera is a trademark of MB-Holding GmbH & Co. KG, marketed by MartinBauer Nutraceuticals; contact details are on the last slide (slide 12). No slide is marked confidential.

items.title: Remember it. Make it. Prove it. Three things your brief forgot to ask
ingredients: MicrobiomeX (citrus flavanol with a prebiotic effect)
Bonolive (olive leaf extract; heard as Bun Olive)
items.to_check: The slides (added 23 Nov 2026) settle the title, his surname and the names MicrobiomeX and Bonolive. Still open: the room; his role at Solabia (not on the slides or in the talk); WATTS'UP is named on Tantus's slides, not on Solabia's own deck.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Thomas Beadnall, presenting for Solabia Nutrition, opened with the brief every brand writes and every CDMO receives: clinically proven, clean label, cost-effective, innovative, ready in Q3, two-year shelf life. He called it impossible and replaced it with three questions: will they remember it, can you make it, can you prove it.

On memory, the name decides. MicrobiomeX, a citrus flavanol with a prebiotic effect, went nowhere as a "flavobiotic" and was repositioned as the co-pilot for your probiotic. An aronia berry extract named Brainberry is now Solabia's second biggest and fastest growing product.

On making it, briefs now ask for several grams of creatine and collagen plus botanicals in one soluble format. Creatine adds its own problem: brands want it in gummies, but heat turns it into creatinine. Solabia and the Polish CDMO Tantus avoided this with a cold-pressed tablet of creatine and Solabia's citrus extract WATTS'UP.

On proof, he said "science-backed" means nothing on its own. What counts is the dose, the population, the endpoints and the study design. Solabia has run randomised placebo-controlled trials on all its ingredients and put each study on its website, with the olive leaf extract Bonolive as his example. He closed by inviting brands to bring their briefs to Solabia.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The standard brief is "impossible"; judge a launch on whether they will remember it, whether you can make it and whether you can prove it [00:01] (slide 2) (slide 4).
- Naming decides memory: "Flavobiotic" did not fly and MicrobiomeX became "The co-pilot for your probiotic", while Brainberry, an aronia extract with the benefit in its name, is now Solabia's second biggest and fastest growing product [00:01] (slide 7) (slide 8) (slide 10).
- Briefs now ask for three to five grams of creatine and five to ten grams of collagen plus a botanical extract and a vitamin complex in one format that is soluble and mixes well [00:01]. The slides show these only as pictures, with no figures (slide 12).
- Creatine in gummies: heat applied over time gives creatinine, which "doesn't really do much"; Tantus's answer was a cold-pressed tablet, no heat, of creatine plus WATTS'UP [00:01] (slide 13) (slide 14).
- "Science-backed" means nothing on its own. The slide's open-evidence test is dose (how much?), population (tested on whom?), endpoints (what changed?) and study design (how was it tested?); he also named the change against placebo [00:01] (slide 16) (slide 17).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high (unchanged): creatine is being briefed at three to five grams a serving alongside collagen and botanicals, and brands want it in gummies and chewables, not only powder [00:01]. The heat problem in gummies is an opening for a stable creatine and for formats that avoid heat. My reading: a CreaWin pitch to CDMOs should carry stability data for cold-pressed and chewable formats.
- Tantus (Poland) is a CDMO already making a creatine chewable with Solabia's WATTS'UP [00:01]; neither deck names the creatine's source (tantus-longevity-concepts, slide 7). My reading: a direct CreaWin prospect, and a sign that Polish CDMOs co-develop concepts with ingredient suppliers rather than only buying to spec.
- Solabia's open-evidence test (dose, population, endpoints, study design) is how an ingredient marketer expects evidence to be shown (slide 17). My reading: our CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea materials should lead with those four items, study by study.
- A benefit in the name beat a mechanism word [00:01] (slide 7) (slide 10). My reading: relevant to how we name concepts for customers.
summary.Quotes:
- "We want a clinically proven, clean label, cost-effective, innovative product, which is ready in Q3, and it's got a two-year shelf life. Sounds like a great brief. Sounds like a great product, but unfortunately, it is impossible." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
- "Only problem with gummies is when you apply the heat over time, what happens? Creatinine." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
- "It's probably one of the most used phrases in the industry, and it's also probably one of the most dangerous because it means absolutely nothing, really science-backed." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
- "Brainberry is now the second biggest product in their portfolio and the fastest growing." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm Thomas Beadnall's role at Solabia.
- Ask Solabia or Tantus whose creatine is in the WATTS'UP chewable, and whether CreaWin stability data would interest them.
- Look at solabianutrition.com for how it lays out studies (dose, population, endpoints, study design).
- Question: does Solabia or Tantus have shelf-life data for creatine in cold-pressed tablets against gummies?

- The deck is "Remember it. Make it. Prove it.", subtitled "Three things your brief forgot to ask." and "A different way to think about a successful launch.", by Thomas Beadnall of Solabia Nutrition (slide 1). Spoken, the subtitle was "three things that your brief forgot to tell you" [00:01]. His role is not on the slides; he said he has worked with Solabia "for a while now in their ingredient portfolio" [00:01].
- MicrobiomeX is a "Citrus flavanol with a prebiotic effect on gut microbiome" on the slide (slide 6); spoken as a "flavonol" that is not a prebiotic but has a prebiotic effect [00:01]. The slide's word and the spoken word differ.

summary.Summary:
Mateusz Korgul and Victoria Lesiovski of Tantus, a Polish CDMO, asked how a longevity trend becomes a product people actually take. A trend changes nothing on its own. It matters only once a product reaches the market and becomes part of a daily routine.

Consumers want healthspan, not only lifespan: years spent active, capable and independent. The industry answers with ever more complex formulas, but they argued the real question is what makes biological sense in a product, not what else can be added. Longevity is a marathon, so format, dose and ease of use decide whether people keep taking it.

Their process has four steps: trend, ingredient, formula, market. Suppliers are partners who bring research, safety dossiers and formulation know-how, not vendors filling separate orders.

They showed three concepts. The first, made with Solabia, is a chewable tablet of 3 g creatine and 400 mg of Solabia's citrus extract WATTS'UP, sold on physical function with age rather than sport: "Chew it, don't shake it." The second is a daily healthy-ageing capsule of Kaneka Ubiquinol, VitaCholine and active B vitamins. The third is a tablet of Nuritas's PeptiStrong plant peptides for muscle with age. Their close: keep it simple, make it last.
summary.Key takeaways:
- A trend does not change anything on its own; longevity becomes a product "when it fits real life - and stays there" [00:31] (slide 13).
- Complexity is not the answer: the question is never what else to add, but what "genuinely makes biological sense in this specific product" [01:05] (slide 4).
- Concept one: 3 g creatine plus 400 mg WATTS'UP in a chewable tablet, formulated by Tantus and Solabia, for mobility and muscle resilience "without requiring athletic sports positioning" (slide 7). Spoken as "400 grams" of a hesperidin-based ingredient [04:45]; the slide's 400 mg differs from what was said. The slides do not name the creatine's source.
- The slide's image gives four reasons people stop taking creatine powder: water needed, a shaker to carry, grit and aftertaste, and it will not dissolve ("Half of it sits at the bottom") (slide 8).
- Concepts two and three, from the slides only: Anti-Age by Tantus, one capsule a day of 100 mg Kaneka Ubiquinol, 300 mg VitaCholine and an active B-complex; and a PeptiStrong tablet co-developed with Nuritas and Vivatis Pharma (slide 9) (slide 10) (slide 12).
- Tantus wants long-term suppliers who bring clinical research, safety dossiers, technology know-how and new concepts, not transactional orders [03:09] (slide 6).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high (unchanged): creatine is Tantus's lead concept. A 3 g creatine chewable is built and sampled with an ingredient supplier, but the slides name only "3 g Creatine", not its source (slide 7). My reading: Tantus is a direct CreaWin prospect, and the first question is whose creatine is in the tablet and whether that is fixed.
- Creatine is sold here on mobility and muscle resilience with age, without sports positioning (slide 7). My reading: the ingredient we sell into sports brands has a second customer in longevity brands reached through CDMOs like Tantus.
- The four reasons people stop (water, shaker, grit and aftertaste, poor dissolving) are the case for the chewable (slide 8). My reading: a CreaWin pitch for chewables and tablets should answer taste, grit and tabletting with data.
- Tantus prefers suppliers who bring dossiers and formulation help over suppliers who sell powder [03:09] (slide 6). My reading: our pitch to CDMOs should include stability and formulation support, not price alone.
- Muscle health is framed as healthspan, and the slot is filled by plant peptides with an open pipeline on dose, format and endpoints (slide 11). My reading: Tantus builds muscle-with-age concepts with ingredient partners; a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea concept could be offered the same way.
summary.Quotes:
- "We know that longevity is a marathon. It's not a sprint, and that's why the most promising formulations don't make sense when users are not willing to use it consistently." Speaker 2 (Victoria Lesiovski) [02:09]
- "At Tantus, we aim to build long-term relationship with our suppliers, rather than treating every order as a separate transaction." Speaker 1 (Mateusz Korgul) [03:09]
- "We didn't want to develop just another creatine powder that you have to scoop and shake and mix and drink." Speaker 2 (Victoria Lesiovski) [04:45]
- "Longevity becomes a product when it fits real life - and stays there." (slide 13)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Tantus whose creatine is in the chewable, whether the supplier is fixed, and how many tablets make the 3 g dose; offer CreaWin with stability and tabletting data.
- Contact Mateusz Korgul and Victoria Lesiovski for a CreaWin introduction.
- Ask whether Tantus would build a muscle-with-age concept with CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea, as it did with Nuritas.

summary.Summary:
Thijs Bosch, CEO of The Protein Brewery and formerly a seller of dairy and fava proteins, presented Fermotein, a whole-food mycelium powder grown by biomass fermentation in Breda, in the Netherlands. His pitch was that one ingredient can carry protein, fibre and longevity bioactives together.

Fermotein is 50% protein and 30% fibre, and is rich in spermidine and vitamins. EFSA gave its safety opinion in 2025 and EU authorisation followed in 2026; approval took five years, he said. While waiting, the company built its market in the US, in "all-in-one nutrition": powders between protein powder and meal replacement, priced against the whole supplement basket. Ka'Chava is the model, growing fast in measured retail without discounting. In Europe the brands still sell meal replacement, and he asked the CDMOs in the room to embrace the all-in-one concept.

His evidence so far is laboratory work: prebiotic effects in a gut model, GLP-1 release in human colon tissue, and longer lifespan in nematodes. The slides say plainly that this is not evidence of an effect in humans. Two human trials with Wageningen come next.

He closed on scale: 10 million servings sold in 2026, three active US customers and €70 million raised. The company is not yet profitable.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Fermotein is 50% protein with a complete amino acid profile, 30% fibre ("unique fungal fibres"), spermidine at "7x more than wheat germ", vitamin B6, vitamin B4, calcium, iron, zinc, phosphorus and magnesium (slide 5). Spoken: chitin and chitosan fibre, spermidine at about 1,700 mg per kilo, seven times "beet germ" as transcribed, and choline [00:00].
- Approvals: self-affirmed GRAS in the US and Singapore (SFA) approval in 2024, EFSA safety approval in 2025, EU authorisation and market launch in 2026 (slide 3). He said "since the summer of this year" after five years, with Australia and Canada pending [00:00].
- All-in-one nutrition is worth $0.5 to 1bn in the US against $8.6bn for protein supplements and $4.9bn for meal replacement (2025), and is priced at about $5 to $7 a serving against $1 to $2 for protein powder and $4 to $6 for meal replacement (slide 6) [00:00].
- Ka'Chava: $47.2M measured retail sales excluding direct sales, up 24.4% in dollars and 39.9% in units over 52 weeks to 07/12/2026 (SPINS); single-serve multipacks grow fastest, up 254% to over 1,000%, at the highest price per serving (slide 8). He called it "super profitable" [00:00].
- Evidence is preclinical: in a TNO gut model Fermotein raised butyrate, propionate and acetate and microbial diversity; in TNO human colon tissue it raised GLP-1 against a blank; in NemaLife's C. elegans study median lifespan rose 21.7%, 28 against 23 days (slide 11) (slide 12). He said 22% [00:00].
- Next: a 16-week human RCT on biological ageing clocks in adults aged 40 to 60, led by Dr Pol Grootswagers of Wageningen; a human spermidine bioavailability trial; and a NemaLife follow-up on lifespan and muscle health (slide 13). He said the ageing-clock trial starts in quarter one [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high, unchanged: a non-animal protein ingredient for active nutrition, now authorised in the EU, competing for the same brief as IsoClr: Pea (slide 3) (slide 5) [00:00]. My reading: at 50% protein it sells protein plus fibre plus longevity, not protein content; it will meet us in all-in-one and superfood blends, not in clear protein drinks.
- All-in-one is priced against the whole basket, at about $5 to $7 a serving against $1 to $2 for protein powder (slide 6). My reading: a premium European format where IsoClr: Pea and CreaWin could be the protein and performance pillars; the European meal-shake brands on his slide, BOL and vybey, are worth approaching (slide 10).
- He says Europe has not yet adopted all-in-one messaging (slide 10) [00:00]. My reading: a CDMO pitch for a European all-in-one shake, built on our ingredients, is open.
- The longevity science is laboratory-only and the company labels it so (slide 11) (slide 12). My reading: a fair benchmark for how plainly to present preclinical data in our own collateral.
summary.Quotes:
- "And we are the first mycelium protein company that has EFSA approval. So since the summer of this year, we can finally sell in Europe" Speaker 1 (Thijs Bosch) [00:00]
- "...it's mainly into the all-in-one nutrition segment, which hasn't really evolved yet." Speaker 1 (Thijs Bosch) [00:00]
- "Preclinical in vitro, ex vivo and invertebrate-model results; not evidence of an effect in humans." (slide 11)
- "Packs got smaller. Price per serving did not." (slide 8)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm Novo Holdings as the largest shareholder (transcribed "Nova Holdings"; not on the slides).
- Find the 2026 EU authorisation in the Union list of novel foods: conditions of use and specifications.
- Ask for the TNO reports (2026 15116 and 15096) and the NemaLife study, and the size and start date of the two Wageningen human trials.
- Which European CDMOs are among the 80+ EU prospects, and in which formats?
summary.Detail:
- Title slide: "Remedy Gdańsk – October 2026 – Thijs Bosch, CEO" (slide 1). His 15+ years in proteins run through Fonterra, Cosun and The Protein Brewery (slide 2); he said he ran a European dairy protein business at Fonterra, then sold fava proteins at Cosun [00:00].
- Slide 8 is marked "Property of The Protein Brewery · Strictly Private and Confidential" (slide 8). Its Ka'Chava figures stay internal.

items.title: Translating Longevity Science into Relevant Consumer Outcomes
ingredients: NAD boosters (nicotinamide riboside, nicotinamide mononucleotide, nicotinamide)
items.to_check: The title and his role are from his slides (added 23 Nov 2026). The room is unconfirmed. The paper he called an April 2026 meta-analysis is not on his slides, which show an October 2025 review, and the sprinter's name (Kenton Brown) rests on the recording only.

summary.Summary:
Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett's Global Product Formulation Lead, runs the team that formulates its own-label products worldwide. He asked how longevity science becomes something a customer will buy. His answer: consumers may buy a story, but they judge a product on the outcomes they feel.

He opened with a tortoise to argue that ageing badly is not biologically fixed, so the category is about living better, not longer. H&B's data on millions of customers show that repeat purchase goes to products with one clearly communicated benefit, such as joint function or brain function. Shoppers ask when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs. His slides set the test an ingredient must pass: evidence, dose, outcome, communication and consumer relevance.

Two case studies followed. NAD boosters have a strong molecular rationale but very limited functional outcome data, and of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was. Curcumin, H&B's second best-selling ingredient, shows the other path: a meta-analysis of 11 trials found it improved knee osteoarthritis pain scores. He also named cheap basics with strong evidence: fibre, vitamin D, calcium and protein.

His conclusion for suppliers: bring ingredients with both a biological rationale and human outcome data, and help retailers translate the science without over-promising.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Mechanisms make promises and sell, but outcomes retain customers (slide 6). Shoppers ask whether and when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs (slide 8); when trials show a benefit at four, six or eight weeks, H&B can sometimes put that on pack [00:25].
- H&B's test for an ingredient has five parts: evidence (high-quality science), dose (the effective, studied dose), outcome (which endpoint improves), communication (legal and responsible) and consumer relevance (does it matter in everyday life) (slide 6).
- The outcomes consumers buy are energy, memory, strength, mobility, sleep, appearance and feeling younger or better, not NAD+, sirtuins, telomeres or PARPs (slide 8). H&B's biggest own-label sellers carry one clear benefit, such as joint function, joint comfort or brain function [00:25].
- NAD: of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was [00:25]. NR reliably raises blood NAD metabolites and NMN or NAM raise it in some studies, but functional outcome improvements are "very limited" (slide 13).
- Curcumin is the "tangible outcomes" case: a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (n=1258) found curcuminoids improved VAS and WOMAC pain scores in knee osteoarthritis against comparators or placebo, and formulation matters because bioavailability varies widely (slide 15).
- Cheap interventions with strong evidence (fibre, vitamin D, calcium, protein) beat novel technologies on evidence and cost; US shelves are "protein plus fiber" [00:25]. None of this is on his slides.
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance stays medium: a major retailer's test for ingredients, adjacent to our range; the slides name none of our ingredients.
- The formulation lead at one of our customers' biggest retailers checks evidence, dose, outcome, communication and consumer relevance (slide 6), and wants ingredients with "both biological rationale and human outcome" data (slide 17). My reading: CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea dossiers for retail-led brands should lead with the studied dose, the endpoint that improves and when the user feels it, before any mechanism.
- Strength and mobility are two of the seven outcomes he says consumers buy (slide 8). My reading: a healthy-ageing pitch for CreaWin and pea protein should speak of strength and getting out of a chair, not muscle protein synthesis.
- "Everything is protein plus fiber" in the US, and protein is among his cheap, evidence-rich longevity interventions [00:25]. My reading: pea protein with fibre is a brief European brands will copy, and IsoClr: Pea's taste and clarity are the arguments inside that blend.

- "Not a single customer knew what NAD was. There was over 1000 people that we surveyed." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]
- "I'm sure if anybody's been to the US in the last six months, everything is protein plus fiber." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]

summary.Detail:
- The deck names him Alex Glover MSc, RNutr, Global Product Formulation Lead, Holland & Barrett (slide 1). Every slide carries the date 04/11/2026; none is marked confidential (slide 2).
- Agenda in five parts: from lifespan to healthspan; consumers don't buy longevity, they buy outcomes; the longevity evidence gap; NAD, NR and NMN as a "molecular outcomes" case study; joints as a "tangible outcomes" case study (slide 2). He skipped it in the talk [00:25].
- The tortoise: a photo, then a survival chart labelled with an average lifespan of about 72-80 years for humans and 150-200 years for the tortoise (slides 3-4). He said humans live about 10 to 12 years with a disability or poor health, while a tortoise lives most of its life without [00:25]. In his words, "we're not in the business of making people live longer; we're making them live better" [00:25].
- H&B's data on millions of customers show what they buy and how often. A customer panel, the "Stay Healthies" around 50, talked about playing with grandchildren and getting out of a chair, not sirtuins or telomeres [00:25].
- The evidence chain on his slide runs mechanism (pathway), biomarker (surrogate), function (performance), clinical outcome (quality of life, disease endpoint) (slide 9). He said suppliers get "stuck" in the first two; his sleep example was the Pittsburgh scale, which means nothing to a shopper [00:25].
- Biomarkers are real signals but often not validated surrogates; a biomarker change is not a change in how someone feels or functions; in supplements, biomarker shifts often precede but do not guarantee outcome benefits (slide 10).
- NAD: a central redox cofactor that declines with age, behind the hypothesis "boost NAD = boost healthspan"; blood NAD is not muscle or mitochondrial NAD, and more in blood does not guarantee more where it matters; measurement is improving but interpretation is still hard (slide 12). NR can raise the muscle NAD metabolome, with mixed outcomes; NMN and NAM outcomes are mixed or early (slide 13).
- The NAD paper: he spoke of an April 2026 meta-analysis and one trial on walking speed in the over-60s [00:25]. The slide shows a different source: a review published 13 October 2025, "NAD+ precursor supplementation in human ageing: clinical evidence and challenges" (Vinten et al., Nature Metabolism 7, 1974-1990), beside three trials: chronic NR in healthy middle-aged and older adults (Martens et al.), NR in aged human skeletal muscle (Elhassan et al., 2019), and a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled NMN trial in healthy middle-aged adults (published 8 December 2022) (slide 13). The spoken date and the slide differ; the walking-speed trial is not on the slide.
- Curcumin is H&B's second best-selling ingredient globally, about "one bottle a minute"; he gave the on-hold claim as joint flexibility and comfort, with evidence on knee osteoarthritis, movement, function and systemic inflammation [00:25]. The slide cites Hsiao et al., a meta-analysis of high- and low-dose curcumin in knee osteoarthritis, and a critical review of curcumin reviews (Chen et al.): adverse events were similar at high and low dose, and curcumin sometimes compares favourably with NSAIDs (slide 15). Systemic inflammation is not on the slide.
- His conclusions: the most compelling retail categories are those where consumers can feel or measure the outcome (mobility, cognition, vision); curcumin, UC-II and anthocyanins show mechanism aligning with real-world outcomes; NAD boosters show strong rationale but limited evidence for tangible benefits "so far"; the retailer's challenge is to translate emerging science without over-promising (slide 17).
- Fibre, vitamin D, calcium and protein: he said the nutrition slide was missing from the deck [00:25]. He gave about 9% lower coronary heart disease risk for every seven grams of fibre, called fibre one of the biggest nutritional predictors of longevity, and costed vitamin D at about two cents per 10 microgram serving from H&B's own label [00:25].
- He believes about 80% of how we age can be influenced. He closed on an 81-year-old sprinter he named as Kenton Brown, who ran 100 metres in 14.4 seconds [00:25]; the slide shows the sprinter in a USA vest without a name (slide 16).
- The talk was one unbroken Otter turn, so every spoken passage sits in the [00:25] block.

summary.Summary:
Viktor Tsevsky and Matthew Kwembowski, co-founders of 2waves, pitched a platform for the three sides of the supplement market: brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers.

They started from a growing market, which Grand View Research puts at more than 60 billion dollars by 2030, and from how badly its sides find each other. Brands have no view of their category, offers come in no common format, inquiries are incomplete or do not fit, one inquiry runs across many email threads, and many get no answer at all. That costs time and lost business.

Their answer is a first module for new partnerships, quoting and negotiation. One inquiry reaches every manufacturer or supplier in the category. Offers come back in one structure to compare, the negotiation history stays in one place, inquiries are matched to who can make them, and every decline carries a reason. Matthew had begun on data security, with every company verified before joining, when the recording ended.

The conference organiser, Pawel Gruszczynski, sits on the project's board as strategic advisor.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The market is framed as three sides, brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers, with Grand View Research's forecast of over 12 percent growth a year to more than 60 billion dollars by 2030 [00:13].
- The cost of today's process is operational (hours organising inquiries, hunting agreements in email threads) and lost opportunity (offers never received, inquiries never answered) [01:50].
- One inquiry reaches all manufacturers (or suppliers) in the category; offers come back in one structure, "two offers or 15", ready to compare [02:46].
- For suppliers and manufacturers: inquiries are matched to what you can produce, so you see opportunities that today never find you [02:46].
- Every company is verified before joining; the security module answers losing control of information once it sits in an inbox [07:42].
- Pawel Gruszczynski (Remedy, the conference organiser) is strategic advisor and board member of the project [02:46].

summary.Summary:
The day's closing panel brought together a retailer (Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett), a CDMO (Martina), an ingredient developer (Matt), a food lawyer (Joanna) and a pharmaceutical company (Alexandra). The moderator asked what each wants in the next two or three years, then turned to regulation, supply and AI.

They agreed that the consumer comes first. Alexandra wanted evidence-based claims and better communication, Martina a focus on what consumers actually need, and Alex a few claims done well, starting from the consumer's problem rather than piling on ingredients. Matt wanted a revolution in clinical trials: high-dose studies in people with real problems, published where consumers' chatbots will find them.

On regulation they differed in tone. Joanna wants food law to be a shield for innovators, though the claims system was written for vitamins. Matt was blunter: a three-year longer approval in Europe than in the US almost makes innovation impossible.

On supply, Matt warned of a fish oil shortage reaching shelves next summer. Alex described pre-bought stock and protecting the claim shoppers buy. Joanna said blaming the supplier is no defence.

On AI they wanted a human in the loop and peer-reviewed sources, and Matt warned that anyone who cannot use AI will not be able to work in two years.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Matt: trials in this industry study healthy people for short periods, so effects look small; he would run high-dose studies in people with real problems and publish, because consumers will find it through chatbots [02:52].
- Alex: consumers want evidence but not the EFSA wording; "throwing the kitchen sink" (90 plus ingredients, 35 claims) muddles the message; do a few things well for a defined audience [08:33].
- Joanna: EU food law and the claims regulation were written for vitamin C and D; innovators must combine what is legally possible with showing what trials found; food law should be "a shield", not "a heartbreak" [05:36].
- Matt: same safety package, three years longer approval in Europe than the US; cost today, income later, so the delay "almost makes the innovation impossible" [14:53].
- Matt: fish oil supply is collapsing for aquaculture now and reaches supplement shelves next summer; aquaculture buys the alternatives with higher willingness to pay [18:48].
- Alex: H&B holds up to nine months of pre-purchased stock on core lines; shoppers give three or four seconds at shelf, so protect the claim they buy (heart, eye) and find the alternative [19:36].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Two of five panellists take creatine daily, including H&B's formulation lead [00:30], [00:57]. My reading: creatine is now a default daily supplement for industry insiders, which supports CreaWin's move into everyday and healthy-ageing products beyond sports.
- A retailer and a CDMO both say the brief is the consumer problem and a few claims done well [08:33], [11:13]. My reading: our customer-facing materials should give one outcome per ingredient with the trial that shows it, not a list.
- The fish oil shortage [18:48] is not ours, but H&B's response, protect the benefit and find the alternative, shows how a retailer treats any supply shock. My reading: supply continuity and traceability for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea are selling points to put in front of buyers now.
- Europe's three-year approval lag [14:53] means novel protein and creatine formats will launch in the US first (my reading).
- Chatbots rank peer-reviewed science [03:45]. My reading: publishing the CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea evidence where AI assistants can find it is now part of marketing.
- Relevance medium: regulation, supply and retail views, adjacent to our ingredients.

summary.Summary:
Marit Weinstra of HMT, the Healthy Marketing Team, a food and health branding and innovation agency, opened the probiotic programme. Her question was how to win in a biotics market that has grown into a jungle of products. Use keeps rising, yet in seven of eight European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics.

She traced four eras. Yakult made good bacteria a daily ritual. Activia made the benefit tangible, and brands began competing on CFU counts. Then survival technology became the story. Now the shift is from adding bacteria to nourishing the gut ecosystem, with the gut barrier as the gateway to the rest of the body.

From that she drew four rules: quality and proof over "more is better", feeding the ecosystem, benefits consumers can measure and feel, and everyday food formats. Her examples were mostly American: Pendulum's Akkermansia products for metabolic health, a prebiotic fibre brand, a digestive brand that sets expectations week by week, and Poppi.

Her conclusion: in Europe most of these claims cannot be made, so the brand has to carry them. Value is moving from what is inside the product to what the consumer gets. A strong probiotic needs a "Double IP": the science and the brand.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Biotics have never been more popular: probiotic use among US adults rose 287% from 2009 to 2023, and European online probiotic sales have grown 15-25% a year since 2020 (slide 2). Yet in 7 of 8 European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics (slide 6); she said this without figures [00:24].
- Rule 1, from "more is better" to quality and proof: a number on its own no longer builds trust, so be an expert brand in a niche (slide 14). Shelves show 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU [03:59]; her niche example is Pendulum, an Akkermansia-based US brand for metabolic health (slide 14) [03:59].
- Rule 2, from adding bacteria to feeding the ecosystem: "eat more plants" instead of strain names, plants and fibre consumers can see, and a gut they feed themselves (slide 15); fibre brands lead this language [03:59].
- Rule 3, from belief to measurable and felt benefits: early adopters measure with microbiome tests, apps and personal scores; the mass market wants less bloating, regularity and energy, and buys again only if it notices a difference (slide 16). Her example sets expectations at week 1 and months 1, 2 and 3 (slide 17); she said "for one week, for one month" [03:59].
- Rule 4, from supplement to everyday food and formats: products designed for the person, not the bacteria; "the best biotic is the one people actually take every day" (slide 18). Poppi is her example [03:59].
- In Europe you cannot claim most of it, so the brand carries it: BioGaia's baby drops say "for colic & digestive discomfort" in the US but "one of the world's most researched lactic acid bacteria strains" in Europe (slide 20), and Activia names its strain, Bifidus ActiRegularis (slide 21) [03:59].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance stays medium: nothing in the talk or slides covers protein, creatine or sports nutrition, but the branding argument transfers to our customers' categories.
- The question has changed from "what's in it?" to "what does it do in me?" (slide 11). My reading: the same shift faces sports and active nutrition brands, and it favours ingredients whose effect a user notices; that is how a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea pitch should be framed.
- Activia's branded strain on its ingredient list and BioGaia's research claim show how a European brand carries what it cannot claim (slides 20-21). My reading: an argument for branded ingredients, and for getting the CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea names onto customers' packs with a story told within claim rules.
- HMT lists B2B2C communication among its services, with Suntheanine as the case (slide 24). My reading: HMT is an agency, not a buyer; it could brand our ingredients to end consumers or support a customer's launch.
summary.Quotes:
- "...there are too many options out there, but there's not enough clarity in this industry." Speaker 2 (Marit Weinstra) [00:24]
- "...numbers alone don't build trust anymore with the consumer" Speaker 2 (Marit Weinstra) [03:59]
- "So in Europe, you can't claim most of it, and that's when the brand has to carry it." Speaker 2 (Marit Weinstra) [03:59]
- "...science opens the doors, but it's a brand that keeps you in the room." Speaker 2 (Marit Weinstra) [03:59]

Slides carry "© 2026 – Healthy Marketing Team" (a few © 2023 or © 2025); none is marked confidential. The last slide offers the slides by QR code and gives marit@thehmt.com (slide 25).

- Era 4: from adding to nourishing, with a new language: ecosystem, barrier, balance, holistic, outcome led, fermentation, whole food approach; Nordic Rebalance's OatBiotics Gut Barrier (ReFerm) is pictured (slide 11). Moving the focus to the gut barrier, where the gut meets the rest of the body, "exploded the category" (slide 12) [03:59].
- The four rules slide reads from "More = Better", "Adding bacteria", "Belief & promise" and "Functional supplement" to "Quality & proven ingredient", "Feeding the eco-system", "Measurable & Felt Benefits" and "Everyday food" (slide 13).

Era 4: from adding to nourishing, with a new language: ecosystem, barrier, balance, holistic, outcome led, fermentation, whole food approach; Nordic Rebalance's OatBiotics Gut Barrier (ReFerm) is pictured (slide 11). Moving the focus to the gut barrier, where the gut meets the rest of the body, "exploded the category" (slide 12) [03:59].

The four rules slide reads from "More = Better", "Adding bacteria", "Belief & promise" and "Functional supplement" to "Quality & proven ingredient", "Feeding the eco-system", "Measurable & Felt Benefits" and "Everyday food" (slide 13).
Rule 2's pictured example is LOAM Prebiotic Fiber Formula (slide 15); she added that the language has moved from one prebiotic fibre to plant diversity [03:59].

Rule 3's example is the be levels digestive product, whose own claims shown on the slide are 90% less bloating and gas, 92% an overall improvement in digestion and 89% more regular bowel movements; its timeline runs from lighter digestion in week 1 to balanced digestion by month 3 (slide 17). items.title: Novonesis and Montefarmaco: the Lactoflorene partnership, from science to consumer product

speakers.name: Ariel Annoni
speakers.role: Responsible for the Human Health business across Central and Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa (as she said it)
